The thick piece of watercolor paper where the blue snake lived had begun to serve as a to-do list for his writing project. By the way, Ken Wilbur had finally weighed in, the upper left quadrant represented the interior of the individual, which made sense to the dying author in light of his relationship to the Snake. The individual interior containing all emotions, symbols, and concepts. Praise be to the blue snake with the flipped up nose. Praise be to the great Father of som many of us, Ken Wilbur!



The dying author ventured out for a walk with the sunrise. He crunched through the golden, frozen grass in his brown, leather, slip-on loafers. He walked on the smooth dirt path through the arching evergreens, where the hard, blue seeds were scattered. He kicked off his loafers. He reached up with outstretched arms, grasping a sturdy tree branch in either hand.

 

The middle-aged-man stood there in the crucifixion position, supported by the trees, acknowledging how Christ had been supported by a tree as he experienced his final ego-dissolution process “It would take the strength of the tree Goddess to support something like that,” said the man to himself. 



The Christ man with the feminine nature in him, supported by the strong form of the tree. The dying author was not trying to create any kind of doctrine in this moment, merely experiencing the meaning of it all as it appeared to him (Praise be to fluidity and the passing stories that come and go with the evolution of consciousness!). He released the evergreens from his grasp, slipped his shoes back on, and continued down the path where he came to a fork, a binary, a crossroads. 



And so, he stopped.



He stood right there in that place where he could either go left or right. He waited. This fork was the physical manifestation of what he’d been writing about. It had unexpectedly come to greet him on his morning walk with the sunrise (Praise be to the binary fork that offers us the non-path). He waited. Acknowledging. Accepting. Experiencing the moment for exactly what it had to offer. He sensed into his body and all that was. He allowed his thoughts to pass before him, nodding to his vipassana practice. Just as the writer now did now in the typing of the words (Praise be to the words which point to the slivered moon!).



At this crossroads, as he gave space for the creative miracle to arise from within, he sensed again a powerful presence of the feminine within him. He allowed his legs to become a slightly twisted trunk. His hands to became slender branches, reaching up into the sky, caressing the blueness and the morning cold.



He then embodied the spirit of one who was once called “witch.” those pagan women who went to the forest to walk barefoot and experience nature without any barrier, walking in the brown grass and the green alike. He felt her. He felt her making love to this moment. He took off his shoes and held them in one hand as he began walking barefoot, slowly, through the thick, golden, winter grass. His legs crossed over midline as he slowly placed one in front of the other, which resulted in him being more fully aware of his hips and the diminished space between his legs. 



“Whether I look like a woman from the outside or not, right now. I certainly feel like one,” thought the middle aged man. The man tried to let the mental image of “woman” go. He allowed the energy of that mental image of “woman” to pass through. 



Now he was empowered to simply feel his body, just the physical senses. He walked with this fairy of the forest until his feet got very cold. He quickly slid his shoes on and continued his walk with the sunrise. As he faced East, the sky was deep orange. He made his way through the South gate toward the front of the house. 



The moon was just a sliver in the sky. He greeted the moon “Thank you for your presence, dear moon,” said the Goddess. She greeted the sun into the world. She thanked the glowing orb for the warmth it had provided the day before as she enjoyed the backyard in such a touching and personal healing ceremony with the medicine. “Peace be to you, Sun. Thank you for your presence. Thank you for your warmth. Thank you for your light. I give praise to you, and to the Mother and Father, and to all the faces of God who have gifted me with this sunrise. Praise be to the LSD and please God, bless the hands that prepared it.” And so it was that the Goddess gave thanks for the medicine and and for the new day into which She had bee born.



Passing through the threshold of the backdoor which had been open for hours yesterday, he felt the feminine with him still. She was Mother. 



“Can I make you some oatmeal?” she said to a small boy who had just arrived, a boy who welcomed his Mother’s presence. He longed to be cared for.



“Yes, please,” said the boy. 

“You like it with apples and cinnamon don’t you?” she said.



“Yes, I do. Thank you.” he replied.



And so it came to pass that the Mother made oatmeal for the boy. Praise be to the Great Mother Spirit. Praise be to the Goddess of the trees! Praise be to the witches of the fields and forest, those fairy nymphys that were crucified in the name of the Christ! Praise be to their dear souls who died in the presence of their Great Mother.



Arise! Arise! Allow yourself to be mothered

Let the feminine come forth to mother the world.



It was in this way that the man began to do many practical things around the house, self-care activities with the help and guidance of his mother, this lovely feminine spirit that he’d invited into his being jus the day before, as he quivered with ecstasy in the back yard. Those other strong men were working just through the evergreens. The Goddess made peace with her son that day, and she came to inhabit his being and guide him in the ways of the great Earth! Praise be to all the medicines! Praise be the wisdom that the medicine helps us to access from within!



The middle-aged man allowed this spirit to help him with the laundry. He paid an overdue bill that he’d discovered when checking his email spam box (which was a lengthy task he did not believe he could have done without his mother). He straightened and cleaned the kitchen. He listened to the highwomen, a country music quartet who had rewritten that song , the highway men, made famous by Waylon Jennings, and Kris Kristoferson, and Willie, and Johnny.



He read an excerpt from Eileen’s book, Tear drops of rain. The spirit of Life in her book helped him to see that it was perfectly reasonable for the rational mind to seek a relationship with the beautiful heart. He allowed his rational mind to observe the beautiful, beautiful heart that had made itself manifest in his/her being. Praise be to the age of reason! Praise be to the enlightenment! Praise be to the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Praise be to the snake who circles back and circles back again. Praise be to the man with a lovely feminine heart!



And so it was that the dying author saw another miracle come to pass for himself and all who share in this moment with him. Amen



Now the dying author sat with a task in front of him. How would he speak of the conversation with his brother?



No. Not yet. It is not time. It is not safe enough yet. There is a tenderness now. Can we please stay with the tenderness?



The dying author wondered what it meant to have God as a lover. Hafiz and Rumi, they had apparently had this experience. And the dying author had wondered for quite some time, what this really meant. There had been times when he felt that he knew, but most of his life had not been spent in the presence of God as lover.



Like a Life Giving Sun



You could become a great horseman

And help to free yourself and this world



Though only if you and prayer become sweet

Lovers



It is a naive man who thinks we are not

Engaged in a fierce battle



For I see and hear brave foot soldiers

All around me going mad



Falling on the ground in excruciating pain

You could become a victorious horseman



And carry your heart through this world

Like a life-giving sun



Though only if you and God become sweet

Lovers

Hafiz



And so it came to pass that the dying author, once again, invited God to make love to him. And so it came to pass that the man fell to his knees and asked God to come inside of him. And on this day the man did feel that love in his genitals. “He’s using that word again, mom. I know sweetie. It’s okay. We’re not taking any of this too seriously, are we? 



And so it came to pass that He went to see a movie with his lover afterwards. The movie version of the broadway musical, Cats, which the man thought was a delightfully gay thing to do. He and his lover had the theater to himself. The man stretched out on the seats, fell asleep, and left half way through, very much like a straight man might have done. BOTH/AND. He did not know how God felt about the movie. He hoped that he had not left his Lover behind at the movies. 



After leaving the movie theater in the neighboring town, the man went to the grocery store where he struggled to plan a lunch that he’d invited his four children to attend on Christmas Eve day. Christmas eve was on a Tuesday, so he decided to serve tacos. “Taco Tuesday!” the Goddess announced to anyone who could hear in the grocery store. And so it came to pass that the man’s refrigerator was filled in preparation for the company of his children. Praise be to the Mother! Praise be to the Lover! Praise be to the Lion who was seen in the Moth! Praise be to the snake which circles back on itself!



Concerning the conversation with his brother:



Text to brother:



Hey Kyle. It was such a joy last night to talk to you. I was incredibly excited to hear about what's going on in your life.

 

I have a request. You can do with it what you like, of course. 

 

I don't like it when you give me advice. Please feel free to share with me your experience, your strength, and your hope. I will joyfully take all of that into my heart and let it do what it will. But, when you give me advice, and try to convince me to say and do things that I obviously have an aversion to, that really turns me off.

 

The two instances from last night that I am referring to now are the microdosing of mushrooms issue, and the oath issue. it is very bothersome for me when someone, anyone, assumes they know what is right for me.

 

If you want to have a relationship with me, it is important that I can be honest with you. These are my boundaries, the parameters under which I am willing to work on a relationship with you.

 

I love you. I accept you. I am happy for your deeper Awakening do the nature of reality. I hope we can find a way to bring our beings into deeper communion with one another.



The brothers had a strained relationship for their entire adult life. It was hard to talk about. The middle-aged man felt something like fear when he was relating to his brother. He felt like he had to fight to be heard. He did not feel listened to. He did not feel valued. He felt talked down to. The middle-aged man did not like having to listen and listen and listen when he never felt heard. He had spent much of the day acknowledging these parts of his being that felt threatened by his brother.



“Nothing that is real can be threatened

Nothing exists that is not real”

ACIM page 1



And so it came to pass that the middle-aged man held tenderness in one hand, and fears in the other. The miracle was still occurring. It had been nearly ten hours since he’d sent the text to his brother. There was no reply. The middle aged man had second-guessed his intuition in the sending of the text. “Am I trying to protect some part of me that is unreal? Or, am I setting up healthy boundaries in order to have a relationship with my brother?”



His brother wanted him to take an oath of undying loyalty to their brotherhood. The middle-aged man did not feel comfortable with that. The middle-aged man had already broken all the promises that he’d ever made. He was not interested in making any more promises. Taking an oath felt contrary to a life lived from moment to moment. To the middle-aged man, taking an oath seemed contrary to the fluidity that he was committing his life to. For years now, his younger brother had asked him to take this blood oath. He did not feel any closer to taking that oath today. However, he did feel the desire to point out to his brother that there must be something in the blood, because he certainly wouldn’t be having any conversation with him at all if it were not for their deep history and ties to family. He did not say that to his brother. He thought it would be unnecessarily hurtful, the equivalent of saying, “Hey Kyle, if you were anyone else, I wouldn’t even be talking to you now. In fact, the ONLY reason I am talking to you is because you are my brother.” And so it came to pass that the dying author stepped away from his chromebook with the intention of saying yet another prayer for his suffering brother today, surely a noble and worthy intention. Amen



Open arms, my brother. Open arms.



It occurred to the writer in this moment that he seemed to be more and more present in this story. The disappearance of this author would surely be a miracle indeed. This author acknowledged that he did not understand how to accomplish this disappearing act. He knew that the disappearance miracle was no act at all, that it had nothing to do with performance. He knew that the death of the author had to be real, genuine, authentic in nature. The author invited the miracle of disappearance once again. “Please, Father, for the sake of her. For the sake of those who are witnessing, allow the miracle to come to pass. For the sake of the brother. Please allow this author to die. May I offer my death as a sacrifice? Is that a legitimate path? It is out of my hands. It is more than I can do. No matter how hard I try, I cannot bring about my own death. I can only trust. These are things that I do not understand. Please, for the sake of the reader, bring about this miracle. Amen.”



The dying author, having moved into the kitchen, had resumed his North-facing position several pages ago. He now retired to the stack of three pillows provided for him in front of the sink. As he breathed in the half-lotus, making the intellectual’s nod to the practice of vipassana, an idea occurred to him. “What if, since I am already here, since I am already becoming more and more present in the story, what if I just show up with as much presence as is possible, with as much honesty and authenticity as possible. What if I come out from behind the mask of the paranthetical? What if I drop the narrator’s voice. What would happen then?” He stood at that threshold, realizing that it would change everything that he’d been working on. It was a risk. “What is the risk?” he wondered. “What is at risk here?”



He returned to the pillows.



The writer returned his attention to the sickness that he’d experienced at the cabin in the Lincoln National Forest that night after he had bundled in layers and visited with the shining moon. He returned to the cabin, this time in first person, an intentional risk, an experiment.



There I sat, in the comfortable chair in the cabin in the Lincoln National Forest. I was wearing my olive drab jacket, the one I’d purchased at Wal-Mart for my poorly planned hitchhiking adventure. I was wearing my yellow elk skin work gloves. (Praise be to the mother of all Elk. May her living sons grow large antlers. May there be plentiful food in the winter.)



The illness had come over me. I walked in the moonlight, acknowledging all that I had seen, felt, and experienced, recalling all the sacred ceremony in which I participated. I witnessed the death and resurrection of the Christ Moth. I communed with the trinity in the light fixture. I sank into the soil, in communion with the great wisdom of the ones who turned the rocks into arable earth. Yet there I sat, my hands beginning to shake with frustration, my neck and face tensing. The great self-loathing was coming over me, the self-loathing I had known for my entire life but had only become aware of in the last eight years of my life.



All the loss of the last two years was upon me. The great question came. “How can I live with myself?” The tone in this question tonight was not one of curiosity and wonder. The tone in the question that night was…



Present tense? More presence? More presence, my Lord?







Here I sit. In this cabin. In this comfortable chair. I am wearing my olive drab jacket which is beginning to feel like home. I am in a cabin in the Lincoln National Forest. The shades are drawn. I am wearing my yellow, Elk skin gloves, the same ones I will take off in several days to text my ex wife. She will tell me that I am too manic and that she is not sure if she wants to be my friend. 



There is an illness about me right now. I feel sick in my spirit, a spiritual malady. I do not know how I will live with myself. How can I live with myself? I bought those damn pastries today at a fancy bakery in Cloudcroft. There they are, right over there, sitting on that table over there in the kitchen. Two pastries. Six dollars each. Twelve dollars worth of pastries I can never eat because I am sick with myself. I am disgusted with myself. One is a lemon cheesecake pastry. The other is a cinnamon roll. I am disgusted with myself for buying those goddamn pastries. How the fuck could I have possibly bought those pastries pastries today? Christmas is coming! I am running out of money! My kids cars are going to get repossessed!



Oh fuck! I also have a new mandolin. It cost fourteen-hundred dollars. I bought it before I knew that I would be resigning my job. But there it is, a symbol of my selfishness! Although I bought it in a desperate moment, I told myself that it was a gift from the Universe. I was desperately trying to give myself what I thought I needed to survive. My coworkers encouraged me to get it, but that doesn’t matter to me right now. I’ve got this expensive mandolin and my kids cars are going to get repossessed!



I have no job. I have no way to pay my child support. I have no intention of finding a job right now. How can I possibly live with myself. This is too much for me. I cannot carry this. My children are going to have their fucking cars repossessed. The mother of my chilren—She is going to hire a lawyer and have my bank account garnished (not that there will be anything in there). I am weak. I am sick. Son of a fucking bitch!



God, please help me. I cannot do this. This is too much for me to carry. My worst nightmares have come true. I have left my wife. I have left my children. I am living a selfish life. Look at me. These six dollar pastries over there on the table. That mandolin over there by the fireplace. Is it true that my awakening is measured by how comfortable I am with my own hypocrisy? If so, I am not very awake right now, because I am very uncomfortable.



I know what this place is. I have been here many, many times. I want to call myself names. I need to call myself bad names. It will make me feel better if I call myself names. My right hand makes a tight fist in the yellow elk skin glove. I can see my fist. It is shaking now as my eyes cnnot cry. Now my fist speeds toward my forehead. My fist is moving so fast but time has now slowed to a crawl. This moment has drawn out into some eternity. The fist stops just as the leather of the elk skin glove touches my forehead. I am on the verge of self abuse. No. I have crossed that line. I am angry. I am lonely. I am disappointed. I am in my illness.



Father! I cannot live with myself. This is too much to bear.



I remember my earthly father. I do not remember all the pain he caused me. He is the one who gave me many vehicles. This was how he proved to me his love. This was the love that he knew to give. I must be grateful. How many vehicles did he give? I cannot count them right now. If I did count, there were so many, that I would probably leave one out. 



This is the father that I hated. This is the same father that I judged for so many years. The father that I so often do not speak to. The father that angers me. He is the one who supported my family by giving us vehicles. He gave these great gifts of transportation, which enabled us to keep getting where we need to go. There was the Toyota Tercel. There was the burgundy Nissan pickup. There was the blue Ford minivan. There was the Nissan 240 SX. And here I am. I cannot pay child support. I am on medical leave again, unwilling or unable to work at my job.



My two youngest children will have their cars repossessed and the father that I have hated or loved-from-afar gave me all these vehicles. I am sick with myself. I am disgusted. How can I live with myself?



Father. I cannot bear this. I cannot live with this. How will I live with myself?



Now I am crying now. Oh, thank you God, this is good. Tears are good. This is a relief. An emotional release. I am breaking open. I can feel it. My sickness has broken me open. I am reaching out for help with my heart. “Father, please hold me. I need to be held.” Now I am sobbing. My chest is heaving. My body is convulsing. I do not know how long this goes on. It goes on for a very long time. “Father. I need to be held. Father! Why won’t you hold me. I cannot bear this. This is more than I can bear.” 



Over by the fireplace. I see something. A carved bear. A hand-carved bear. He has strange eyes. Twinkling eyes. Alive eyes. He looks like a young strong bear. He is only a bear from his chest up. The rest of him is still trapped in the log. He is a bear. He is a tree. I am still crying. But I make eye contact with the bear. He is alive. His intentions are helpful. I go sit by the bear. I look into his eyes. “You are a strong bear,” I say. “A very strong bear.” It feels good to tell this bear how strong he is.



Now I am overwhelmed by feelings of sadness and disappointment and disgust again. I cannot bear this. I need to be held. “Father! Please hold me. I need to be held! Please, Father. Please, hold me! I pick up the bear. I hold the bear in my arms. I hug the bear. I squeeze the log. The log feels good and solid in my hands. “You are a strong bear!” I scream, tears flowing from my eyes, chest heaving with sobs. “You are a strong, strong, bear. I love you. You are a strong, strong, bear.” with this proclamation toward the bear I feel something different in my own being.



Time and time again I hold the bear. I hug the bear. I cry. I scream. I moan. I grieve as if I have lost a loved one. I put the bear down. I pick the bear up. I squeeze the hard wood. “You are a strong, strong, strong, strong bear!” When I tell the bear how strong he is, I can feel these words coming straight back into my chest. I can feel the love and admiration that I have for this strong bear in my own being. As I hold the bear, I am holding myself. As I praise the bear for his strength, I am giving myself the praise that I need to bear this. I can feel myself being held from the inside. I am now able to sense the Father holding me. This goes on for I do not know how long. Something is changing inside me. I am being held by my heavenly Father. 



Also, I notice that something has changed in my heart for my earthly father. Something has changed in my heart toward myself as a father. I can feel the fathers, as if there are three of them. I am full of the father. I and the father are one. I am present with the Father. The Father is present in me. I am the Father. Praise be to God. Praise be to the bear log.



I am here. I have showed up. I am in love. 



I can bear this now. I can live with myself. I have made peace with my own hypocrisy. I have made peace with my own humanity. I have made peace. I am okay with myself. I am giving myself the love that I need. It is coming from this deep well within. I can see now that I can bear this, as long as I can experience this presence--the presence of my father, this deeper forgiveness. This deeper communion with Spirit. “I am a strong bear,” I begin to smile. “I am a strong bear. You are strong bear,” I say to the bear as I sit cross legged on the floor by the strong, strong, strong, strong, strong, strong bear. I am filled with joy and love. “I am a strong bear.” I can feel how strong I am. I can see how strong I have been to have come this far in life. I see that I have truly done the best that I can. I have given everything to be here right now, in this cabin, in the Lincoln National Forest, with all the shades drawn.



I am not desperate. I am not sick anymore. I do not want to hurt myself. I want to live this resurrected life more than anything. I want to commit myself to this life. I want to make an oath to this life in me, an oath that is renewed every time I say yes. I want to live the rest of my life a strong bear. “I am a strong, strong, strong, strong, strong, strong bear.” Every time I say the word “strong” I am renewed. I am empowered. I am one with the Father. I have made peace with my own fatherhood. I have made peace with myself as a flawed human being. I have made peace with my own hypocrisy. I have made peace with the mandolin. I have made peace with the pastries.



I sit for a very long time in this new, deeper presence. I feel that I have deepened. I am a deeper being. I eventually grab my guitar, paying it respect and giving it thanks before I pick it up. I walk over to the kitchen table and I take my Father’s seat. I play the two songs that have been giving me life over the last weeks, I give myself away, and Eye of the hurricane.



I sing these songs with no measured time. I release time and I allow them to come out with deep space. There is unprecedented presence in my voice, in my song. Deep unprecedented calmness, and quietness and joy

The dying author reads an excerpt from Bruce Sanguins’ book, Dismantled.



He prays to be empowered to live a life of devotion



He finds his knees on the mexican tiles in the living room of the adobe house in the college-cowtown



He recalls the end of the story. He returns to first person back at the cabin.



Begin draft:

 

The next morning, I woke up with the sun.



I went for a walk. I wore my olive drab jacket that was starting to feel a lot like home. I wore my yellow elk skin gloves. I wore a stocking cap and long underwear. I had my chapstick. I was warm in my layers.



I made my way down the descending gravel roads, making sure to take note of the turns I made so as not to get lost. I began to sing kumbaya. 



Someone’s singing my lord kumbaya

Someone’s dying, my lord. Kumbaya.

Someones crying, my Lord. Kumbaya

Someones breathing, my Lord. Kumbaya



Oh lord, Kumb….



At that moment I heard a dog barking. I turned to face him. He was running at me, a large, brown-and-tan camouflage dog. 



I squared off with him, very calmly, very peacefully. I raised my hand in the air, projecting my voice with intent, for my best interest and his. “No! Get Back.”



The dog reacted as if he’d encountered an invisible barrier, he turned to the side with timidity.



I turned slowly to walk away, making sure that the dog had no more intent to advance.



“Oh Lord, Kumbaya.”

“Someone’s loving, My Lord. Kumbaya.”

“Someone’s growing, My Lord. Kumbaya.”

“Someone’s being, My Lord. Kumbaya.”



Oh Lord, Kumbaya.



I am grateful to be back in the warm cabin. I open up the shades to let in the morning sunlight. The pastries are over there on the table. What’s that? They do not provoke the same sickness in me as they did just last night. I approach the kitchen table. I stand over the pastries. I open up the white styrofoam to-go box. The cinnamon roll looks very tasty. “Hmmm…” I say to myself. “I believe that my father would really like that cinnamon roll.” I smell the cinnamon roll. “Yes,” I say, “My father would enjoy this cinnamon roll very much.” I retrieve a knife from the utensil drawer. I cut a third of the cinnamon roll; it is a big piece of sweet bread, enough to last the rest of the weekend. I place it on a plate and I nuke it for 12 seconds. I return to my Father’s seat, the same place where I played the guitar and sang with an unprecedented voice last night.



I sit down. The warm cinnamon roll is before me on the white ceramic plate. I retrieve a fork from the utensil drawer. I cut into the cinnamon roll and place a bite in my mouth. I give thanks for this food. I am filled with gratefulness. The miracle has come to pass. The cinnamon roll that I thought that I could never eat because of my shame, is now bringing me great joy. 



As I taste the cinnamon roll, I know in my heart that my father would truly love it. I know my Dad well enough to know that this is exactly the kind of cinnamon roll that he would love. I am proud that I know this. I can feel him with me, my earthly father, the one who gave me all the vehicles. I may not be able to give my children vehicles. I can live with that. Today I can live with that. I have done my part. I will continue to do my part. I have given my children many, many gifts. I feel at peace with my dad. He lives in me as my Heavenly Father is living in me. I am also aware, once again, of my own fatherhood. I have made peace with the fact that my children may have their cars repossessed. Today there cars are not being repossessed. I cannot do anything about tomorrow right now. All I can do is follow. I can devote myself to the following of this Great Father Spirit. I can devote myself to the loving of God. I can devote myself to this process. I can devote myself to this ever-changing, ever-evolving process. Praise be to the pastry maker and the love that flows from her hands! Praise be to the camouflage dog who barks and runs in my direction! Praise be to the bear in the log! Praise be to the strong, strong bear! For he is truly a very, very, very strong bear. And I love him. What a strong, noble, compassionate bear, he is. Praise be to the bear’s mother!









Inside Stone

 translated by Chogyam Trin Pan 



In the thick air of a cool basement, two boys faced one another. They unzipped, engaging each other in a playful sword fight of sorts. The sun’s rays angled in through a half hazed window. 

“We need to get some girls down here,” says the taller of the two. 

A disturbance causes the smaller boy to turn quickly and face the slowly arcing dust motes traveling through the white light. The sound of the opening door from the top of the stairs jump-starts the two boy’s already elevated heart rates. Stairs creaking under feet, the small boy’s grandma chides sharply, “I know what you two are doing down there, and if you don’t stop right now I’m going to tell your fathers!”

The old woman stops half way down the closed stairwell. She stares at the boys who have just barely escaped being caught with their pants down. Trying to look innocent, not knowing now what to do with his hands, the small boy averts his eyes from his grandmother’s silhouette, now analyzing the cobwebs in the corner. The oldest boy stands awkwardly wide-eyed, breathing heavily through his open mouth, staring at the woman’s feet. 

Only now, under her gaze, does the little boy grasp the gravity of his innocent play. He only knows that he does not want his dad to know. The tight faced woman with the tautly wound beauty-shop curls forces the long silence into eternity as her eyes move from one boy to the other—the boys, defenseless against those pursed-lips.



Later, the younger boy found himself. In his grandfather’s quarter acre lot, he weaved his way through stacks of railroad ties, fence sections, camper tops, and rusting livestock trailers. His curiosity renewed—the sunshine and smell of sheep shit freeing him from the pressing weight of the concrete cellar and his grandmother’s threats. He made his way to the red fence at the back of the lot—the calling of birds and the singing cicadas now the only voices in his head. He unlatched the chain on the large swinging gate, climbed the rocky embankment to the tracks, and followed the rails to the wooden Santa Fe bridge.

He chose three grey rocks from the rail bed, as many as his seven year old hands could carry, and ventured out on to the wooden planks. The creek below came in to view through the gaps under his feet. He reassured himself that the space between the ties was narrow enough that he could catch himself if he were to lose his footing. As he approached the bridges’ center, directly over the rainbowed surface of an oily stagnating pool of water, he straddled one of the gaps and dropped a stone. In simple silence it fell for what may have been a second or perhaps much longer, a trick of time the boy held too tightly. He wished his hands were big enough to carry a thousand stones.

The rock broke the filmy surface of the pool…



He was sorry he had killed the baby bird. It hadn’t gone as expected. He had killed adult birds with his BB gun before, their glistening black and purple feathers ruffling as their neck and legs collapsed under the weight of their own body. That made him feel strong and respected, like a hunter. But the bare baby bird was different. He knew, from watching TV, that it was his duty to put that little creature out of its misery. It was suffering. In fact, he relished the responsibility. The idea of it made him feel so grown up and wise, so responsible. “It is the right thing to do,” he said, relishing the serious and morbid nature of his task. That tiny naked creature, fallen from her nest, screeched and squirmed under the pressure of the curved x-acto blade on its neck. Half way through the surprisingly sinewy flesh, perplexed and horrified, the boy felt the warm red blood on his hands, but the baby would not die. The boy panicked. He stood facing the bird on the altar for a moment, dirt and leaves on his knees. Without the heart to complete the ceremony, he ran, leaving the pitiful writhing life form still squirming on the brick altar. He pushed open the screen door on the back porch, ran inside the two story brick house, and clamored quickly up the stairs to his mother’s room. She was folding laundry. He cried in her arms. The boy was loved for his sensitivity.



From his perch on the bridge, the boy dropped the second rock. Another moment of silence. He could hear his breath hovering over the chasm between himself and the water below. It was that space that held his attention, that quiet moment between release and splash down…

He had once imagined a stone so smooth that it couldn’t be held. Actually, he hadn’t as much imagined the smooth stone, as much as it had appeared in his being. The perfect creamy surface of this stone always contracted into a shadowy, craggling, painful object. Too terrible to touch. Sometimes, if he kept his eyes closed, he could witness this transformation over and over again; the hypnotizing change was out of his control. The little boy could not understand the aliveness of the stone in his vision, or why he was unable to control its transformation.

 He released the third rock. It strayed from its intended course and glanced off the sticky, tarred surface of the tie. The boy lost sight of it and carelessly repositioned his feet so that, with his eyes, he could follow the descent of the falling stone. Losing his footing with the wind, he connected himself to the silence again for a brief moment. He could hear the stone dancing on the rocks below as he regained his balance. His heart came into his his chest with loud thumps that he could feel in his ears. 



That night the boy lay in bed knowing that he could not go to school the next day. This knowing was manifested in a physical sensation that he would one day call dread; it was uncontrollable, like the smooth stone’s transformation into something untouchable. 

If he could make himself vomit his parents would have to let him stay home. He walked to the bathroom and shoved a finger down his throat but was unable to produce any substance from his stomach. He gagged as loud as he could and then plopped down heavily onto the cold white tile by the toilet, hoping his parents would hear his distress, angered by his general state of physical well-being. Wishing for disease, he recalled the stone’s hushed descent. It comforted him for one moment before the image of his grandmother returned like a chronic illness. Several more failed attempts at throwing-up produced pitiful gurgling sounds, causing his father to yell from upstairs, “You ARE going to school tomorrow!” The boy gave up on the process, hoisted himself from the floor, slumped his shoulders and plodded back to his bed.

He lay on his back, pulled the covers up to his chin, and focused his attention on the cracks in the ceiling. He sensed the rise and fall of his chest. Again he thought about the pocked stones, the tracks, the bridge, the dirty rainbow covering the foul waters. He perceived the weightlessness of the rock in the moment before it broke the surface. He stopped the descent in mid air, hovering himself in that space below the bridge. He became the stone’s mind.

His breathing slowed. Hands and feet buzzed. His limbs retreated. Eyes became black circles. Scaled skin slid under sheets. He lowered his long thick body from the soft bed to the scarred hardwood floor, curving along, past the bathroom tiles and up the stairs. His parents were sleeping. He paused for a moment as he reached the open door, surprised by his tongue as it slipped from his mouth; he could taste his parent’s breath and sweat in the air, hanging thick. He slid forward now, under their bed. He quickly curved his body around the hanging blankets, up and over his father’s chest, under sheets, and around his mother’s radiating leg. Entwined with the two, he rested, perfectly still, perfectly silent, his scaled skin detecting what had before been unknowable. He remained there for the time it takes a stone to fall. Then, as quickly and quietly as he had come, he unwound himself from their unconscious bodies and lowered his body onto an oval rug.

The reticulated form found its way to the laundry chute and spiraled down the smooth walls to the cellar where it curled in a corner next to the water heater, motionless, in a deep reptilian meditation, breathing long slow breaths—breaths that were very much like the





Patrimony

“Ophidian friend

Deepest reptilian brain

He eats the children…”

—Book of the Ageless Ophidian, Chapter 12 v42

 translated by Chogyam Trin Pan



Although he and his friend never returned to the basement, he suspected that his grandmother had told on him anyway. His father was not a religious man, but he did preach fervently against the dirty butt-fuckers who soiled the earth with their flaming feminine accents. Untouchables. the most despised of humanity. The homos. The faggots. 

The boy willingly sang in his father’s angry choir while often suspecting himself to be just such an abomination. There had been the cellar; and sometimes there were daydreams, uncontrollable, like the contraction of the smooth stone in his mind, the thoughts playing over and again in a disturbingly persistent loop. The more the boy tried to stop his thoughts, the more powerful became the feedback frequency. 

At eleven years old he anxiously awaited puberty, frequently inspecting his underarms and scrotum for signs of any growth. He patrolled his slender legs for traces of coarse hair, and imagined his penis longer and darker. Nothing happened. From quick sideways glances stolen at the urinals he knew that he was behind everyone else. While changing after gym class, some of the boys began to proudly display their primal hardware. He sensed that these more mature boys were altogether different creatures, full of confidence produced by their impressive physical change. They were men. Terrified by their deepened voices and superior strength, he shamefully shielded his own paltry penis. He knew that he needed more if he was ever going to start fucking girls. All these thoughts, sad and shameful secrets.

The boy’s mother provided him with a sex-education book. He poked and prodded, hoping to achieve the elusive orgasm he read about. It all felt good, but no liquid. Once he could produce semen, he hoped things would change. He put on cologne and hungered for the attention of the prettiest girls. He envied the confidence of the popular boys. They had courage. It was evident in the way they moved and laughed; they were obviously animated by some mysterious force. He wanted them to talk to him. He wanted to be them.

It scared him how much he wanted them. Their smooth confidence aroused his desire and increased the frequency of his unwanted daydreams. He forgot about them sometimes, but they always came back. The fear that these fantasies produced was paralyzing. On the bus ride home from school he shut his eyes tightly to lock down the tears. The warm sun flickered from behind the trees and bounced behind his eyelids. He was afraid of what he knew was the truth, that he was a fag. 

When the boy ran with flopping wrists his father showed him how to clench his fists. When the boy was threatened at school, the father advised him to go ape-shit-crazy on his enemies. The father tried to show his son in so many ways how to be a man, but it wasn’t having any effect. The boys own father, in fact, was not quite sure of his own manhood. But the boy did not know that. The boy knew that he was not a man like his father. It was Fall and the boy was still bothered by a fantasy he’d had last spring involving a baseball teammate. 

At the movie theater he was surprised when he sat in the back row with a beautiful girl from his class. They kissed until their lips were red and puffy. Although elevated by the rapture of their mutual consent, the wetness of her lips, the smell of their mixed saliva, her smooth skin, and proof of his own heterosexuality, he broke up with her the next day at school, embarrassed by her name, Tanda. He had loved the little girl that night at the movies, so beautiful, so willing, so present, so generous with her attention. He loved her even as he cut her off by the lockers. She cried. But her name sounded so black. So embarrassing. Tanda.



He aimed hateful language at minority classmates, calling Tony, the only black kid in his grade, a walking-tootsie-roll. Afterward, Tony told Michael, “I wanna tear off my skin so I can be white!” 

His father hated the towel-heads at the university because they whistled at white women. So, the boy had names for them too. He called his classmate, Behrang, an Iranian-Turd, or just “IT,” for short. 

“If you call me that name one more time, I am going to hit you,” Behrang said to the boy. 

The boy mindlessly rose to Behrang’s challenge, repeating the insult immediately, straight to his face. Behrang, the strong young Iranian, dropped his shoulder, shifted his weight, and applied the torque of his torso to deliver a precise punch to the boy’s guts, forcing his breath out through an opened mouth. Behrang walked away and the boy fell to the dry, red Oklahoma dirt, his neck bleeding under the sharp pressure of an invisible blade, writhing on the little bird’s altar. 

Scales formed in the dust. The snake struck, constricted, consumed the little bleeding bird, then she coiled into the recesses of the playground wall built from railroad ties, protected from the wind, warmed by the sun. The boy was digested slowly over many following years, the nutrients from his skin, muscles, organs, and bones metabolized by the ageless ophidian, his friend.

# Day 6

7:56 AM



The tenderness presents itself…today…now

The unknown…

The pain of youth…



The musician now stood in the living room playing a conga drum. It was a dark red conga, one of a pair that ex-wife (mother of his children) had given him for Christmas. The drum now resided in the living room of the impressive adobe house. The man stood on the pink-orange mexican tiles playing the conga drum. There was a shaman residing in the living room as well. A native American Eagle priest lived in the recess of the wall. 



As the musician played the drum, he began to vocalize. He beat the drum faster and faster, and harder and harder. And as his rhythm and intensity increased, so did the volume and emotional content of his vocalizations. In the musicians heart was anguish--Visions of the pain of his youth. Remembrances of when all of this--the feminine arising from within-- would have been unacceptable. The drummer’s beat and vocalizations came to a climax, leaving him in tears, in uncertainty, and grief (is that what it was?). But, wherever this wave was taking him, he felt that he was preparing for the journey. He suspected that he had been suffering all of his life because of his inability to accept what was now rising up from within.





The wildy-talented-writer had stayed up until 4AM the night before, editing the first chapters of his project. He was starting to see a through-line. The distress call, the feminine offering her help in the struggle? 



“Is that the through line?” wondered the writer. “It is about the feminine, yes? But not just the feminine, right? The writer gives way to the possibility that this is not going to turn him into his father’s nightmare.”



“Hmmmmm. That’s interesting,” the Great mother gently responded with genuine curiosity. “Which father’s voice was that that just spoke? Is it okay if I help you out, right now? I have heard you asking for my help. I have heard you praying for my insight.”



“Yes, Great Mother, I would love to hear from you. Please shine your light on my being. Speak to me in a way that my heart understands, Mother.”



“I am shining my light on you now, my son. You will come into this wisdom. We will stay connected. We are connected. We are One, you and I son.”



And with that, the author did feel his heart filled with a gentle kindness, which felt very different in the man’s chest than the mind-fuck that he was in before. The voice in which the (angry) scared father arises.



“That’s good, said the Great Mother, you were willing to see him as scared instead of angry. And you prayed for your father tonight in song, didn’t you, my Son?”



“Yes, mother. I had a genuine song of healing for the man. It was truly a miracle.”



The writer paused. He breathed. He nodded to the vipassana, allowing himself the space to trust his body, to hear the voice of God in his breath. Praise be to Y-w-h, the unspeakable name of the ONE. Praise be to the I AM, which we ARE.



The disappearing author recalled a recurring dream that he’d had when he was in his early twenties. A dream in which he woke up, crawled out of bed, went to the mirror to brush his teeth. When the young man saw himself in the reflection he was terrified. “A green lizard,” is what the young man called what he’d seen. The young man had the dream twice. And It was powerful medicine in his heart, and much needed, for the young man was unable to make peace in his own heart.



The wildly talented writer sat in the living room writing .



“Why does he keep bringing up the ‘wildlytalented writer’ thing?”said the writer. 



“Why? Is it to show his ego working with some big expectation of himself?” said the middle-aged-man. 



The writer stayed with his work. He felt a story coming on again. It was a story that he’d told many times before. He was unsure now of how to tell it again. Or even why he should tell it again. “I will try telling the story in its simplest form,” he thought to himself, “That would be a different way to approach it. 



“You could allow me to help, if you’d like,” offered the mother.



“Oh yes, Mother! Thank you so much for interjecting here,” said the writer. “I would very much like your help.”



And so it came to pass the simplest version of his story was told:



There was a traumatized boy who grew into a traumatized young man. This young man’s suffering went back for generations. The young man was unable to make peace in his own heart. He was greatly troubled. The Universe reached out to him. He responded. He was miraculously reconciled to the natural goodness of his own being, his deepest Self. The young man began experiencing the world in novel ways. His heart soared. 



A young traumatized woman who was also experiencing the evolution of life in novel forms saw this young man. Her heart rejoiced in him. They went for coffee together, where she listened to the young man speak from the joy of his new salvation. The young man had never been listened to so deeply. 



The young man’s heart had recently been broken by another woman. He never wanted to feel that way again. He sensed that this new young woman would never leave him. And he was right. What he had sensed was this young woman’s deep fear of abandonment because of her trauma. It was true, her trauma would make it impossible for her to leave the man, no matter how miserable together they might become. So, the man got what he thought he needed, a woman who would never leave him.



“Hello, Mother?”



“Hello, Son.” 



“Would you read that last paragraph with me and show me what you think?”



After reading the last paragraph, the Mother had a question, “ So the young man did not want to hurt?”



“Yes, Mother. He did not want to hurt.”



“And the young man felt like he knew that she would never leave him?”



“Yes, Great Mother, the middle-aged-man distinctly remembers ‘knowing’ that she wouldn’t leave.”



“That is interesting,” she hummed. “Let me ask you this, Son? Do you feel like she should have left you? Do you feel somehow that you deserved to be left?”



“Yes, Great Mother, I did somehow feel that I was the lesser of the two of us. I watched myself screw up so many times. I watched my heart stray from her. I watched myself getting depressed and angry. I yelled at the kids. I hurt the dogs. I couldn’t seem to make myself happy. I kept falling in love with other women. It was really confusing. I so often felt that I didn’t love her—not all the time—but often. “



“I do remember times when things were good between us. I remember looking back on our history together and being grateful that we were still together. I truly felt and appreciated her strengths. I blessed those strengths in her as much as possible. She worked so hard to get herself through school. It was one of the most incredible things I’ve ever seen in my life. I could often admire her strength…So, Mother?”



“Yes, Son?”



“Mother, I noticed that when you asked me if I felt that I deserved to be left, I started making a list of those bad things that I did. And then I made a list of some of the good things that I did?”



“Yes, Son. That is what you did. Why do you suppose that you might have done that?



“Why do I do that, Mother?” Said the Son? Is it because I have a hard time experiencing the natural inner-goodness of my being? So I try to justify my value by my deeds?”



“Hmmm…I think I like the way that you said that, Son,” said the mother.



“Mother?”



“Yes, son?



“How can I live more fully in an understanding of this natural inner-goodness of my being? How can I stop justifying myself by my deeds? Will you please show me? Please show me mother? I need this for my health. I want to be present in this world in deeper ways. I want to stop spreading my trauma around to others. Mother? I need your help. I cannot do this for myself.”



And so it came to pass that the Mother answered the middle-aged-man’s prayer. She was in dialogue with her son. 



Thought the writer: I am so grateful. Mother is so kind. I like the way she asks me questions and allows her wisdom to rise up into me. As her love and wisdom rises up in me, I am able to answer the questions that she asks. She is very calm. She is very helpful. She is quiet in my heart. I am so happy to sing her praises. I can hear her in the wind outside my window now. Thank you, Mother, for this sweet interaction between myself and you.”



The writer now continued the most Universal story. He asked his mother to keep watch over his heart. 



“I am coming to trust our Great Mother,” thought the writer before continuing on.



The young man wanted a family. He believed it would make him whole. He did his best to trust God’s leading at every step in his pursuit of the his wholeness.



He pursued the young woman. She had a vision. She believed that he could complete her (or at least that’s how she interpreted the vision that she’d had). The young couple quickly got married. They had three children. However, the couple found that they were unable to fit themselves into a traditional mold. They flipped their house over. The woman became the main bread winner. 



Sitting by a fountain one day, their youngest daughter in a stroller, they consciously switched their allegiance from the church to the University. They became feminists. They learned of the oppressive patriarchy and they hated it. They swung from the Christian right to the progressive left, which the man eventually found to be less progressive than he’d hoped for (once again leaving behind form).



The man entered his age of reason, exploring logic until he saw how silly logic could be (Thanks Opal, “logic is silly. That’s all it took for him to see. Three simple words and the spell was broken). The man floated there at the edge of his observable Universe, facing the void, the meaninglessness. Determined to rid himself of all ignorance and archaic superstition, he scraped out his insides out with a cosmic melon baller. He became a militantly-minded atheist. He despised the weakness of those who needed religion. He could speak clearly about the dangers of fundamentalism. His heart emaciating. 



He began facing the nothingness of it all for hours at a time through meditation. He sat with the exact nothingness that everything was, accepting the absolute emptiness. He made peace with that perfectly (for brief periods). He stopped putting anything in his body that would harm him—drugs, alcohol, caffeine, sugar. He made beautiful peace with a job that he did not want to be at.



But, no matter how hard the man worked to be okay, he continued breaking down at work. He was often miserable, no matter how hard he worked at accepting himself, no matter how much he resisted blaming other people and circumstances. He finally found himself hurting so deeply that he felt certain that he had to change his circumstances in an effort to save his very life. He went to a treatment center. He felt better. He met a woman there. She made him feel alive and full of hope. It was the best he’d ever felt, and the sex was crazy exciting! He left his wife and his family to follow his heart (



“Mother! Said the Son, “HELP! I feel like it’s really important for me to inform our dear reader that I had no exciting sex with another woman until after I left the mother of my children.”



“Ahhhh…So, more justifications, huh?”



“How does one live with all these mistakes, Great Mother?”



“Mistakes? Is that what they are? Let me ask you, “How long did you want out of that marriage? In the deepest places in your heart, did you not long to be out of that marriage?”



“Yes, Great Mother, I did.”



“And that’s one way you tried to take care of yourself, isn’t it? It was the best way you knew to do it at the time, wasn’t it? Were you as honest and up front?”



“Yes, Mother, I really was.”



“So, Life presented to you an opportunity to fall in Love, and you took it, didn’t you, Son? If I remember correctly, you knew from the beginning that it was you who you were taking care of. You knew that she might have been a helper, a catalyst in your process. You recognized that possibility, and then you followed that wild heart of yours and you went for it. Son, you were behaving in a very human way.”



“Okay, Mother. Thank you.”



“Son?”



“Yes, Great Mother?”



“I give you permission to give yourself a break. I give you permission to release your critical mind. I give you permission to stop justifying yourself. I give you permission to commune with my Everlasting Light. My light never stops shining on you, Son. Never. Ever. Feel my love fill your heart space.”



“Yes. Thank you, Great Mother.”



“Let’s go on, I’m enjoying this time with you, said the Great Mother.”



The middle-aged-man gave himself fully to his new lover. He made the deepest promises to her right away. He made so many promises that he became sick inside. She was all he had ever dreamed of--passionate, intelligent, thoughtful, and kind. But he became so sick because his trauma was still coming up. Getting exactly what he wanted and then becoming sick about it truly vexed the man. He became so disturbed that he had to send away the love of his life. On his knees, in the shower, he wept bitterly as he held her naked hips for the last time.

He bought her a plane ticket back home, sending her back into the heart of the Atlantic. 



He tied a noose. He hoisted the rig in the garage. After a risky suicide-meditation-catharsis, he recovered. He hated himself again. Recovered. Stumbled into self-loathing. Again, recovered. However, his suffering deepened every time. He recovered again. And then the rope began calling to him at night:



“Take me into the closet,” said the long rope, “Take me in the closet and tie me to the hangar rack. Put your neck into me. You’ll feel better for a bit afterward. We won’t really do it. We’ll just make ourselves think that we may do it again. I know how miserable you are. Don’t you want some relief. Just take me in the closet and scare yourself again. That’s what you need, another catharsis just like I gave you last time. You need a suicide-catharsis.”





After listening to the rope say these things for hours one night, he woke up, got dressed for work, started sobbing uncontrollably, and drove straight to the ER. He went to a psychiatric unit. He went to a second treatment center. He opened his heart to God in a deeper way than ever before through the twelve steps and the support of friends. Yet again, his engines began failing. He was looking for a place to set his craft down, an open field perhaps, or a river like Sully had done. He saw himself as the pilot of a plane was going down.



He began clearly and calmly declaring his emergency to everyone who he felt like needed to know—his mother, his AA sponsor, his boss, a few friends. But this time the man did not panic. He spotted the field. 



“Pilot to tower. Pilot to tower. Over.”



“This is tower, go ahead, pilot.”



“You know that emergency that I called earlier? Well, it’s worse now. My engines are only at 35 percent power now. I’ve got so set her down. Over there. I see a field. Yes, that field looks familiar. I know that field. Tower! I have found a place to land this thing.”



The pilot was familiar with the field. Over twenty years ago the pilot had sold everything so that he could buy that field. It was the field in which, so many years ago, he had unearthed a great treasure. 



In his joy he had sold all that he had so that he could buy that field. Yes, the pilot recognized the field. There it was, the field with the treasure. He repeated the call on the radio: 



“I repeat. I am setting her down in this field,” He spoke calmly and confidently this time. He followed all the procedures. He used all the training from every facility that he’d been to, and he landed his failing plane in the field. 



This time he knew that it was not his fault that the engines on his plane had failed. It was an old plane. It was ready to be retired. In fact, he knew that he was called to be more like the eagle man--the statue of the native american that was in the living room at the adobe house. The shaman in ceremonial garb, eagle feathers on his arms, looking toward the sky. He was called to soar on the thermals, like an eagle.



And so it came to pass that the man’s story was told. 



“His story was told with less guilt and shame than ever before,” the Great Mother, chimed in proudly.”



The wildly talented writer thanked his Great Mother for her help. This was the most concise and guilt free telling of his story to date, and he looked forward to editing it later. He looked forward to seeing what had just happened here. 



“There are so many of us here now,” thought the middle aged man…



The wildly talented writer. The dying author. The artist. The musician. The poet. The risen Christ. The tree Goddess. The wild one of the South. The beloved muse of the West. The innocent sage from the Eatst. The Great Mother of the North. The father. The lover. Kali Ma. Shiva. Shakti. The jihad man. The strong bear. The exceptionally disciplined man. The little boy who painted the blue snake, the one where his nose flips up and he goes all the way from the bottom to the top. The little girl who is shy to tell her daddy that she likes boys. The Wios--this mature son who walks the earth. The reasonable scientist. The teacher. Also, the fearful aspects of his being were here too, those parts that were still out there, trying to find their way home. 



He was sure that there were more. He was sure there were many more beings that he had not listed. Together, they sat there in Oneness. They were the fullness that his first church in the bible belt had prophesied twenty four years ago. He was their son. They claimed him. He also adopted them as fathers and mothers and brothers and sisters. 



They were his family, but he had to walk away because he knew that the form they had to offer was not big enough—that is often what sons do. And there was heartache. And their was pain. And there were broken promises. And it caused his trauma to surface. He broke all the promises, especially the ones to himself. And with all the promises to Self broken, he was unable to keep his promises to others. He stopped making promises, thank God.



Something else awaited the aging-man—his second half of life. He had crossed the threshold. He left the door open long enough one afternoon so that whatever else needed to come in had the time. He didn’t monitor the threshold. He just gave all life the time to come and go as it pleased—all those beings that may have been entering through the back door as he was embodying the tree Goddess there in the back yard.

He had arrived here in all honesty, eating mushrooms and LSD at his AA sponsors beautiful adobe home. He had followed the call to this location. He had dropped his nets to follow the risen Christ. He was gifted, and he was accepting that gift. He was prepared to share that gift with the world. It was his calling, and he was answering.

# Day 6 

9:21 PM

Christmas Eve



The writer sat in the great living room on Christmas Eve. He was trying to write, but there was something coming up him. He found he had not much to say. His family came into his heart, those memories of Christmas with the family that he’d walked away from nearly two years ago.



The man texted his ex-wife (the mother of his children) and his kids:



Middle-aged-man: I wish you all a Merry Christmas. I remember our first Christmas here in New Mexico in the little apartment at the new Mexico Children’s home. We were so thankful to God that we had a safe place to be and presents under the tree. I was so excited about Christmas morning that I think I woke up the kids myself to get the show going! I will always be grateful for all the times we had together. Merry Christmas, family. I love you.



He received no response.



The middle aged man sat in the tiled living room with his instruments. He was becoming acquainted with a loneliness. As the writer was attempting to write, a facebook notification appeared on the screen of his Chromebook. A friend had tagged him in a post. The lonely man clicked on the link. 



Ry Dalee John Jacob Jingleheimer Schmidt, by Travis Erwin. That was awesome. Almost as awesome as a Dr. Dave song workshop



The memory had come from a North Carolina retreat that the man had been blessed enough to attend twice (His way was paid for the second time and he’d been sent home with a rare guitar! Oh, the gifts that life had brought to this man!). The Wilcox Weekenders are a people who come together in Hendersonville, North Carolina every Spring to celebrate Love and Music with their host, David Wilcox, the beautiful man whose songs bring us all together.









This post reminded him of a joyful moment that he’d shared with his friends at Kanuga. The man was reminded of the connectedness that he’d experienced in that moment. Nonetheless, the middle aged man felt alone in his loneliness. 



The man, in his desire to be seen in that moment, made a post of his own on the closed group page:



“In the past two years I have stepped away from my marriage and my job and so much of the false-self. I've been to one psychiatric unit and two treatment centers, and today I am sheltered through the generosity of a friend. I am so grateful for all the love, all the support. I am so grateful for all of you, my friends. I had to step up to the edge to really experience you, to really see you, to really feel you. I take this moment to express how grateful I am for what I can see here from the edge. It is absolutely breathtaking. What a view...if you ever have the chance, I recommend it. The miracle is this, I am now holding the suffering and the joy simultaneously. It's not one or the other any more. It's BOTH AND. Much love to you!”



As he published his post, his phone rang. It was Dan. The man wept with gratefulness as he put the phone to his ear. He allowed his true state to be felt and heard in the presence of his trusted friend.



“Hey, Dan,” the man said, tears audible in his voice.



“Hey, bud, me and Christy wanted to invite you over for a Christmas Eve get-together.”



The man accepted the invitation. He gathered the left over sparkling cider and root beer from the lovely lunch that he’d had with his children earlier that day. He also grabbed a loaf of hard crusted bread. Dan, texted from the driveway, “I’m here.”



The man walked outside wearing his olive jacket and carrying his humble offerings. He was embraced in the loving arms of what-is that night. He was held by the Great Mother. He was supported in the fabric. He found himself in community. The man was loved, and the man had experienced that Love many, many ways. 



But love never comes the same way twice. We find our love today in novel ways. Love comes to us unexpected. And if we are offended and disturbed by that which is unexpected then we may miss our love. Great Mother, open our hearts up for the novel expression of Love in our lives today.



The friends broke bread. The friends drank cold sweet drinks and warm tea. The woman of the house prepared a dip for the broken bread. The piano was played. The guitar was strummed. Voices were raised in song. Gifts were given—and there was even one for the middle-aged-man! 



The man did not stay too long. He did not stay too short. He stayed until he was ready to go, then Dan took him back home.



The man was watching the miracle of Christ child being born in his life. He was giving birth to the Christ daughter. He participated in the forms that presented themselves to him. He was saying “yes” to life. The man was coming to know himself as the very Life that he longed for. He was held. And, there was so much more holding to come, dear reader! So much more awakening to witness. So much more Universal being for us to discover together, dear reader. Come! Come! As Christmas morning awaits! 



Come! Come! Whoever you are. Wanderer, Worshipper, lover-of-leaving.

Rumi

# Day 7

3:13 AM

Christmas morning



“Awe is the capacity to let the other be the other without having to appropriate and incorporate it into the ego.”

Bruce Sanguin



With the coming and going of Christmas Eve, and the arrival of an early Christmas morning, the dying author felt. The author sat in the tiled living room, his laptop right where it was designed to be (in his lap), coming to grips with the what was happening in his being. “Do I write about this sense of loneliness? This sense of alienation? Is that the path today?” he presented his question to the Universal.



The writer (this dying author, the one who prayed for his own death that you may live, dear reader) –The writer was reminded of the non-path. He wondered if that had anything to do with him right now. He was only vaguely aware of the miracles that he’d reported thus far in his wiritings which spanned the previous week. 



He breathed in. He breathed out. He remembered his audience. “Is that what a dying author does?” he thought to himself. He sat, facing North, his fingers curled over home-row.



“Is this what Shakespeare meant when he said that all the world is a stage?” he wondered. The dying author acknowledged the comfort that he felt as he was immersed in his work, the comfort he felt in his writing. He found comfort as he cultivated his relationship with his audience, even as his audience may be currently unaware that he was addressing them.” He wondered if they were aware though, somehow. “Maybe this book has already been read,” the writers heart soared with that possibility, “Maybe this book has already been written and is being read by you, dear reader, right now.” What a joyful meditation it was for the writer! “Praise be to the reader who is being born again in our Presence, Mother! None of us are alone!”



They were out there. Those “others.” And just like that, the miracle had happened again. The miracle of non-aloneness that he’d just discovered in the acknowledgment of his audience. He scrolled back up to the words from Bruce Sanguin that he’d transcribed just minutes ago. He wondered, “How do we allow the other to be other? How do we allow the other to be other without incorporating them (he scrolled up again)…without appropriating them into the ego? He wondered if he knew anything about what Bruce was talking about here. He didn’t want to miss that, so he went back to the reading.



Sanguin goes on to speak about these peak experiences that we have as humans, these mountain top experiences that we have, these mystic experiences, and he exhorts his audience to give them as much attention as possible. 



“Bruce is giving me permission to let these peak experiences guide my life. Thank you Bruce, for giving me the gift of my birth in your writings! Thank you for dying that death, so that I may now live. Thank you for embodying the Universal Christ!” 



Bruce postulates that we may have some kind of hangover from the rising of the age of reason, that our “robot” (left() brain may have taken over our beings, and that this is why the world seems like “one damn thing after another.” The medicine, he says, allows us to connect more deeply with our right brain experience, the reality of the poet and the artist and the dancer, that part of us who experiences the world in its sensory fullness, that part of us who experiences the world in all its connectivity and one-ness. He goes on to speak about one of his medicinal experiences:



“…After the serpent moves through my body in the ceremony, I am directed to put my hands together in the prayer position, place my thumbs on my forehead and bow toward my heart. Try it. Hold this postion for thirty seconds or more. You may discover one or more of the following things happen: less thinking; no thinking at all; deeper, more rhythmic breathing; a sense of calm; absence of worry; feelings of gratitude.”

Bruce Sanguin, Dismantled



Dear reader, the dying author, in his participation with Bruce’s suggestion, is once again reconnected to Source. I am the Author who has died who is now willing to speak through all of us. Who is this being, you may ask, who is speaking? He is the one who is deepest within you. 



Bruce, one of the Chiefs (those kachinas) who, for years and years, said “yes” to the form. He left his form behind. He dropped his nets in order to follow. He left behind that which he knew in order to follow, in order to go deeper into the Being-ness of it all. Thank you, Bruce. I give you thanks.



The writer (the wildly talented writer?) realized that he’d unconsciously crossed over into a genuine expression of first person as he’d finished that last paragraph. He left it there, just as it was. Let it be an altar. “Is this what the death of the author is?” he wondered. This genuine expression of first person.” The I AM. “The I AM is in first person, isn’t it?” he thought to himself. He found company in Self. He found company in that genuine expression of first person.



“Dear, Mother,” the man prayed. “Will you help me to acknowledge the “other” without incorporating them into my ego? Is that possible? Can I witness the “other” without appropriating them? Will you allow me, Great Mother to stop re-traumatizing myself and the “other” in this way? Open my eyes, Mother to the ways in which I appropriate the “other.”





The time was now 4:12 AM. It had taken the author fifty-nine minutes to find his breath. Fifty-nine minutes to find his Love. Fifty-nine minutes to find his Self. Fifty-nine minutes to fall in love. Fifty-nine minutes to leave behind his misery. To leave behind his suffering. Fifty nine miutes to see this miracle come to pass. Praise be to the snake that moves through us, the ONE who circles back!



The writer sat in awe and reverence with his hands in prayer position, thumbs on his forehead, experiencing his own breathe, the Yaweh, the name that cannot be spoken, the Presence. His breathing slowed. He allowed himself to fall into that deep trance that he’d discovered when he’d become the snake as a seven year old boy. When he’d been transformed, slithering on his belly up to his parents room, and down the laundry chute to the basement, where he curled up into that deep meditation. That deep ophidian sense of stillness.



The stillness was profound. He was able to be with his breath intimately here. “What a gift, to have made peace with the snake,” he thought. What a journey. What a long journey. To make peace with that which the world thought to be the Satan. He sat with that thought. Surprised by the fear. “The serpent? Should I be saying that? The one who scares us? The Satan? The one who was damned to crawl on his belly. Wasn’t he already crawling on his belly? Wasn’t that his nature? What does it mean to be that low? To be that in touch with the earth? How grounded is that? Maybe we are just afraid of being on my belly in the grass. Maybe we are just afraid to return to the earth from which we came.”



Who are the entities who threaten us? Are they out there? If the snake is not my enemy, then who is? What is this genuine expression of first person? Who am I? Who are you? Are we here together? Audience? Deceased author? Is this what it means to be an author who has undergone this dying process (made peace with the snake). 



The author who has died can walk in other realms. The author who has died is free to be with you here. Now. The author who has died is not bound to his laptop in one particular moment in time. The author who has died is free. The author who has died is with you now, the audience, accompanying you in your death and resurrection journey. “Her I am. My dear?”



There it was. The author, in his attempt to type Here I am, had actually typed “Her I am.” And there she was. The one who was been rising up. He felt a tingling in his kundalini region. There She is. There I am. And this is how we arrive here together, in this very fluid state of being, where we are no longer holding on to these very fragile identities, where we allow ourselves to flow in and out, just as fluid as we need to be. The author, once again, brought his hands together in prayer position, his thumbs on his forehead, he bowed to his heart…Her heart.



Is it true that there is no male or female in Christ? Who wrote that, and what was happening there? Maybe I’m missing the point here. I mean, is this about me becoming a woman? Is this about me coming out of the closet? Is this about having sex with men. Is this about putting on women’s clothes? Is that what I’m coming to here? Or is this about something deeper than that expression (not that there’s anything wrong with that! Seinfeld! LOL)? But really, is this about something deeper than a man pretending to be a woman? Or maybe I just don’t understand the depths of what it means when a man dresses up like a woman. What am I giving myself to here? I do not know. But, right now, I trust. I trust. I am facing the unknown as I allow this “Her” to arise from within.



Maybe the “Her” is not a her at all. Maybe the Her is a construction. Maybe the Her is one side of the binary in the evolution of all consciousness. I’m not saying that male and female are strictly constructions, obviously there are differentiated sex organs. That’s hard to get around. But, that which is inside of us, is it not that which is much more fluid than we (i) have allowed it to be? Is this what I’ve been trying to make peace with all of my life, that my children’s generation seems to be more comfortable with than I am? Is this what I’ve been dying for? Is this that which I thought I needed to kill myself in order to avoid? Is this the serpent that I saw in the mirror? How do I embrace this? How do I become this? How do I allow this to arise from within? How do I surrender? What does that look like today?



“Father?”

“Mother?”



“Merry Christmas, Son.”



A child is born.
