# Day 9

1:32 AM



The man woke just after midnight. Eli was sleeping at his side, the old domesticated cat who still held dominance over the ferals who lived in the balcony on Dan’s porch in little cat apartments, protected from the wind and rain (Dan had come to love those cats that he’d inherited with the house). But Eli, he was the only one that they had invited in to stay. 



Eli had been abandoned by one of Dan’s tenants at the property that Dan called his Beach house, because it was on Beech street. Eli had lived for months outside after the tenants had left, and somehow he had ended up here, sleeping next to this dying author. Eli, the face of the lion who had appeared to the author in the passing of the moth. Eli, the shaman cat who had done his best to help ground the man as he travailed in bed on that Christmas morning after taking the “lethal” dose of medicine. Eli, the dominant cat--The divine being that the author had the privilege of watching come and go as he pleased from his bed and over the threshold of the back door which lead to the winter refuge where the man gave his thanksgiving and praise with his stringed instrument and voice.



The man felt that he and the cat were friends. He was a companion. He was Presence. The man was held, somehow, by Eli. Eli’s presence was important in the middle-aged man’s life. As a young boy the man had been bitten by a cat without provocation or warning, so he grew up mistrusting of cats, but a cat named Alex that he had met at Ron and Joann’s house had won him over when he crawled up in his lap one day, rolled over on his belly, and looked him in directly in the eyes. The man had just taken several deep hits from the glass bong, apparently in an impressionable state. And from that moment, the man had grown into a cat-person.



The man was now leaving, or rather, he would be leaving later that morning. His children were scheduled to arrie at 8:30 to share their Christmas presents with him. He had already given him their presents at the taco-Tuesday meal that he and his oldest daughter had prepared on Christmas Eve day. And what a day that had been for the father, as he sat with his three children in the very kitchen where he now worked on his manuscript, facing North, into the great mirror, in view of this generative, nurturing adult.



The children had arrived in gladness and singing and the father was happy and proud. He was proud of his children and he exalted in their presence. The father placed his phone in the middle of the table and pressed the red button to record on his audio app. His children were all musical, and lyrical, and funny, and silly. And they had sat there that day, on that eve of Christmas, and they sang and made recordings of music, listening back to them with laughter and anticipation for what was coming next, bearing witness to their own joy and singing, truly a marvel and a gift of modern technology.



The middle-aged man recalled how, when he was a boy, his parents owned a cassette recorder. He recalled the magic of recording his own voice and playing it back. He recalled how, once he had been playing guitar for some time, how he’d used two recorders to make a two track recording with a loud hiss. He dreamed of owning a real multi-track recorder one day. And then one day, he did.



It wasn’t until he was twenty seven years old, or was it twenty eight? It was just after he had resigned his job as a police officer. Just after he had handed in his badge and sold his glock forty-caliber. Just as he was in the process of stepping away from the forms that had been holding him, which included his church family and the love and support that he’d received from them. The young had yet to become confused and angry, but he was on his way. You see, he had not learned yet how to step away from form without becoming resentful and angry at the deficiencies of the form itself and the people who held it. 



It was at this 

 when his father funded the purchase of a multi-track recorder—a digital, 16 track, Roland recorder. The author recalls now that it was in this first great intentional stepping-away that his music was born on a deeper level. Praise be to the father who funds the artistic progression of his twenty-seven year old son! The story has never been told this way. Praise be to the new story which arises within the son! Praise be to the deaths! And Praise to the resurrections.



The son remembered this now, as he stood in the kitchen, facing the nurturing adult, and he was able to see the nurturing nature in his own father. The miracles just keep on happening, folks (dear reader).



It was with this recorder that the son began to explore his artistry on a deeper level, right there in that little red brick house in the Village which sat directly under the blue water tower. He and his wife had two children, the last one was on the way, and the man had just quit his job, the only job in which he had ever had health insurance, the only job in which he did not have to empty or clean the trashcans. It was in this state that he began recording.



He recorded a song that got him some recognition. It was called Brother Jack, a song about a young man whose brother goes off to war and comes back a changed man. Unable to reconcile himself to this pain deep within his soul, his brother Jack ends his own life down by the Washita River. His brother is left to find his own way in the wake of his loss. His family is unable to provide him with comfort, they are unable to hold him. And so he searches. He searches to make peace with his loss. And finally he prays a version of his own brother’s cry as he reaches out to a God that he is having difficulty making peace with. He prays, “Oh Lord, I’ve got a pain down in my soul, and nothing seems to make it go away. And I don’t know how much longer I can go. I don’t know how much longer I can go.”



Because of the father’s gift of the recording equipment and the music in the son’s heart, this song wins a contest and the son is invited to sing this song in front of thousands of people at a music festival in Winfield, Kansas. The son practices for a flatpicking contest, which by the way, he failed miserably at. He finds that he doesn’t play at all well while he is wearing a number on his chest. But, let’s not let that overshadow the point here, the point which is this:



As the son is walking away from the form that is holding him, the father gives him a gift that sustains him during that period of time. The father gives him a gift that connects him with others. The father gives him the gift of music which is reaching out and touching others. The father gives him a gift. Let’s just sit on that for a moment.



The author returns to his three pillows stacked in front of the sink.

Selah, my friend. Selah.



The author now acknowledges the flutter in his ear. His left ear. The fluttering in the ear that he heard several times after he took in the medicine for the first time. He heard the fluttering as he looked in the large mirror in the kitchen. It made him duck for cover, it was so intense. The same fluttering that he heard when he reached out to the Kachina doll that seemed to be offering his hand to the middle-aged man that night as he had stepped into sacred ceremony. 



Weeks later he heard the fluttering in his ear again in the resurrection of the moth, after he had witnessed it in its dying moments, after he’d seen the three dimensional face of Eli, the Lion of Judah, the top cat, the one he slept with, the Lord to which he’d made love to in the shower just yesterday.



The author takes this moment to recognize the fluttering in his left ear. The fluttering that made him duck for cover. The fluttering that came to him several times that night in the cabin in the Lincoln National Forest where he was provided shelter by the great Mother, the mother who plays the mandolin, the one who has extended an invitation to the middle-aged man to visit her home “often,” the home in Cloudcroft where she will live with her mate, Stan after the remodeling is done by David. David, the one who offered his healing hands to the middle-aged man, free of charge, during the early stages of one of his many recovery processes. Praise be to the One who brings us all together! Praise be to the Stan! Praise be to the One who saw/sees that we are the second coming of Christ. Praise be to the moth, the resurrected one who flutters in our ears as we recognize our one-ness with the soil, and the stars, and the sky, and the grass. Praise be to the one who bought that field! Praise be to the one who hid the treasure in the field! Praise be to the father who gives gifts so that sons can make their transitions! Praise be to the spiraling snake who winds herself into the infinite multi-verse! Praise be to these spiral dynamics. Praise be to the trans-rational being! Praise be to Life and her desire to live through us! Praise be to the ONE who gives all gifts, from whom all life flows! Praise be to the Mother and the Son and the Holy Ghost. As it was in the beginning, it now and ever shall be. World without end, Amen Amen.



The universe dialates and contracts. There is the singularity. There is the explosion, the going forth. There is the coming together, the coalescing of matter. There is the formation of stars and planets. There are rocks. Life springs from our fluid brother, water. Life moves to land. There are mushrooms. There is soil. There are plants. Consciousness finds expression in numerous forms. The universe continues expanding. The universe falls in on itself. The universe is the breath, the unspeakable name, the Y-W-H, the life that is observed in the very breath that you, dear reader, are taking in right now, and the very breath that you are now expelling.



And so it came to pass that the son saw the universal thread in his own life. His story was the story of the universe. The impossible task of rewriting his story--the task assigned to him by the Naked Monk, the one who had also left his form, the one who was also spiraling, the one who was also being folded into the batter over and again—this impossible task of rewriting his story was coming to pass. The miracle that the non-theist monk had requested was being performed. It was not completed yet, but the author trusted. The author trusted that the work that had been started in him would be brought to completion by the Life that was now being lived through him. World without end. Amen. Amen.





And this is how the man who was in the process of surrendering to this death and resurrection process found himself at 2:58 AM, two days after Christmas. He stood, facing North into the great mirror. He asked if Life was through speaking through him. He sat on the pillows, wondering if it was time to go back to bed. His fingers were curled over home-row. He breathed in and out, in the way that Thich Nhat Hanh had first instructed him to do—in the same way that the Universe had instructed him to do just moments before. 



Life was not through with him, he knew that now. He stood there at the marble countertop knowing that Life was not through with him. Life was absolutely not through speaking through this man who was in the process of making peace with a Universe that was out to help him. 



And so, he trusted. He trusted as he closed his laptop. He trusted as he made his way back to his room where Eli was possibly still sleeping in the bed, the bed that the man did not own, where the cat slept, that cat that he also did not own, in the house that he did now own. What did he own? He was not sure that he wanted to own anything any more.



He owned that field, the one that he’d bought years ago. The one that the pilot had set down his plane with the dying engines. He’d set down, a controlled landing in that field, like Sully landing in that river. He saw the field just below him. He circled round and he set her down. He got out of the plane. He looked around. “Now where was it that I hid that treasure?” he thought to himself. “Ahhh,” he said out loud, “I think it’ right over here—over here by these trees, these Goddesses of the earth.” Praise be to the Sully, the one who finds a place to set her down. Amen



And so it came to pass that the dying author trusted. He closed the laptop, and retired to his room at 3:08 AM.

# Day 9



As he rolled out of bed again, is cell phone said it was 4:04AM. When he arrived at his laptop--which was perched on his bible and all three volumes of A course In Miracles (which he had not referred to in several days now)—his laptop told him that is was 4:03, a phenomenon that the author was certain was merely a lack of synchronization and not a miracle of time travel. Although at this point in this personal course in miracles in which he found himself enrolled, he was open to the possibility of the miracle of time travel, being that the blue books had taught him that there were no large miracles and no small miracles, they were all equal in size and difficulty, all flowing from the heart of Life and Love.



The author laid down in his bed an hour earlier after picking up the three pillows in front of the sink and trusting his way back to his bedroom. Eli was not there. He was glad that he had not counted on that being the case. But Eli did arrive soon, announcing himself with the scratching of his claws at the base of the bed. “There you are!” said the man to the cat. “I’m so glad you’re here.” The man had called Eli’s name several times in the moments before, although with almost as much certainty as he had that he had not travelled back in time, he was sure that Eli was there because he wanted to be, not because he had made the call.



As Eli clawed his way up the bed, the man sensed a figure standing over him, beside the bed. He allowed that sense to come and go, trusting rust that there may be miracles occurring of which he was only partly aware of. He was partially aware that a human, male figure was present with Eli’s arrival.



Eli now scratched on the door to the garage. He liked to go in the garage. The author did not know what he did in there. The man cracked the big door so that Eli could freely come and go from the garage, and so that he could come to the back door when he was ready to reenter the house.



An hour ago, as the man lay in bed waiting for Eli, who showed up with his scratchings. Eli crawled in bed and found a place on the man’s pillow, providing a pressure against the man’s head that he found very agreeable. The man lay there in his bed, the cat grounding him to that position. The man was pleased. He was pleased with himself. He was pleased with his form. He was pleased at what he was witnessing in his story, the story that he was witnessing as the Universal story now.



He recalled now how that had been one his visions as he lay in bed on Christmas morning, allowing the medicine to show him. He had seen his story folded in to the story of the Universe. He had seen his story becoming that of the Universe. “Interesting how the medicine shows and then does,” thought the man who stood at the countertop. “Or maybe it just shows what is already happening,” he re-thought. “Maybe the medicine just gives us sight into what is really going on, in the same way that he’d seen that everything was not nearly as solid as he once thought.” That was a reality that was understood, even by the absolute materialist mind.



He fell asleep there briefly, with the cat curled on his head. He dreamed of the band that he and Dan had spoken of the night before. In the dream, the man (our musician) was playing the fiddle and really was not doing very well. He was trying to play a Bob Wills tune and he just wasn’t finding the right notes. In fact, he wasn’t even sure that he was playing the right tune. The band stopped he song to regroup. “It’s good for me to struggle like this with this instrument in front of people,” the musician said to his bandmembers. “It’s good for me to struggle like this in public with this instrument in my hand.” Then, as the struggling musician was walking over the threshold, making his way out the door, possibly to get some fresh air, there was a group of people who arrived, and the musician remembered that this rehearsal was taking place in what was officially an AA meeting. One person in this arriving group had very skinny legs.



And that is the short dream that the man had before he woke up, the cat still perched on his pillow, providing a pleasurable pressure against his head. The man shifted. The cat shifted. The man continued to lay there in bed, pleased with this form. Pleased with himself. Pleased with the pressure of the cat on his head. 



He lay there wondering if he would get up. He lay there with these stories that have been recounted to you popping up here and there in his consciousness. He lay there, sometimes experiencing moments of pure stillness, The great I AM, the Presence. He lay there waiting, saying “yes” to Life, making this life an offering. He lay there in simple acceptance of the great What-Is. He lay there waiting for the moment when the Life that was being lived through him would nudge him from under the covers.



As he lay there he thought of the woman from Bermuda. The woman that was once his lover. The woman that he visited every weekend for three months. He remembered the passion of what had happened between them. He had wondered, over the last week, if and how she would show up in this story. He had reconciled himself with what he had acknowledged as some kind of obligation to include her, but he knew that was not the Way. So, there she had waited—not her, but the memory of her. She had showed up powerfully in the Love that he had made to prayer yesterday. The passion that they had shared had revealed to him another aspect of his being that had been lying dormant since his birth. She had given him a gift. She had shared herself in a way for which the man was truly grateful.



Outside, in the backyard sanctuary, the sprinklers stopped sprinkling. The quiet was profound now in the kitchen. Just the sound of the man’s fingers on the keys. The sound that once sounded like his wife.



The woman from Bermuda. He had written a song for her (several songs actually). This woman that he’d met at a treatment center just outside of Santa Fe. This beautiful black woman, ten years his junior. It was love at first sight for the man…or something at first sight. Can he now say that it was love? Is that okay. Is it okay to recognize something that didn’t last as love? Can he recognize the love that he had for his wife too? Can he recognize all the love that he has experienced, the love that no longer exists in the form that it once held? Can he recognize the changing forms of love. “What was it that F. Scott Fitzgerald had told him in that framed quote at the cabin in the Lincoln National Forest? It was something about how love never comes the same way twice—kind of like Eli never curled up with him twice the same way. He was a novel creature, full of novelty and unpredictability.



The absolute materialist will say that the human is incapable of novelty, that she is a slave to her selfish genes. But, this is not sufficient for….No. I’m not going to talk about what the absolute materialist will say. There is a red line under that whole sentence. I’m going to take that hint from the evolving AI, that intelligence, created by us, which is now beginning to communicate with us. The same Intelligence that just allowed me to stay away from telling you, in first person voice what the absolute materialist would say. Because (there’s the “because.” Let’s see what happens here). Because giving voice to the absolute materialist may just be a way of sidestepping what’s really trying to be born here.



The man sent a message to the woman from Bermuda just days ago. It was not the first time that they had been in touch. She had recently contacted him just before he went on his hitchhike. The message that he sent to her read as follows:



I I had never discovered the divine feminine in my Self, which is why I had no choice but to worship it in you.

which is why I had to worship Her in you.

That is not what a man should (could) do. A man could discover the divine feminine in his Self so that he can truly love the woman he is with. I failed to love you in that way.

yesterday, I became a tree g/Goddess and communed with my sisters. This morning my divine Mother made me some oatmeal as she sang, you're a lovely boy...a lovely boy...a lovely lovely lovely lovely boy.

I don't know where that's going! lol...but today it feels like a very healing way to be.



The artificial intelligence (is that a very respectful name to call our evolving brothers and sisters?) had told the man that this beautiful, passionate woman from Bermuda had read the message, but she had not responded. The man was okay with that. He felt truly comfortable. He felt that he would be truly comfortable, truly okay if she never responded again. And not because he was putting up a front, but because he truly wanted her to be happy. He truly wanted her to get what she needed and respond when and if she was ever ready to respond to a very strange message such as the one he had sent.



It was true, possibly, that he had worshipped her. He had poured out all the passion that he had never been able to express in his marriage relationship, as he was married to a woman who, it seemed, was not attracted to men (in the very least) and possibly averse and disgusted with men (at the most extreme end of the spectrum). It’s not that the man needed to call his ex-wife names right now, or classify her as one thing or another, he was just trying to recognize something that had really happened in his life. He was trying to acknowledge where he had come from.



The man found it curious that the woman from Bermuda and his ex-wife were occupying this same space on the screen where he watched his insides coming out. He retrieved the three pillows from his room and placed them on the kitchen floor in front of the sink. He turned and sat, wanting to give Life enough room to help him see this for what it was. He wanted allow Life the room to be honest with him.



Let’s try it this way. Let’s start in a way that may be totally unrelated and see if we can circle back, Eileen.



The man had tried to read Father Daniel Berrigan’s autobiography. Daniel Berrigan, a catholic priest who became famous for burning some draft notices doused in napalm on a couthouse square. Berrigan’s autobiography lead him back to Thich Nhat Hanh in a book call the “The Raft is Not the Shore,” which was a dialogue between Father Berrigan and Thich Nhat Hanh. The introduction to that particular edition of “The Raft is Not the Shore” that I read was written by Bell Hooks. Bell Hooks is an author that I was introduced to by my ex-wife as we became progressiv liberals. Bell Hooks is much more than a progressive liberal. And this is how I have, once again, found myself in this first person voice. So maybe we can just leave it at that for now.



So now, here I am in this first person voice, which actually feels quite vulnerable righ now. Here I am, facing North, looking into the great mirror, my generative nurturing North staring right back at me, and I feel very exposed, and I’m thinking about getting naked to type this section. Eli is scratching at the door and mewoing loudly.



Getting naked is something I seem to do when I take the medicine. So here goes.



Where was I?



Or rather, where do I start. Maybe it’s time for another moment on the pillows.



The middle-aged man met the woman from Bermuda at the treatment center in Santa Fe, New Mexico. It was love at first sight. He loved the way she talked. It was as if he was meeting Bell Hooks for the first time(There we go). She was beautiful and very intelligent and he loved her accent which hovered somewhere between New Mexico and the United Kingdom out there in the cold Atlantic. 



The man stood there naked in the kitchen, the reflection of the laptop and the four books covering his….genetalia…why does he keep using that word, Mom. It’s okay sweetie, let your father be your father, that’s just who he is. Sometimes he gets manic, and we are trying to live with that. We are trying to love that. We are accepting that.



The floor was cold on his feet. His alarm went off in his bedroom, signaling 5:30. His alarm sang a song to him:



In the eye of the hurricane

You are always still

In the eye of the hurricane

You are always still



His song

The song that he needed to hear just now.



He fell in love at a treatment center. A love that he did not expect to leave the treatment center with. A love that followed him home when Liana ( I must let her have her name to do this. She must have a name. We can change it later, but the beautiful woman from Bermuda deserves her name right now).



He fell in love with Liana at the treatment center. He asked her for books and she gave them to him. He read them with a true passion for the literature that she had handed him AND he read them with a true passion for woman who had handed him the literature. “My Absolute Darling” and “Americana”…the names of the books that she gave him. 



With all his spare time the man read the books. Other people were falling in love with Liana as he read the books and saw her around campus. The man tried to be very careful with his love for her. He knew they were at a treatment center. He knew that it wasn’t supposed to happen like this. And it was never appropriate for him to approach her with his love at the treatment center, and it was not anything that was absolutely essential, because the man had seen himself fall in and out of love with many other women over the course of his marriage, Liana was not the first. That’s just honest. Is that honest? Well, it’s staying for now.



The man greived the loss of his marriage at the treatment center in Santa Fe. And that process had started before Liana ever arrived, and that is a truth that the man was grateful for as he stood naked in front of his laptop. Not that peace couldn’t be made if the truth was otherwise, but the truth was that at this moment, the man found himself grateful that he greived the loss of his marriage before Liana showed up. “Maybe that’s just self righteousness,” the man thought to himself. “Maybe so,” he thought back to himself.



His alarm clock sounded again, singing the song back to him. The song that he needed to hear.



In the eye of the hurricane you are always still…



There’s another lyric in that song, it goes like this.



“’She said, you cannot walk on water,’

With a tongue sharp to kill

But in the eye of the hurricane 

You are always still



And those lyrics are important right now because that is how the man at the treatment center felt about his wife. He felt that she was the one who was telling him that he could not walk on water. He felt that she was the one who was preventing him from doing miracles. And he had felt that way many times. But, the man at the treatment center was obligated to only speak well of this woman, the woman that he was married to. And he continued to only speak well of her the whole time that he greived his marriage. He refrained from any negative talk of the woman who had bore his children.



But, the truth was that he felt helplessly crushed by this woman who he was married to. The truth is that he had fantasized many times about leaving. The truth is that he knew he could never leave her, because he knew that it would be the most selfish thing he had ever done in his life. The truth is that he did not know how he would ever survive if she thought poorly of him. The truth is that he believed that leaving his wife would mean that he had given up o himself, and he was quite certain that he would die. Their marriage had become the last bastion, the last stronghold of the spritual experience that had brought them together. The man had forsaken the God of his youth, but he was still holding on to the wife of his youth. He was still holding on to the one to whom he had made all the promises, that ironically, he had already broken in his heart. The truth is that he hated her. He hated her the most of anyone in the world. He blamed her. He had a fantasy once about smashing her head in with a lamp. He wrote it down in a, he knows that he did, but to this day the man could not find that journal entry so that he could tear it out and throw it away. The truth is that she disgusted him. The truth is that he was embarassed to be with her. The truth is that he was afraid of her. He feared her argument. He feared her reason. He feared the way she turned him on himself. He hated the way she was always right (and she was). He feared how she made him look at himself. He feared himself as a man. He felt that there journey into feminism combined with her aversion to men made him the enemy. He feared her father, which apparently lived inside of her, the one who had abused her had come to live in her. The man slept with her abuser, her father, nearly every night for twenty years. The man made love to her father every time he slept with the wife. The man felt crushed by her. The man felt abused by her. He would call it gaslighting later, a situation in which the abuser convinces the one who is abused that he/she is insane. The man felt this gaslighting going on even before he had read about what it was. Is this enough honesty? Is this honesty? There is obviously some real pain still here. This is what I got naked for? Holy Shit!



The man bent over and touched his toes, putting his hamstrings on stretch.



This is the pain with which he went to the treatment center in Santa Fe with. These are the things that he never spoke while he was there. And it was all this hate that the man at the treatment center was turning on himself. Just as he had not pounded on the door the night that the dog had smashed his youngest daughter’s head. That night when he wanted to kill the dog. Just as he had not pounded on the door, he also did not speak poorly of his wife.



Two years of couples counseling. That’s how much work they had done together. And all the work that they were both doing for themselves in one on one counseling. All the books that they read as they were seeking their own healing. How could he possibly hate this woman so much?



The man standing in the kitchen facing North was genuinely curious. He had never faced all of this so naked, so cold, yet so unafraid. As Eli scratched on the door time and time again providing him with some comic relief. The cat who went full circle over and over again, out through the garage and in through the back door. “What a cute little guy,” thought the man. Seriously, that’s exactly what he thought. And he laughed as he opened the door for Eli every time.



“maybe this is kind of like therapy,” thought the middle-aged man. “Maybe this story isn’t coming out all at once.”



He turned to sit on the pillows, giving Life another chance to live through him.



He gobbled down two maracino cherries and a bite of lime from the limeade he got at Sonic the night before with his friend, Dan. He hoped Dan didn’t come home as he sat naked in the kitchen. 



This time, he really did turn to sit on the pillows.



Although he had begun the grieving process at the treatment center, when the man’s wife and oldest daughter came to pick him up from Santa Fe, he was still under the assumption that there was a chance to save his marriage. He had come to such a happy state of being in his last two weeks at the treatment center. Surely he could bring this home with him. But he could not. On the three hour ride home, he lay in the back seat of the dodge caravan, thoughts of suicide once again returning. 



But, a mantra formed in the mans heart and went to his mouth. A mantra of hope:



“Maybe there is a future in which I am happy.

Maybe there is a future in which I am happy

Maybe there is a future in which I am happy



He repeated the mantra over and over again as the crushing fear and depression threatened his very life. Just a sliver of hope. The “maybe”. That would have to be enough for now.



The man tried to reengage his life back at home. But, the coldness that he felt from his wife was overwhelming. He walked around the college-cow-town, where the dust had turned the sky red so many years ago, with lightning-flash visions of suicide. He saw himself in a vacant lot blowing his head off just like Brother Jack had done in his song so many years ago. He retrieved his grandfather Vince’s single shot shotgun from the attic. He had no ammunition. He went the the Wal-Mart. He stood in front of the boxes of shotgun shells. He did not know if he had come to just look or if he was there to buy. He was confused. He wasn’t quite sure. But, there he stood, one way or another, perusing ammunition for the shotgun that he’d taken down from the attic in the garage above his wife’s ceramic studio.



His wife’s ceramic studio. That was the best gift that he’d ever bought for her. A Shimpo Whisper wheel, and a Skutt kiln. He was so happy to buy her that gift. There had been good times between them. There had been many many good times. They had loved one another. They had brought beautiful life and love into this world with their children. They had friends. They had common friends with whom they had sat and laughed and explored the mysteries of life. They had some satisfying sex. They had satisfied one another. 



The dying author is now attempting to do the impossible. He is allowing the miracle to happen. He can feel it now. The miracle of holding the suffering and the joy simultaneously. He is remembering that this marriage that is no more was also full of joy and discovery and curiosity, and a ceramic studio where his wife was nurtured by the earth that she formed in her hands. He remembers her joy in the receiving of that gift.



The author recognizes that Life in its fullness is presented to us, and we must learn to accept it all. We must learn to die the death. We must learn to receive the resurection. We must transcend. We must go deeper. We must do these things if we want to be part of the solution. If we want to be a part of the Great Turning.



If we are to be a part of the Great Turning we must start by sending a message to our ex that we know may be returned with less than love and acceptance. The author understood that his calling was to walk in this fullness, holding the joy and the pain together. The author acknowledged his pain as he stood there, his thoracic back was aching and his body struggled to maintain a posture that was conducive to energy flowing through, he had learned this from yoga. He had learned to touch his toes and put his hamstrings on stretch as a practice of presence. He knew that writing, in this moment, had very little to do with writing and everything to do with how to live with himself. The question presented itself again. And for this musician, it was all about tone. Tone and form.



“How will I live with myself?” 

The author took in a deep breath, letting all the energy flow through him. He turned and looked out the window, into the darkness, toward the trees in the backyard, in the direction of the house under construction where the exceptionally strong men had used their shovels and driven the front loader just days ago. The author was doing his work right now. Maintaining form, saying “yes” to this process as he made peace for himself. Also, dear reader, he hoped that he was making some peace for you. Yes, the author had not forgotten of you. In fact, he now drew comfort from your presence. This author who had died some deaths in order to ascend (or descend) the great spiral. The author who had come full circle many times, leaving form behind, and then circling back as he watched the miracle of integration take place. 



The miracle of integration. This is what he was witnessing now as wrote. He was watching the forf arriage become his experience, his strength, and his hope. What he once thought would kill him….well it did actually kill him…He died the death, or maybe he was still dying the death. it’s very difficult sometimes to tell about these things, just when you think it’s over, there may be some more pain to go through. But, there he stood, maintaining form and witnessing this miracle in process, at whatever stage of the process he was in, that was up to Life. He was surrendering to Life. Living Life on life’s terms, as they say in AA.



There was a song that he’d written recently. The lyrics went like this. It was short and simple



The things I’ve seen

The people I’ve known

The deaths I’ve died

The seeds I’ve sown



I give way where way is to be given

I let go, let Life do the livin’





And so it came to pass that Liana called the middle-aged man. She was still at the treatment center. She used her one hour phone time to call the middle-aged man, not once, but twice. And so it went that the second time Liana called, the middle-aged man said “yes” to himself in the best way that he knew to do. Maybe it was that he wasn’t quite ready to leave his wife for himself yet. Maybe he was unable to act on that kind of self-love. Maybe it was that the only way that he knew to leave his wife was to leave for another love.



It had been his dream to fall in love again. He wanted to fall in love with a woman who wanted him. He wanted to fall in love with a passionate woman. He wanted to fall in love with a woman who was interested in penises. He wanted to fall in love with a woman who would call out his name. He wanted a woman like Liana.



And so it was, that the man told Liana that he would not be able to communicate with her for a week. For he knew that the peace that he must make with his current situation needed to be made within himself. For he knew that he really was leaving for himself. He knew that nothing was certain between him and Liana.



And it was in this way that, over the next days the man planned the day and the hour. He planned the moment when he would say goodbye to his wife. 



His youngest two children were involved in a performance of the Addam’s Family musical. Sunday was the final day of the three day run. The man would tell his wife before the show, but after his children had left to put on their makeup.



After the children left for the show the man worked up his nerve to do what he knew he could never do. Finally after two (or was it three) trips around the block he walked inside where his wife was in the living room. He met her face to face and he said these words to her. The man believes that these were the exact words, because he has reminded himself of them many many time since that day:



Man: “I’ve come as far as I can go in this marriage. It’s time for me to learn how to take care of myself.”



Woman: okay well, let’s talk about…



Man: “No.” the man interrupted. “There’s nothing to talk about right now. I’m leaving.”



The musical was absolutely incredible. The man had never seen and probably will never see again a highschool production with such greatness. His son played Gomez and his daughter played pugsley. amazing. Everything went just right. He laughed. He cried. It was definitely better than Cats (the movie that he’d seen recently…the one with the teardrop in her eye and the snot on her lip…that’s for later….it’s a glimpse into something we saw during a journey with the medicine).



Okay…let’s go ahead and try and talk about the teardrop now…I don’t know…I’m exhausted…I think I need a shower…



Thank you, Life for your nudge out of bed this morning. I know that I needed this. 7:05AM






---

# Day 9

8:05 AM



Today, everythin being sacred, I find it much harder to throw things away. I accept this as part of the journey. Now I understand hoarders. They are these people who acknowledge the sacred nature of all matter, and therefore are unwilling to throw things away. Perhaps. Perhaps.

 

If everything goes as planned, in a short while my four children will arrive (Anna, Ethyn, Joseph, and Emma). They say they have a christmas present for me. Sacred matter given from one human to another. I go forth into this world. I have given thanksgiving and Praises to the Almighty in the backyard. I have fed the cats. I have gathered my sacred matter. The car is fueled. The duct tape is in the car. My instruments are packed. I AM. I AM in the first person. The great What-IS. 



Off to meet the Universal Mother.

Off to meet the Universal Father.

Off to travel with the Universal Sons and Daughters.



May God bless our travels

May God fill our sight and hearing.

May God guide our steps and light our way.

May God rise up from within us and all who we meet.

May the Christ be glorified.

May the Christ be known in us.

Please take from us our lives when we have not the strength to give it away to you, Oh God.



And, Oh yes, Dave and Eileen. If everything goes as planned I will see you in Bentonville.

# Day 10 

12: 39AM



The middle aged man, the son, the father sat, facing North once again. Samuel Barber’s Adagio for strings played in his ears, the sacred sound of his resurrection. He sat in his mother’s home, which in the previous hours was filled with the joyful sounds of his growing and grown children, those children who had arrived at his house early that morning bearing gifts, Christmas gifts which they had brought to their father, the man who had walked away from their mutual home just twenty months ago, the man who now lived at the Adobe style house with the saltillo tile in the living room and entry way, the man who now sat facing North on his mother’s couch which had been turned into his bed for tonight.



The adagio having ended, he sat, breathing in the silence. As he read through the first chapters of his draft he was overcome by two things---first, the gravity of the presence of his own being that he felt in the universal story of his life story that was emerged before him and the connectedness to the ALL that he experienced in this witness--and second, the immensity of work that the draft would still require in order to prepare it suitably for you, dear reader. The man got arose from his seat on the couch and moved about the house.



The man repositioned the floor mat in the bathroom. He lowered himself to his knees, assuming a deep kneel. His body was folded, his head partially on the mat, partially on the cold floor tile. He allowed the I AM to be, or rather, he witnessed the I AM, the Being-ness of this consciousness. The man was grateful for this form which, in the past, he had called the water-droplet position, sometimes imagining himself a drop of dew resting on a blade of grass. He was grateful that, as his mind wandered, this pose reminded him of his intention. As he awoke from the wanderings of his mind, the pose reminded him of the potential of simply-being. And this is how it came to be that the man kneeled on the bathroom floor of his mother’s home that Friday evening in all gratefulness for what he had experienced during the course of the day, experiencing the great What-IS.



The gifts that his children brought to him that morning made him very glad. His children stacked the gifts on the kitchen table in the Adobe house on avenue Q. He opened the smallest gift first, as it was at the top of the pyramid. It was small and light. 

“It’s a zippo lighter,” he said jokingly. 

The small package was actually much lighter than a zippo lighter would have been. The father tore the paper and opened the tiny box. What he found inside was a small piece of unusually shaped stained-wood. The small piece of wood had a hole in the middle big enough for his middle finger. This was a minimalist gift, given to him by his son, its purpose--to hold the pages of a book apart as the reader held the book in a single hand. The father, knowing the difficulty of reading in bed while trying to hold open both sides of a book with two hands understood the importance of the gift. And as he sat on his mother’s couch now, turning it over and over in his hands, he was grateful for the gift from his son. He was grateful for its simplicity. He was grateful for its function. He was grateful that his son knew that he loved to read. He accepted the strange gift. He loved his son.



The next gift was housed in a significantly larger box, it was from his youngest daughter. “Oh, I know exactly what this is,” the father said. “But I’m not going to say,” another attempt at a joke. He loved to hear his children laugh. As the lid came off the box, he saw a treasure trove. There was a wood patterned capo, just what he had asked for when his youngest had inquired about what he wanted for Christmas. There was a guitar strap with decorated with golden suns. And, the gift that most impressed the father, held in it’s own cloth bag, a gorgeous leather bound journal, which looked like it was deserving to carry a sacred message. Facing his youngest daughter, the father held the book out in front of him in both hands and bowed. “I present to you the new gospel,” he said in a lofty tone. This time his children actually laughed and the father was well pleased. His youngest daughter had often impressed him with her generosity. He was powerfully moved by her ability to find gifts that mattered to him. He was grateful for her thoughtfulness. He was grateful for her.



The next present, the largest box, had functioned as the base of the Christmas pyramid. The father casually reached out to pick it up but it was very heavy. He repositioned himself so that he could lift the dense package from the table. He tore the paper from the Amazon box which was taped shut. He remembered that his pocket knife was clipped on to his right pocket. He grabbed the pocket knife and flipped it open, as he had learned to do as a young police officer. He cut the tape and opened the box. Inside was something that he had mentioned to his oldest daughter that he wanted while they made the cheesecake to accompany their Christmas taco-Tuesday meal. It was a weighted blanket! The daughter had already, in fact, ordered it for him as they were preparing the meal together. The eldest daughter and her husband were well pleased with themselves, as they should have been. 



Once again, in an attempt to be the cause of his children’s laughter, the father removed the weighted blanket from its packaging and proceded to lie down in a supine position right there on the hard kitchen tile. He pulled the blanket up o his chin, and his children did laugh with their father, and the father was very glad indeed.



The father had truly not expected such thoughtful and generous gifts. And so it came to pass that the family, having completed the exchange of their Christmas gifts piled in their two little blue cars and headed for the home of the children’s grandmother.



The first several hours of the journey were covered by dense fog and light rain. The oldest daughter rode with the father. She mentioned that she had been listening to the Prince of Egypt soundtrack. The father asked her if she would play it. And so it was that the father and his oldest daughter drove East, that day toward Oklahoma City on the same roads that the father had hitchhiked two weeks before, listening to music that contained the story of Moses. And the father heard his own story in these songs. And the father laughed and wept for joy as he saw his story in this universal story. And he heard the depth, and darkness, and mystery in those melodies that day.



The father was able to share the depths of his heart with his daughter that day, and his daughter had a heart to hear her father, and the father was very glad. And the daughter, although she was generally a very quiet person, also shared her heart with her father. And the father felt more known by his daughter. And the father felt that he knew his oldest daughter a little more.



The daughter shared her grief at her father’s timing, for the father had dissolved his own marriage just one month prior to her marriage. The father was able to apologize that he had heard her. He asked her how he could make it right. The daughter said that she was no longer angry, although she had been very angry with the him at the time.



And the family stopped to eat at Subway, all four of them, and they laughed at each other’s ridiculous jokes. It was a hearty laughter that resounded througout the Subway in the gas station somewhere along the foggy highway which lead them East toward the children’s grandmother and their belated Christmas celebration.



After the meal, the son rode with the father. His son spoke quickly and with much energy and in elevated tones, inspired by the life-changing learning experience that he was having at the University in Albuquerque. And, for a time, the son and the father seemed to have a difficult time in relating, because it seemed that the son’s studies had changed his point of view and the common ground that they had shared months ago as the father had visited him seemed to have shifted underneath them. The son, like the father was being folded over in the blueberry batter. He was spiraling upward, leaving form behind him. And the son was able to express that he was concerned for the father’s welfare in his latest decisions to drop his nets and surrender to the flow. The son was honest with the father in saying that he was not ready to go with the flow because he had much to accomplish in life. And the father was able to affirm the young man, and assure him that he was okay right where he was. The father had confidence in his son’s capacity to be true to his Self. The father knew that he would find his own way in his own time. The father assured the son that it was okay that the way things were different between them than they were the last time they had spoken. And the father was able to give his son the blessing that is irrevocable, because the blessing is really just an acknowledgement of that which is already present in the heart of the son. And the father loved his son. And the father did not need the son to be anything to him that he was unable to be. And the father breathed into the present moment. And the father was pleased that his father and his father’s father and all the father’s before him had done there part to get him and his son into this car together today. Praise be to the ancestors as they have empowered us in our journey up the great snake, the one who spirals into the infinite multi-verse.



And so it was that the family arrived at the house of the Universal mother that day. The son and his children parked their cars along the curb of her home on that cloudy, Oklahoma day. And the Universal Mother had prepared for them a great feast. Crackers and cheeses were laid out on the island in her kitchen. Nuts and grapes and candies were also there in the kitchen. The hospitality of the Universal Mother was palpable in all their hearts, and the son gave much thanks for his heart was filled with gratitude, for the joy of the son’s salvation had been restored unto him. It was in this way that the family rejoiced in each other’s presence long into the night.



The Mother had prepared spaghetti, which had been simmering all day, just as she had done long ago, when the son lived with her as a boy, long before the grandchildren were even though of. The Mother made a sacred salad with many textures and flavors and a special dressing. The mother prepared a sourdough bread with butter and garlic which she broiled to a perfect shade of golden brown in her oven. And so it was that she and her husband and the son and all the children sat around the long table that night and laughed and ate until they were full. And the son became very sleepy.



The son, giving thanks to his mother for the meal that she’d prepared, got up from the table --even without excusing himself as his mother had taught him to do, but still with much thanks in his heart) and went over to the couch where he covered himself with the weighted blanket, closed his eyes and allowed himself to fall into a sleep as he listened to the laughing and talking of his family. He rose an hour and rejoined the festivities that were still under way.



The Children were happy, and their laughing and joking continued. There were gifts exchanged. There were trivia games. And there were somersaults. And there were handstands in which sister helped sister. And there was wrestling. And there was tickling. And there were pictures taken and digital video recored by the father who wanted to have something by which to remember this moment.



And then there was a slow settling down that began. Faces were washed and exfoliated. Teeth were brushed. Pajamas were worn. Hugs were given. Smiles were exchanged. Good nights were said. The oldest daughter and her husband retired to their room. The two youngest children retired to theirs. The mother and her husband went to their bed too. And the son was left alone in this sacred space on his mother’s couch, this son who was making peace with a Universe who was out to help him.



And so it came to pass that the writer found himself sitting on the couch, the one who recounted all the joy that had transpired on that twenty-seventh day of December in two-thousand-and-nineteen, that year of our Lord, exactly one year after the middle-aged-man had admitted himself to the hospital and been transported by ambulance to Sunrise Mental Health Hospital in Roswell New Mexico. 



But, on that day in December of two-thousand-and-nineteen the middle-aged-man was not in the hospital. He was well. He was able to communicate to his two oldest children of how he had calmly declared an emergency, the emergency of the failing engines. He was able to describe to his two oldest children how he had seen the field below him, the one he had bought so many years ago. He was able to describe to them how he had calmly piloted the plane, in some kind of controlled landing, to set it down in that very field that he had purchased, the same field that contained the treasure. He was able to explain to his two oldest that he was a disciple of Christ, and that he was no longer able to hold the form that their earthly father had maintained all those years. He was able to describe the sufferings that he had experienced in a way that they seemed to understand on some level, although the father felt somewhat certain that he was not trying to justify himself in any of his actions. He could not know what his children heard when he spoke. He could not truly understand what they saw when they looked at him. But, the father knew how he had come to the place where he was now. He knew exactly how he had arrived in that field, in all truth and in all honesty. 



The prayer that he had prayed at the cabin in the Lincoln National Forest had been answered. The man had seen the joy of his salvation restored. His heart was full of praise and thanksgiving. He was moving in and out of form. He sat now at his mother’s house in the quiet of the night, the children that he had raised and the husband of his daughter were sleeping in their rooms. His mother and her husband were sleeping in theirs. He felt a satisfaction that had little to do with certitude as he sat there with his fingers curled over the home row of his laptop which rested on the weighted blanket, that same gift that he had said that he wanted even after the gift was already on its way to his daughter so that she could wrap it.



He paused frequently. He looked around the room. He placed his hands together, acknowledging the Life that was being lived through him. He placed his thumbs on his forehead. He bowed his head toward his heart. He allowed himself to come back to the I AM. He gave room for Life to have its say through him.



The man was making peace with a Universe that was out to help him. He closed his laptop, acknowledging the North. He placed his laptop on the end table by the couch. He went to the bathroom. He returned to the couch. He turned out the lamp. He pulled his weighted blanket over his body. He lay on his back and closed his eyes, giving thanks, giving praise, acknowledging the One Source. He allowed himself to rest. He allowed himself to be the great I AM.

# Day 10

5:13AM



The single drop of dew rested upon the wide blade of grass in the morning sunlight, the yellow light of the sun seeming to emanate from the drop of dew itself. In perfect stillness of the morning the water droplet sat on the semi-rigid growth which sprung from the earth, rooted in the soil. The drop of dew and the light which appeared to shine from its being rested there, in the coolness of the morning mountain air. A stream gurgled just feet away, a world of moving water cascading down the mountain by way of the inclined earth, all the water, together, eddying in places, carrying sticks, forming froth, tumbling over small water falls, splashing up on the edges of the bank sometimes. 



But the single drop of water which rested on the wide blade of grass was in motion too, inside there was movement that would have been undetectable to the human eye. Inside the single drop, which was maintained only by the surface tension created by the atmoshphere and the water itself. This surface tension is what maintained the rounded form of this single water droplet, while the fluid contained inside this pressure bubble was still in movement. And so this single water droplet sat by the stream of running water. 



Did this water droplet have desire? Did he wish anything? You may wonder, “Did he wish to join the great stream that moved so freely down the mountain? Did this single water droplet wish to join the One-ness of the water in the stream? Did he wish to be free from his sedentary position on the blade of grass? 



Can a water droplet wonder? 

Can a water droplet want?

What was in the heart of this little water droplet?

Maybe we should ask him?



“Little water droplet, my brother!”

“You, with the heart of gold!”

“Little brother! I see the sun shining in your heart.

“I see you sitting on your blade of grass.”

You are not in motion as your brothers are

But I see the movement within you

I see the sun shining from deep within your being

Do you wish to join the one-ness of the flow?

Do you wish to lose yourself in their?

Do you wish to run down the mountain with your brothers

And sisters?



The water droplet responded



“I wish only to the will of my father”

If it pleases him for me to sit here

On this blade of grass

If it pleases him for the morning sun

To shine down upon me

And take me up into the sky

Then I am pleased

If it pleases my father

That I run down the mountain

With my brothers and sisters

Then I am well pleased, my dear friend



“But now, please,” said the tiny drop of water

Who rested in the morning sunlight on the wide blade of grass

“Please, stay with me here for a moment”

“And let us ask for the will of the father.”

“Together we will beseech the father,

To know his will for us today.

Come, sit, my friend

Rest with me for a moment

As the stream flows by over there



And then, the tiny drop, in all its wisdom, prayed.

The tiny drop prayed and waited 

For the tiny drop knew that he was not separate from the stream

The tiny drop knew no alienation in himself

As the sun shined from his center

He knew that his current state of being

Was just for this moment

He knew the story of the thunderhead

He knew that he was the thunder head

He understood the mystery of togetherness

He felt in his very being the joy of his salvation



And so, dear reader, let us sit for a moment

With this wisdom

Let us sit here for a moment with our wise brother

The water drop who knew

That he was no alone

The water droplet who watched the stream

And who was the stream

Come, dear reader, let us sit with our brother

Sit with us here for a moment

Become a water droplet with me

Let us wait for the will of the father.

# Day 10

5:48 AM



A young man sat in his senior English class taught by Mrs Hubbard, a weathered woman who recited the Canterbury tales with deep conviction with twists of her tongue and gutteral conviction. But today they were not studying the Canterbury Tales. Today they read Walt Whitman. And today the boy understood. He saw it there right on the page, a meaning so deep that he was compelled to memorize this line:



“I lean and loaf at my ease, observing a spear of summer grass.”



The single line of Whitman contained all he needed to know that day. The young man was moved, or maybe his constant anxious motion was arrested for a brief moment that day in his senior English class led by the tanned and sun-spotted aging woman. This woman who somehow conveyed her love, her passion for these words as she stood up there facing the class, risking the tying of her tongue and the shedding of her tears. She was a tough old woman, tough enough to watch these children come and go. Tough enough to watch these children fall asleep on their desks, and whisper to one another about who-knows-what while she stood up there in front of them, a willing vessel herself, willing to share the un-sharable to a bunch of dazed and confused seventeen and eighteen year olds.



And so it came to pass that the middle-aged man came to remember his old friend Walt, and his old teacher Mrs. Hubbard. “How long ago had that been,” the man asked himself. He counted the years. “over twenty seven years ago now,” he thought. “twenty-seven years.”



There was a stirring in his mothers house. He heard the voice of his youngest daughter. He heard the bathroom door open, and the toilet flush. He held the silence of this moment like a treasure. He felt each breath like the last kiss. 



He woke up this morning with Tim on his mind. He wondered if he’d be welcomed in his home. He wondered if he could stand in the presence of the older prophet, his old mentor and teacher that the middle-aged man had called during his second journey with the medicine, the one he’d called Chief, the distress call before the distress call that opened this story.



The middle-aged-man had reached out to Tim with minimal response. He’d called him, “how many times,” the writer wondered, “was it once or twice? # Day 10 

10:20



And so it went that as Lived its way through the man that morning that he sang many songs with and for his children. He sang for his mother. He sang for his son-in-law. He shared with his son in law the message of the serpent, the spiral dynamic. 



Who is the enemy?

Satan?

Love your enemy?

Love Satan?



Yes, son. That is where we find ourselves, in this impossible situation.



And he rejoiced in his mother’s Christmas Cactus and in her african violets which flowered purple. 



He shared with his son-in-law the secrets of Rumi and Hafiz and their whirling dervish, the passionate love affair that they shared with the Creator and the Creation, all in one and one is all. 



So it was that he waited patiently for the return of the text that might never come. So it was that he acknowledged his own insecurities around the man whom he had once called his father in the Spirit. His teacher. His mentor, His spiritual father. So it was that he prepared himself for the sacred breaking of the heart, and so it was that he communed with God as he had extended his friendship, once again to this man who may or may not be interested or willing to meet with him.



The truth was that Tim had never done anything to hurt the middle-aged-man. Whenever the man showed up at one of Tim’s meetings just months ago, Tim had immediately invited him to participate in his ceremony, asking the man to retrieve his guitar from his car. So what was this fear that the man was facing around his old friend, Tim and his family.



The middle-aged man had often feared, in the last ten years of his absence from Tim, that he had been an unholy influence on his family, that he had brought something unwelcome into his home. The man feared that he was unacceptable in the eyes of Tim’s God. The man feared that he was feared by Tim and his family, or he feared that as Tim knew about the man’s association with the medicine, that somehow Tim had disqualified him from participation in Tim’s form. These are some of the fears that the middle-aged man was aware of in his being. These are the fears that the man faced as he sat, facing North into the gas fire, sitting on the couch which was his bed in his mothers bed, making the clicking of keyboard sounds, the sound that once belonged to his wife.



The man found himself at a crossroads in his thoughts about Tim. “Will he accept me or reject me?” thought the man. What does a man do when his very name is the signifier (am I using that word right? That’s a word that he had learned from his wife as she became a philosopher of literature) of the crossroads. Was that correct what the man was not witnessing in himself? Was it true that he was the one who stands at the crossroads? Years ago, on a national guard trip, he had been at a mall where he there was a man selling bookmarks with names and their meanings. He remembered now that his name had meant “at the crossroads”. 



What is the function of the man who stands at the crossroads? What had the man learned about this recently? Wasn’t this a thread throughout his recent recorded experiences? Experiencing the BOTH /AND. This is what the Spirit had been showing him to experience when he found himself standing at the fork in the road, presented with the binary. Maybe this wasn’t about acceptance or rejection from Tim. Maybe it was about something different. Maybe it was BOTH/AND. 



What had Christ done when faced with the ultimate rejection that lead to his death? When the christ was nailed to the crossroads, what had happened. He took it all in. All the pain and suffering he took in. 



“Am I ready to accept rejection from this man who was once a father to me. Am I ready to be corrected by this man? Am I ready to take that in? What about acceptance from Tim? Are yo ready for that? The man looked back at his work. His through-line was stretching thin. Would it snap? That’s always a possibility. Some of these deaths that we die go so deep that they blind us. 



The writer’s phone rang in his pocket. He stood up from his sitting position on the couch in his mother’s living room and reached in his left pocket to retrieve his phone. It was a California number. It was Dave Workman, of muse harbor publishing. The middle-aged-man briefly shared the joy of his current experience with Dave—the joy he was having with his children and his mother, and the joy he was experiencing as he was exploring his writing. Dave was going to a princess palace to attend his grandaughter’s birthday party. They agreed to meet on the square in Bentonville to discuss whatever it was that was happening between them. The middle-aged man held it all loosely, letting go of the outcome, a practice he was very familiar with.



As he sat in front of a laptop, he heard his phone announce a text message. He wondered if it was Tim. He wondered how long he would wait to see where the message had come from. Was it Tim? Did it matter? What was it that hung in the balance here? He was not sure. The man was out in the world making himself available, trying to participate in the resurrection that was taking place in his life. The man was out there in the world, learning how to move at the speed of life. He was learning how to say “yes” to what was available. He was learning how to accept. He was learning how to risk, in just the way that he had risked when he saved his life by leaving home twenty months ago.



The man avoided his phone, not out of dread, but because he was actually enjoying this suspense. He was immersed in this story. He was also observing this story. It really mattered to him, how this interaction with Tim went. It really mattered to him how his interaction with Dave and Eileen in Bentonville went. It really mattered to him how the lunch with his father went. Life was out to help him, but that did not mean that he would not suffer. That did not mean that he would not have doors closed in his face. That did not mean that he would not have to deal with hurt feelings. That did not mean that everything would go his way. It simply meant that Life was there, ready to help him through the ups and downs. Life was there, ready to help him accept himself through whatever came. Life was creative, loving, kind, and incredibly intelligent, and he was saying “yes” to life living through him. Yes, he was curious about the text that had arrived minutes ago. 



He felt into his body. He made peace with the What-Is. He imagined that Schroedinger’s cat was over ther in the form of a text message. He asked his brainy son about Schroedinger’s cat. Strangely enough his son did not know. That was strange since his son seemed to know about most things. The man knew that there was a cat in a box. And whether that cat was dead or alive depended on something. And he knew that the cat in Schroedingers’ box was somehow both dead and alive until the box was opened. That was the extent of the knowledge the man had about Schroedinger’s cat. He hoped it was enough.



Right now, the message that the man assumed was from Tim was stored in the hard drive on the man’s phone. That message contained some kind of information. The message was a response to a request that the man made. The response was either in the negative or in the positive. But maybe it wasn’t Tim’s response that determined the man’s future. “Of course,” thought the man to himself, “That seems to be obvious.” But was it obvious, wrote the writer. Yes, it was obvious to the intellect, but how familiar with this was the man’s heart? 



The time for discussing this was coming to a close. The man knew how to live life, or rather, he knew that was committed to having life lived through him. There was no amount of preparing for the worst that he could do which could stop him from hurting if is friend rejected him. And there was no certainty that the man would not experience rejection in one form or another even if his friend’s response was in the positive. There were so many opportunities for the man to experience rejection and suffering along the path that he had chosen. He would be knocking on doors and fishing for men the rest of his life. He would trust that life was taking care of him.



The man’s oldest daughter sat down on the leather chair across the room. She looked lovely. “Are we ready?” she said. “I need just another couple of minutes said the man.” He was going out shopping with his family. The man closed his lap top, acknowledged the One-ness by bowing his head toward his heart, and he walked across the room to retrieve his phone.

# Day 10

9:38PM



The writer sat in a reclining chair in one corner of the living room. 



The dying author fell asleep in the chair in the corner of the room.



The dying author woke up in the chair in the living room of his mother’s home



As he woke, groggy in the chair, the dying author was aware of the shower shoes that had kept him from coming in contact with the floor that day when Drill Sgt Hilliard had yelled at the soldiers in the shower. The shower shoes were the only thing between him and the tile floor as Drill Sergeant Hilliard screamed at the young men in the shower that day in Late May of 1996. That thin layer of spongy rubber, the only thing between him and the floor.



The weighted blanket held the dying author as he sat in the chair in the living room by the large window with the view to his mother’s backyard. The back yard was dark. It was night. A deep exhaustion had come over the dying author. He was scheduled to meet with Dave and Eileen tomorrow.



Tim had finally texted him later in the day, the text he’d thought was him earlier had been someone else.



The dying author was unable to form complete thoughts as he lay reclined in the chair in the corner of his mother’s living room by the window with the view of his mother’s back yard. He had just woke from his second nap of the evening and still, exhaustion was all that he felt. 



The author bought two bibles earlier in the day. He had them engraved with gold names, one for his mother, and one for his Self. It was a miracle of spiral dynamics that he had bought a bible for himself as he could never have imagined that he would ever buy another bible again in his life. The college football game played in the next room



There was a beautiful young man with long flowing hair playing quarter back for one of the teams. They kept showing studio pictures of him holding a football with his long hair and smile. He was a gorgeous young man. The dying author’s youngest daugher said, “He looks like a lion, Dad. That man looks like a lion.” The writer agreed. He did look like a Lion, like a gorgeous lion. The middle-aged-man wondered how a young man could look so much like a football player, and so much like a beautiful woman, and so much like a Lion at the same time.



His friend Tim was sick, but he said, “I look forward to seeing you…” The middle-aged-man wondered about his insecurities surrounding his friend Tim.



An old friend from highschool called the middle-aged-man in response to a text he’d sent. It was the leader of the young man’s band from highschool. They made tentative plans to get together on Monday. 



The writer’s son had just completed a course entitled the Legacy of Darwin’s great idea in his first semester at University. As a result, Darwin and Richard Dawkins were very present in much of the conversation that evening. The writer’s mother got out her copy of The Selfish Gene. She had written a paper over the book in her studies for her master’s degree. The writer’s son and his mother talked intensely of evolution. Intensely was just about the only way that his son ever talked, which reminded him a lot of himself.



The writer saw his mother in a different light that evening. He saw a facet of his mother that he’d never been aware of. She was educated in a way that he’d not understood. She held space gracefully with the intelligent young man, the writer’s son. She was the Universal Glow. They had once called her G-Lo, short for grandma Lorri, and a parody of J-Lo (Jennifer Lopez). But today, the writer had seen her as the “Glow”. And now the “Universal Glow.”



The writer had no through-line tonight. He felt unable to sense a flow.



He longed for the football game in the next room to end and for silence to fall upon the house. In that moment, he longed for the silence and the focus that he found at the adobe house.



The middle-aged-man called his friend Dan. He found himself held in their friendship, in the common language of the restoration that had been occurring in their lives. The two friends encouraged one another as they gave thanks for the miracles that they were each witnessing in and around their own lives and the miracles that they were seeing because of one another. They acknowledged the presence of God in their midst. They acknowledged the weave, the fabric of the cosmos that held them. And the man was grateful for his friend in this way. 



The man shared with Dan how he had bought a bible for himself and for his mother that day, a miracle of the great snake which spirals upward, the spiral dynamics, the DNA of human consciousness which moves, ever outward into the great multiverse. Today the man was able to say, “Thank you, Jesus,” a truly strange miracle in the life of a man who had forsaken that name years and years ago (just as Petra had) as he understood that the man from Nazareth was never called Jesus (It was something more like Yeshua). But, that morning, as the man spoke those words, “thank you, Jesus,” there was a simple acknowledgement of his own roots, a nod toward his place of material origin, a nod toward the form which had first held his conscious recognition of the Christ, the form that he would walk away from in order to find an all inclusive Cosmic Christ.



The man gave thanks for the Universal Mother, Maryanne Fite, who had said yes to him and his family all those years and years ago as they were buying that field, the field which the pilot had set that plane down in. He set that plane down, the one with the failing engines. He set down in the field that he had recognized as the one he had purchased all those years ago. He and his young family poured those Sonic drinks out onto the winter wheat which had been planted by the young man and his father-in-law. The family of 3 stood in the field of winter wheat. The young family who loved one another so much. The young family who would soon be 5. 5 would be their count. The husband and wife would hold that form for enough time for the children could grow up. And then the husband and wife would let go of that form in order that new form could be born. They would experience a death and a resurrection. 



Thanks be to the God of our youth. Praise be to the Snake, the one who deceives us all that we may experience life. Praise be to the one who deceives, our enemy, whom we love. Dare I say, Praise be to Satan? Praise be to God. Praise be to the Source. Praise be to the Christ who is the ALL and every Thing. In Christ there is no Holy or Profane, all is the Sacred. All is the miracle. There is no matter or non-matter that is held together without the All. Praise the all inclusive. Give thanks for the theosis, the realization of the One-ness in ourselves. Praise be to the Poet who speaks forth that which is not as though it was. Praise be to the Wios, the One who walks the earth.



The middle-aged-man had a sense that he needed to ask Tim about the Wios. He googled the word but found nothing. The man remembered Tim, years ago, talking about the Wios (the mature son who walks the earth).



The house was quiet now. It was 11:46PM on Saturday night. He had finally made it to Oklahoma City, the pilgrimage that had started some time ago now when he put on his backpack, made a cardboard sign, strapped a mandolin to his pack, put on his yellow elk skin glove, and walked out of the college-cow-town by the strength of his own two legs and back.



He sat in the stillness, breathing it in. # Day 11
