The writer awoke with a start just minutes ago. He awoke from a dream that he did not know now. The writer paused now, closing his eyes and waiting for the power of the dream to aprehend him. “The writer paused now,” The writer repeated to himself, for it was in this sentence, “The writer paused now,” that he detected the Great Turning, or the Great Folding Over which he had first experienced in the blueberry batter, and which he had more recently became familiar with when he had consumed the large dosage of the medicine on Christmas day. And this is the great turning to which he had awoke with a start when he heard the bathroom door close just a few minutes ago now. “There it was again,” thought the author, “The place where the past meets the present…or…where the past becomes the present?” 



The writer paused now.



A statement in the past tense which contained the present.



This reminded him of the Course In Miracles lesson that he’d read and practiced last night just before he went to sleep. “Let’s see, what was the lesson?” wrote the writer. He bent over, reached down into the space between the couch and the coffee table to retrieve the thick blue book.



Lesson 9: “I see nothing as it is now.”

Lesson 8: “My mind is preoccupied with past thoughts.”

Lesson 7: “I see only the past.”



The writer was reminded that by the time the light from the lamp on the endstand reflected off the objects around him, travelled to his eyes, and was then processed and interpreted by his nervous system, there was a certain fraction of a second that had passed, so what it was that he thought he was seeing was actually the past. The writer did not remember where this thought had come from, but it had been taught to him one time. The lesson had been taught to him one time in the past. The lesson was taught in the past, that place in which he percieved himself to live, apparently. 



The writer wrote now.



The writer, by his very nature was the observer who commented on the past, no matter how infinetly close he may appear to himself to be in the present moment. “infinitely close,” repeated the writer to himself. This reminded him of a few lines of a Rumi poem he’d read last night. He remembered that the poem was on page seventy-two and seventy-three of the book that he’d purchased yesterday while shopping with his children. He now found his hand on the book which was in the past.



I do not see this book as it is now.

I do not see these hands as they are now.

I do not observe these thoughts as they are now.



This writer—the dying author-- commented on the present which he could not ever quite be a part of. Even when he was not writing, how close could this one who is observing come to the present? Was the observer in the present moment? Was this the whole purpose of the teachings of the Buddha? Was this the purpose of the the Vipassana practice? Was this why the writer now instinctively paused with his fingers hovering over home row, allowing the present to butt right up to the documentation of what he was trying to communicate? The writer now paused, his hand on the Rumi book. He grasped the book, this sacred form which the annointed one had apparently not written while he was here (How could the One who is a parable write the book? The One who is the parable is the one who is written of, yes? The Parable is the one around whom the legends are made, the One around whom the myths are told, the One story of which Joseph Campbell and Carl Jung built there lives around. Can the parable write of itself.) The writer finally brought the book to his own eyes after he reached over to the coffee table to retrieve the gift of his only Son, the uniquely crafted piece of stained wood with which he could hold a book open with one hand.



“…The moon has opened its face

And its wings made of light.



Borrow eyes to see this,

If yours cannot.



Night and day and arrow comes toward you

From a hidden bow.”

Rumi (translation Barks)



The writer, once again referred to the past with the intention of bringing you, dear reader, into this present moment, Just as his Algebra 2 instructor Mr. Watters (his fluid brother) had done for him so many years ago as he traced the infinity symbol, over and over again (as the infinity symbol invites) with a fine dry-erase marker on the overhead projector. The overhead projector fan droned on, the drone which invites accompaniement. The man—this teacher—this teacher of the infinity symbol, taught the form and structure of Algebra while often referring back to this infinity symbol which he traced on the overhead projector, right there for all to see. “Was this an act of subversion,” the writer now wondered. This man-of-water, tracing the infinity symbol, opening up the hidden universe for his students in this public school setting. In a dystopian parallel universe, the thought police might have violently pushed open the door, come in and swept Mr. Watters from the room, taking pictures of the convicting evidence before they left—this obvious attempt to infilitrate and infect the minds of the children under his charge—this infinity symbol still wet with the mark of this thin dry-erase marker which had been purchased with state funding with the exclusive purpose of teaching Algebra 2. The Juniors would have sat stunned as a replacement teacher came in, quick on the heels of the removal of the excessively fluid Watters. The highschool students would not have even taken too much notice as the infinity symbol was erased forever from the overhead projector, and Mr Watters was never seen again.



It was this Mr. Watters, the writer’s algebra 2 teacher who had also introduced him to theis proverbial arrow which, in approaching its target by half the distance every time, is never actually capable of reaching its mark—the same arrow that Rumi had just referred to—this arrow that “night and day comes toward you from a hidden bow.”



The writer now classified this memory of Watters among that of his Mother (The Universal Glow) as she taught him to fold the blueberries into the mixture. These are the examples through which this Universal Man had witnessed the Great Turning, The Great Learning, The Great Folding Over, the way by which we evolve, or move forward as a species—the view of reality by which we can never actually be classied as a species. Thank you, Mr Darwin. Spiral Dynamics: this way of looking at a species as a transmuting expression of consciousness, the same way that Ed, the Marxist, had shown him to see the thunderhead, that which we have reified (and the reified beans which Ed so subtly called our attention to, our neighbors who lived South of the border. Those neighbors which we knew no other way to relate other than objectification, or alienation. Thank you, Mr. Marx).



And it was the dream of this Great Turning that the sound from the bathroom door had awoken the man from at approximately 3AM that morning. This was the dream that the man feared that his consciousness would never return from on that Christmas morning when he had become an infant and longed for nourishment from a thumb--the Universal Thumb of this Universal Man who was now engaged in writing his own story from the Universal perspective of the Cosmic Christ. This author who was now so nobly engaged in this process of death and resurretion. This writer who now tried to answer the Universal-Calling of His-Life. The One who spoke in Parables. The One who was The Parable. The Parable that chose not to write itself, but chose rather, to show itself in its willingness to die for the sake of its own awakening. The parable that showed the way to the eternal by showing itself in the life of Watters, the life of the Mother, in the life and death and folding in of the blueberries which provide sustenance to the evolving consciousness of the Universal Human Being, that which knows no gender, no male or female. Praise be to the One Watters! Praise be to the one who stood in front of us all, tracing the infinity symbol with the fine drye-erase marker! Praise be to the Universal Fan which drones, an invitation to join the One Music. Praise be to the Universal Author who sits cross-legged on the Mother’s couch, fingers curled over home row, breathing in in effort to bring the present moment as close to these words as possible. Praise be to the invisible One Source from which we all flow. Praise be to the God who is available for the making of Love. Praise be to the hands that crafted the Great Mandolin and the Ude and all the stringed instruments from which our hearts are awakened to the Great Potential of Life. Praise be the ears that hear the Great Sound. Praise be to the birds, and to the sun, and to the sky in which they rest. Praise be to the Breath which is breathed by the ever expanding and contracting Univers. World without end, Amen. Amen.



Selah



The man writhed slightly in his seat, allowing the Great Sister Serpent, the Kundaline Serpent to make her way up through his Chakras. He said yes the the Great Turning of the wheels of those Chakras within his being. He said “yes” to the beauty of the female snake who had made an invitation to him on that Christmas morning, these memories that had faded from him so quickly as he tried to save his life from a death of which he was convinced was inevitably coming as the light faded from soft yellow to a dull green, a death which the man had backed away from, the edge from which the man had prayed he could return to the middle of the platform on which his life so precariously rested. 



And then there was his son-in-law, this beautiful being who rested right here with him in this very home from which the writer now channeled these Universal Messages. The Son-in-Law, this beautiful being who was now saying “yes” to his own being. The Son-In-Law whom the Father had blessed yesterday with that irrevocable blessing, the blessing which gives its approval in the acknowledgment of the life that is seen within. The blessing which cannot be taken because it is never given. The blessing that simply awakens the being to his being-ness. The blessing that is the I AM. The blessing that merely points this one to THE ONE. The beautiful son-in-law who would inherit the rising spirit of the times within himself, the convergent evolution of the Being arising from within himself.



The middle-aged-man was honored to have received the gift of Presence from his children this weekend, the truest Christmas present of all, the gift of Presence—the Presence that delivers us from all sin. 



The father had spoken with and heard from each of his children this weekend, including his Son-In-Law, and the father was well pleased in this gift. The father sat on his Mother’s couch, fingers curled over home row, once again a with-ness to this miracle of creation. Once again, the man said “yes” to the universal. Once again, the man said “yes” to that Which-Is flowing through him. Praise Be to the Great I AM. Praise be to What-Is.

I watched a moth last night, Dave. It's wing dust was smeared all over my blanket. I'm sure that I must have crushed him. I watched this moth in his dying moments. I witnessed his death.

He reached out with a quivering antenna. then he began moving, very slowly, up the canyon of this soft red blanket. He moved almost imperceptibly slow. I knew that I could not leave him. Exquisite Stillness



exquisite—extremely beautiful and delicate. highly sensitive and discriminating.



My father is a very fearful man. Of course, he would never admit it. But his fear has eroded a deeply grooved path in his being. Like water which runs through a canyon, my father has no choice but to follow the course that fear has carved through the terrain of his inner person.

My father has never learned that he is not exactly like his thoughts. He is completely identified with every thought and emotion that he experiences. That’s why he is so easily offended. If his thoughts or emotions are challenged he has no choice but to become defensive and angry.

My father suffers deeply. But he has hidden his suffering so well from himself that he cannot understand why he feels the way he does. Because he cannot ease his own suffering he must blame people and circumstances for the way he feels. 

Just last year I asked my father to come and help me. I was going through a difficult time with a recent divorce. My kids weren’t speaking to me. I was plagued by suicidal thoughts. My father was very helpful. He helped me to make the home where I was staying livable. When I asked him for money that he didn’t have, he became very angry, telling me, “You are the reason that I am a bitter old man. I have dreamed of putting a bullet in your head. And I have dreamed of putting a bullet also in the head of your mother.” His eyes were red and tearful and full of rage as he pointed his finger at me from across the table. Although I was also suffering, I was able to ask him to forgive me for the pain that I had caused him.

My father does not have friends. He told me that he has intentionally pushed people out of his life and that he experiences satisfaction when his birthday passes and no one acknowledges him. He has also told me that he is hurt when no one acknowledges his birthday. He has said both things to me. I think I understand how both can exist in separate moments.

It is difficult for me to relate to my father. I know that if I challenge his thoughts and emotions there will be conflict. It seems that merely presenting my own experience challenges him, so I often just let him talk and talk about the way he sees the world, knowing that it will be easier if I just stay quiet.



I am beginning to see how I too, have lived in fear. I am beginning to see how my suffering has injured others. I am beginning to learn how to give myself the compassion needed to allow my fearful thoughts and emotions to dissolve. I am no longer blaming people and circumstances for my own suffering. Now I hope to stop blaming myself and find an entirely new option.



When I was four years old I watched the movie Jaws. The ocean, I understood, is where fear resides. But that’s not really how it is. Fear resides in my own mind. The ocean is just the ocean and sharks are just sharks. I understand now that there is some remote possibility that if I go into the ocean that a shark might eat me. But if I allow my fear to dictate where I go and what I do, then I may never go into the ocean and play in the waves.

When my children were young, we took them to the ocean for kayaking. I and my oldest daughter, Anna, became seasick. Our guide, Max, suggested that we jump in the cool water to relieve our nausea. I felt sure that as soon as I jumped in the ocean that I would be eaten by a shark, but I jumped in anyway, and so did my daughter. I did not want to pass on my fear to her.



This weekend I went on a solo backpacking adventure in the Pecos Wilderness of New Mexico. As I was signing the trail register, I noticed someone had written a warning about cougars. “Stay together!” they wrote. I was by myself. There was no one to stay together with. As I set out on the trail I felt like prey, scanning the mountain above and below for movements of large cats.

After seven exhausting hours on the trail, I pitched my tent, made myself dinner, and built a large fire. The crackling warmth of the flames made me feel safe and secure. It was the first time I had ever been in the wilderness all by myself. I went to sleep watching the campfire from the tent. Two hours later I awoke suddenly. The fire was out. It was dark. There was a mysterious clicking sound close to my camp. I was terrified.

I lay there for some time, hoping that I could fall back to sleep, but I could not. I finally sat up in the tent as straight as I could. I listened to the strange clicking sound. A light rain began to fall on my small tent. The sound of the raindrops hitting the tent just inches from my head was unpleasant. I startled with fear when the logs in the fire shifted suddenly. My brain started inventing other reasons to be fearful, but panic was not an option. I was miles from anyone or anywhere. No cell reception. No help. no comfort.

I recalled my meditative practice and then I calmly prayed. I focused my attention on my breath. I realized that no matter how unpleasant the sound of the rain was, I could not change that. I accepted that I was vulnerable and alone in a dark forest with only a thin layer of fabric between me and the wild. I had no control over any of this. The only thing I had any chance to control was my response to fear.

Eventually the rain stopped. I recalled something I had read earlier that day from Pema Chodron. She had encouraged me to move toward my difficulties instead of trying to push them away. I wondered, “What if I get out of this tent and just sit outside in the dark?” I allowed myself some room to make friends with this idea. Part of me was resistant, but another part of me thought that that might be okay. Minutes passed. As I opened the tent, the sound of the zipper seemed to echo throughout the canyon. I found my sandals and then I sat again, waiting for the courage to go out into the dark, closer to whatever threats, real or imagined, might await me. As I finally emerged I could see the outlines of large rocks and trees. I sat on a large stone by the extinguished campfire. I could still feel some warmth emanating from the darkened coals.

As I stared into the dark forest, I allowed myself to become aware of my breathing. Thoughts came and went. I imagined a sudden piercing howl. I imagined that Golem was creeping around on the rocks just outside my camp. I imagined that a large cougar was stalking me, skulking down the mountain in preparation to attack. But, every time a thought came I allowed myself to return to the stillness that was all around me. I told myself, “none of these imaginations are actually happening.” What was happening in my surroundings was stillness. The mysterious clicking had stopped. The rain had ceased. There was absolutely no wind. I was in the middle of a profoundly still forest. Exquisite stillness.

When I allowed the stillness between my thoughts to align with the stillness of the Pecos Wilderness there was harmony. Stillness within. Stillness without. As the fears came I understood that I had a choice. I could allow my mind to entertain fear, but then I would be missing what was really going on. So I just kept coming back to the stillness, and when I did that, there was no fear. I had no control over what might happen in the next moment. But that was really none of my business. I was much more concerned with what was actually happening, this Exquisite Stillness. I was eventually able to return to my sleeping bag. I slept until the sun rose.



Hiking down the mountain is often much easier than hiking up. Me and my son Joseph have hiked together a number of times. He likes to consider all that potential energy that we store up in our bodies as we are hiking up the mountain which is now being converted into kinetic energy as we make our way down. 

I made my way down the mountain to my little blue Toyota with a cracked windshield. Still sensing the release of this kinetic energy as I drove home from my solo backpack adventure, I called my father. I wanted to talk to him about how I had felt in my role as potential cougar food, because I knew he would understand. He loves to think about the terrors of being eaten alive. Our conversation was the impetus for the words you are now reading.

I have lived for most of my adult life powerless to control how I respond to fear. My fears were so deeply imbedded that I didn’t even understand that they were fears. I participated in psychotherapy; I joined churches; I prayed; I had demons cast out of me; I went to AA meetings; I exercised; I studied; I tried to be a loving person; I became an atheist; I meditated; I became a feminist; I had intelligent and caring friends; I listened to my wife; I went back to school and got a better job; I played music; I got standing ovations; I did so many things to try to fix myself, but fear continued to dictate how I perceived the world. Even when the forest was still, my brain was inventing fears.

I want to be careful here that I don’t sound like I have the answer, but if I am truthful, I feel like I do. I will try to explain. Today the answer for me is acceptance of what-is, and confidence that a power greater than myself is able and willing to restore me to sanity. When I am in the dark forest all by myself and my brain is inventing a half dozen reasons that I should be scared, I now know that I am not obligated to follow these story lines. If I am willing to look inward toward this Exquisite Stillness, I can experience a profound shift in my perception, a miracle of perception change. Today I am willing to experience a deeper Reality than I was able to conjure for myself. If I allow it, this deeper Reality will flow from within me. A well has been unstopped that I had allowed to be clogged by all of my fearful suffering.

All of those things I said about my father, those things are true about me too. And if that is the reality that I choose, I render myself powerless, bound to my fearful story lines. 

No matter how hard I tried, I could not think myself out of my inherited mental illness. But today something has changed. Today I have a reprieve from my insanity. Today I am focused on this Exquisite Stillness.



…And so the first story of the mountain was told by the middle-aged-man, the story of the Exquisite stillness. This was the story of a man who had been trying to make peace with his father for a lifetime, and the story of a father who had also been trying to make peace with his son.



And this is how the writer, the one who was sitting at his mother’s home in Oklahoma City, came to witness again the long journey up the mountain that he had been making over the previous year. For it had been three-hundred-and-sixty-seven days since he had driven his little blue toyota, the one with the severely cracked windshield, to the Emergency room instead of going to work on that December day. It was just over a year since the middle-aged-man found himself walking the circular hallway of the psychiatric unit in Roswell, New Mexico where he had received the prayer of restoration from the One called Clinton (that Universal Crossroads), the gay black man who had interceded on behalf of the man, the man who had just had another cavity search, the one who had just prayed, “God, please help me.”



But there is still another mountain story to be told, dear reader. And the dying author is very much looking forward to the possibility of sharing that story with you. The story of how a man flew up a mountain with a feather and was rocked in the arms of a an evergreen.

# Day 11

8:03 AM



It was time for the man to travel again



And so it came to pass that the writer prepared for his journey to Bentonville, Arkansas to meet with his two new publisher friends. And Vincent, our dear Mr. Van Gogh truly did make peace with the world, and he passed it down to his brothers and sister in this way.



It was with deep trust and affection for all that is that the writer, somewhat hesitantly left his joyful family that morning. He left them in Love. He left them with thanksgiving in his heart.



Amen and Selah.



The windshield of the man’s little blue Toyota was iced over. He needed a tool. He started the engine, turned the heat on high defrost, and picked up Dickey Lee Erwin’s CD case from the middle console. CD cases can make good ice scrapers when its not too cold and the ice is not too thick. The process did not take all that long. He used the neighbors driveway for a turn-around. As he passed house after house in his mother’s comfortable neighborhood, he was reminded of the mandolin that he left behind. His guitar was with him, but his mandolin was not. He turned the car around, as a prayer of willingness to listen, He parked the blue toyota in his mother’s driveway, went inside, grabbed the mandolin, said another short goodbye to his family, then passed over the threshold of his mother’s home again. 



He found the Rucker Brother’s CD, the album that he had written and produced with his old friend from music school back in 2006. The album spoke to him of hope, his friends last name, Matthew Hope. He praised the Spirit of Music which chose to flow so freely through his friends hands in the album they had created together. His friend was truly a conduit, some might say a genius. 



The album played out. The middle-aged-man called his friend Matt. No answer. Voicemail not setup. The man texted his friend Chris with an invitation to call him. No response. The man continued the journey on his own, giving praise for the sense of purpose that he felt in his being, giving thanks for the clarity in his mind and soul, giving thanks for death and the resurrection that he knew in his being, He picked up his phone and accessed its audio-recording app. He raised the phone to his lips.



The man traveller spoke these words that day as he scooted down the Oklahoma turnpikes in his little blue toyota, stopping to pay the tolls along the way. There was something about the name of the traveller that had to do with paying a toll or keeping a gate or existing at the crossroads.



 “I pray that God would keep me rooted, right here in this moment, moving at the speed of life. Gratefulness in this heart. Thanksgiving on these lips. Peace. Peace. Peace to you, my dear reader.”



Maybe following life is like foraging as a hunter gatherer—seeing the nuts and the berries, or following the herd of animals as they migrate. Maybe it’s more like than than obeying a command. It makes more sense to me that it would be like that.



The writer, the middle aged man, the dying author held his phone close to his face and spoke into the audio recording app reveling in the idea of his words being captured in real time as he drove down the road. He passed a sign for Braums where he worked as a soda jerk in his twenties after selling all he had to buy that field. He tapped his brakes, taking his little blue toyota out of cruise control in order to stay with the flow of traffic, in order to stay moving at the speed of life. He was on interstate 244 East heading toward downtown Tulsa. 



Tusla OK, the city in which he and his now ex wife had spent their first married evening. He took the Joplin exit where the road forked (he laughed) and he was reminded of the binary. Yet, in that moment his forward motion did not cease, for he did not wish to cause a traffic accident. His GPS told him that he had sixty five more miles to go til his next fork in the road.



He passed the bartlesville exit. Bartlesville, that town where one of his old friends was from. Kevin, the gifted guitar player that he had made much music with so many years ago in those early year of his marriage. Kevin, the friend who had called him with correction in his heart as the hitchhiker sat at Denny’s. Kevin the man who had spent six years in prison. Six soul crushing years in a federal prison. When kevin’s voice arrived over the cell phone as the man sat at Denny’s the man created space between as graciously and as kindly as possible, simply saying, “with all love and respect, I’m going to hang up the phone now.” He had not heard from him since, nor had he tried to contact him.



The man took a moment to make his heart right toward his old friend. The man took this moment to allow this miracle to happen as he drove through downtown Tulsa, the place where he and his wife had spent their first married night. But today, the man felt his own company, and it was good company. And the man felt the company of you, dear reader, as he drove on those elevated interstates, fifty-eight miles now to the next fork in the road. He marvelled at the joy that was in his heart. This pure, simple, clean, light-hearted experience. He knew that if a word search was done on this manuscript, that the word “experience” would certainly be the most used. “That’s appropriate,” thought the man, “Considering where I came from. Considering that album made by that twenty-something year old man who’d asked him that question, “Are You Experienced.” The traveller laughed out loud at eighty miles per hour.



That fourteen year old boy took that question into his heart. That fourteen year old boy took that album into his heart. He took that creation into his heart. And it was his own creation that he’d made with his old college friend, Matt Hope, that the man took into his heart at the beginning of his journey to Bentonville Arkansas. With fifty four miles to go to the next fork, he breathed in the joy of life. He breathed in all of these connections that he was sensing. He rested in the weave of life, as he travelled at the speed of that life. That’s one of the things he had seen the first time he took the medicine. He saw the fabric of being. He saw the fabric of community. And he saw himself supported in that fabric.



Ther was still the potential for fear in the man’s heart. He felt some, just then, with fifty one miles to the next fork. He felt the fear in his heart. Fea that maybe he’d missed it. Fear that maybe he hadn’t worked hard enough. Fear that he should be at work right now in the physical therapy clinic He almost passed a state trooper doing sixty-five in a fifty-five mile per hour zone.



He passed a billboard for a gentleman’s club called “Sensations.”



Bright orange pylons and arrow signs pointing in different directions signaled construction zones.



Rick Springfield was sheduled to play at the Hard Rock Café, casino, and Resort.



He looked down at his gas gauge, less than a quarter of a tank. He opened his heart to his environment. As he thought of those trackers who somehow see the world through the animals eyes, a red GMC truck passed him on the left. He checked his GPS, sixteen miles to the Stone Creek gas station in Inola, Oklahoma. His GPS indicated his arrival time to be around noon in Bentonville, which would give him an hour to see if he could find Mr. Van Gogh at the art museum which his mother recommended that he see for years now.



And so the road seemed to open up wide in front of him as he approached the horizon on a hill. Tulsa disappeard in his rearview mirror—forty two miles to the next fork in the road.



As the left lane closed down for construction up ahead, the traffic lined up in single file. The man came to a fork in the road of his own—that place all writers encounter when they must choose between one story or the other. 



He was reminded of an image of a chimpanzee who was holding as many oranges as he could carry in his arms and hands, and also he carried one orange in each of his feet as he was walking upright. This was apparently one of the benefits that came with bipedal motion as the primates came down from the trees and began to walk on two legs. Walking on only two legs gave us hands with which to carry food and children. The writer was pleased. He waited at the fork in the road. He paused at the binary. He chose neither story that had presented itself when he had the vision of the chimpanzee, our nearest cousin in the tree of life.



Both lanes opened up again. Then the orange signs reappeared and the road narrowed once again to a single lane. The gas station approached, less than a mile ahead. He drove under massive power lines. He merged into the right turning lane and he stopped to gas up at the sinclair.



He wondered how closely this narrator was related to the observer. He pumped his gas and he went inside. “The I AM simply observes. The narrator is the one who tells story with language,” he thought as he stood at the urinal, speaking into his telephone, wondering if someone would walk in on him mid-sentence.



As he made his way throught the gas station and out the door, he realized he was hungry. He had not eaten that morning except for a few candied pecans from his mother’s kitchen island. Those lovely pecans who had so attractively offered themselves to him as he packed his lunch. Fortunately he had packe some food for his journey. There was a variety to choose from as he had packe three tupperware containers that morning at the home of the Universal Glow. He munched on some of his aunt lindi’s famous cheese log. He ate a couple of pieces of chicken that the family had eaten the night before. He didn’t want to be too full for he was scheduled to have a meal with Dave and Eileen. He dipped a frito in an avocado. He tasted a penut butter cookie. One final bite of chicken. Then he started his car and navigated out of the gparking lot, turned right twice, and merged onto the Interstate.



“You’re packing too much food,” his youngest daughter’s voice from that morning rang in his ears. “I believe you are correct,” he said, out loud as he completed his merge into the right lane. 



The writer was looking for dialogue opportunities. “What else is it that I’m trying to develop in my writing?” he thought to himself. “Oh yes, I want to allow the reader to experience the story with their senses. I’m creating context in which the dialogue can occur when I allow the audience to experience the environment with their senses. And I’m choosing the Universal message as I allow the dialogue to form. It’s not at all important that I remember exactly what was said. It’s only important that I allow Life to show me what was actually being said.”



The man had always been curious about what people took away from conversations. He was also curious about those memories that shape us and move us forward in life. He was curious about first memories. As a father raising his children, he was especially curious about which moments in the lives of his children would be formative, so he questioned his children as they were growing up about what they remembered. 



Just that morning, in fact, one of his children asked the man about a memory. 

“Do you remember when your brother was born, Dad?” asked his son. 

“Yes, I do,” he said. “Let me show you how I remember it.”

The father lowered himself to his knees in front of the fireplace, next to the snake-skin-pattern chair. The rug on which his knees rested was thick and textured with yellows and greys. 

“This is how I remember my brother being born,” he said.



The man held an imaginary car in his right hand. It was an orange volkswagen Beetle that zoomed forward when you pulled it back. He pulled the car back on the thick carpet and then he watched as it rolled forward on the hospital lobby floor. When the car came to a stop, he retrieved it joyfully and repeated the process.



The middle-aged-man’s three children watched intently as the little boy played with his new toy that his parents bought to keep him occupied as he waited for his little brother to be born.



As the little boy stood up he was once again a man, the father of the children who were, for that brief moment, his audience. 

“And that’s what I remember about my brother being born,” he said to them. “I don’t have a memory of a baby boy, but I do remember waiting in the hospital lobby, playing intently with that little car,” he said. “But, you know what?” he questioned rhetorically. “I am not for sure that the car was self-powered like I said it was. I feel pretty certain that it was an orange car, but I’m not exactly sure that it was a volkswagen Beetle. That event happened over forty one years ago. I was four years old. I have played and replayed that memory for myself many times throughout my life. I can’t really be certain of much surrounding that memory, but that’s the story I just told surrounding the birth of my brother, and that evolving memory came to signify his birth in my mind.”

# Day 12

5:32 AM



The next morning, having successfully returned from his trip to Bentonville, the middle-aged-man sat in the living room with his mother. His mother, the Universal Glow, who sat next to the gas burning fireplace. She sat in a snake-skin patterned chair, across the living room from where the man was seated comfortably on the couch—the couch which had served as the man’s bed for the previous three nights. The man’s children, his mother’s grandchildren, still slept in the guest rooms just on the other side of the hallway which was lined with many pictures of all the family that flowed from the Universal Glow loved so deeply.



The man loved his mother. He was deeply grateful for her presence in his life. His mother still held him. Over the last year, his mother had done much to help him hold his own form. The mother had done all that she could do to bring her son into the world, and also, to see him be born again. She had not only witnessed his rebirth once, but many times. There were also births that she had not witnessed, those births in which the mother had not been directly involved. But, the mother had a front row seat to his current rebirth as she sat there in the snake-skin chair. She was able to be so close because she knew that she was only a witness and not an active participant. She watched as her son allowed himself this process. She watched as the son was letting go. She watched, and yes, she was worried, but she knew how to give her son the room he needed to do what he was doing. And the son knew how to allow his mother to be a mother. He knew that she would worry, and he was somehow able to allow her to be just who she was in this process. He was able to feel her worrying for him without allowing himself to be overwhelmed by the worry. And these were the nuances of the push-and-pull in the relationship between the man and his mother—the mother who now sat in the snake-patterned chair in front of the softly hissing gas fireplace.



The son and the mother spoke of the son’s upcoming lunch with his father. Louie’s at lake Hefner. 



Son-in-law asks to trim the father’s beard



Waking up at the speed of life



The man’s youngest daughter sat next to him on the couch. “Do you remember last night?” she said? “I got up to get a drink of water and you were standing over there crying. I gave you a hug and asked you if you were okay, and you said, ‘somethings happening.’” She wanted to talk about her grandfather that they were to meet at Louie’s later that morning. She spoke of her apprehension toward her grandfather. She spoke of a fear that she had in relating to the grandfather. The son was able to explain to his daughter that his father suffered deeply, that his father had never been held in the way that he needed. His father had never been seen or known. His father had been physically, emotionally, and verbally abused by a father who had likely had the same done to him. 



His oldest daughter approached him. They had a similar conversation. The father spoke of the generational suffering. He spoke of the healing process. He spoke of needing to be held. He spoke of Andy Dufresne, the man who crawled through a mile of shit and came out clean on the other side. He gave his daughter thanks for the gift of her being. He thanked his daughter for seeing him. He thanked his daughter for listening. He thanked her for her smiles and her hugs. He thanked her from the bottom of his heart and he was glad.



He prayed for the father who they were scheduled to meet. He prayed for that the father would have his own awakening experience, and he prayed that their meeting today would play its part in the great awakening of the Father in the father.

# Day 12



After the meal at Louie’s, the Traveller (the son?) fell asleep in a bed at his father’s house. He woke from a dream with a startle. He was unable to remember the dream. The son lay on his back, the weighted blanket, that gift from his oldest daughter, draped over his body. His laptop rested on a folded blanket and a large wooden lap desk that his father told him was his to use for writing while he was there.



The writer’s visit with Eileen and Dave yesterday left him somewhat confused about the purpose of his writings. The encounter left the writer wondering who he was doing this for. Was he writing for the purpose of being published, or was he just writing for himself? The writer wanted to be published. Isn’t that what writers want? Isn’t that what the musician always wanted, an audience (or a bigger audience, or an audience that came to listen). The artist wanted to be seen. To be heard.



Text from MOM:



Mom: Happy Monday (winking smiley face emoticon)



Son: Hi mom



Mom: hello…how’s your day?



Son: I’m okay. I’m at dad’s house. I just woke up from a nap. The kids are on their way to Caldwell to see Dan and Laronna



Mom: should I expect to see you tonight?



Son: No, not unless some kind of unforseen emergency arises. I am sowing myself into the soil here. Making myself available for a miracle. Please pray for our peace. I trust the Christ.







The day before, While in Bentonville, Harbor Dave had given the aspiring writer some practical advice. It was advice that the writer had heard before in a writing class. One part of the advice went like this: “Show. Don’t tell.” The idea behind this being that the audience needs/wants to smell and taste and touch and hear and see the environment in which their beloved character is immersed. The audience does not want to be told about the character. The audience would rather experience the environment for themselves, and the best way for this to happen is by allowing them to feel the world through the character’s senses.



The next bit of advice was also simple, at least in concept: “Dialogue”. 



“The audience wants to listen to your character interact with others,” Dave said as they were walking the graveled paths through Bentonville. “They don’t care whether you can remember exactly how the conversation took place, but they want to know what it sounds like when your character speaks out loud. The audience wants to hear your character. The audience wants to hear the Universal voice in the dialogue between your Universal characters. Your audience wants to observe the characters reactions as they diaglogue and interact with one another. And they want to feel something coming out of that. Your audience wants to be reminded of what they already know, the truths that they know but that they have forgotten, those truths that are buried down so deep that they haven’t been in touch with recently. Or those truths that have yet to surface, that the listener is ripe to hear. That’s why the reader reads--to be reminded of these sacred things. The audience wants to know more about what your character is thinking and saying,” Dave reiterated.



“Eileen,” said the writer, “What was is that you were telling me that day? What was the Universal Eileen saying? What is it that I am able to hear from you as we meet now on the Bentonville square? What was the Universal Eileen saying as we walked those gravel trails?



“Look sweetie,” said the Universal Eileen, “I just want you to know that everything is okay. It’s okay to get naked. Everything that happens in the shower is beautiful! You just keep walking away and you just keep walking forward/toward/inward/onward. Keep taking those deep breaths--those breaths that give you an unusually large rib cage that kind of sticks out like your kids were pointing out to you. I just want you to know that I DO see you. You are seen by the Universal Eileen. Listen, you ARE safe. The Univers IS out to help you, and you are on a beautiful path of discovery that I just want to bless right now. Waking up is a process, my dear, and you are right where you need to be in the middle of all that. I know how to play just like you do, believe me, my friend. There is nothing you can do that’s gonna freak me out, because I have been there. I have been where you are. I have run around my house for days without any clothes on and my kids came over and had to make peace with that. The ambulance came to my house and I had to go away for a little bit and I had the honor of making peace with that. I am familiar with medical leave, my dear. So, there’s not a bit of judgment coming from this direction, my dear. You are on the path, because everything IS the path. Be patieint as you watch this all unfold. Know that you are held. Know that you are loved. Know that you are supported. And most of all….most of all…remember that none of what’s happening right now is nearly as important as you think it is. Money? Do you remember what Rumi said the other day? Remember sweetie, it was on page 72. This is what he said:



‘The copper of your being

Has already been transmuted to gold

By Moses Alchemy, and yet you fumble

In a moneybag for loose coins’



You’re worried about money? Sweetie, don’t worry about money. I know people who lived out of their cars for a while, and that was exactly what they needed. It brought them into a deeper experience. So you just don’t worry about what you are going to eat. And you don’t worry abou what you are going to wear. Look at the monkey grass in your dad’s backyard and how it’s nice and green and healthy in the middle of winter. You see those plastic ducks in your dad’s cement pond? Well you are buoyant, just like those ducks floating on that water, my dear. You get to stop fumbling through your moneybag for loose coins. I give you permission to be this, I give you permission to be the you that you have always known you were. Matthew 5. Am I right, sweetie. Didn’t you always admire that about the one that you so affectionatley call Jesus for all those years? Remember Dear, you are not obligated to take all of this too seriously. And believe me, that’s a gift that this world needs very dearly. As you allow the matrix to crumble around you, you are bringing this gift to the world. You remember that man outside the bus station when you were younger? The one in whom I showed you freedom? Do you remember who you went home and shared that with? You are not obligated to make your ex-wife happy, and although you may be legally obligated to provide child support…well, let’s just say that you can’t get blood out of a turnip, my dear. And if your ex-wife (or rather, that person that your ex-wife thinks she is) is hell-bent on squeezing the shit out of turnips, then so be it. But, let me just say that you also can’t get shit out of a turnip. So, in all reality, she’s just gonna be shit out of luck, and that’s gonna be exactly what she needs. She can squeeze turnips from here to your grandma’s house, but she can’t squeeze you. Remember the big blue books that you were resting your lap tops on at the adobe house, the one that is in your suitcase right now? What does it say? Do you remember? “Nothing that is real can be threatened. Nothing that is unreal exists.” So, if you are feeling threatened, what do you do? You just give thanks that what is false in you is passing away. You prayers are being answered. Isn’t that the prayer that you’ve been praying for a year now. How long have you been praying that third step prayer? Do you reember what it says? Of course you do. “Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do your will.” Well, this is one way in which that prayer is beig answered. You are not obligated to take all this too seriously. And, you really don’ have to worry. And…listen to me, dear… YOU DON’T HAVE TO GO BACK TO LIVING A MISERABLE LIE. Misery is completely optional here. You aren’t on some kind of vacation right now that must come to an end. You are answering a legitimate calling on your life, and it was true when the Christ said that you are not obligated to worry. So, don’t worry. And lastly, why don’t you just go ahead and put a little book mark right here, because you may need to come back and read this message. This is the new message from the Source. The new message from the Universal Eileen which comes from the same source from which Eileen’s first email came from. There may be some more I want to say here as you read through it. 



The meeting with Eileen and Dave (Dave and Eileen) started like this.



The aspiring writer stood on the square in Bentonville. The air was cold. The sky was grey. He reached into his pocket, found his phone, and took a landscape picture of Sam-Walton’s first business, the mother of all Wal-Marts. Sam’s old Ford Pickup sat there, enshrined for a capitalist’s eternity in front of his five and dime, where all the magic that we experience today began. As the writer stood, immersed in his screen, attempting to send this picture to a friend with whom he’d once visited this very sight, he felt warm hands wrapping around his waist from behind.

“Oh my goodness!” he proclaimed, before even turning around to see who it was, “It’s so good to see you!”

Eileen smiled. They hugged. And there was dave, fifteen feet away! They had appeared! Harbor Dave and the Universal Eileen. The aspiring writer approached Dave. They exchanged embraces and polite greetings.



“I didn’t realize it would be so cold,” said Dave. “I kind of hoped we’d be able to sit out here on the square, but it’s a bit too much for that, I think. Are you hungry?”



“Yes, I am,” said the man in the olive jacket, “I haven’t had much to eat today.”



“Okay,” said Dave, “there’s a diner just over here. Lunch is on us. We’re staying with my son. He’s a chef, a real foodie. He feeds us all the time, but I could still eat.”



Dave lead the three of them along the West end of the square until they came to a café on the corner called the Pressroom. The sounds of the restaurant bounced off solid, grey concrete floors. The acidic smell of coffee rose from behind the large island bar. The hostess lead the three of them to a square table on the other side of the coffee and wine bar. Another party of five were already well into their meal, consuming somberly in a little cubby under a multi-colored, textured light fixture.



“How will I keep this up?” thought the son as he lay on his back at his father’s house. “What is the point of all these details?”

“Just keep going,” said an imaginary Harbor Dave, “You’re creating a space for something to happen here. Just put in the work here. Give yourself to this space. Allow this space to create itself, and then just see what happens.” 



The son laying on his father’s bed wanted to object. His heart was broken somehow. He was exhausted by his meeting yesterday with Dave and Eileen. He felt somehow disappointed, like he didn’t get exactly what he’d wanted, even though he’d tried to shore himself up against any such disappointments (He’d rather say that he had surrendered himself to the will of God surrounding the possibility of disappointments, but how could he really know for sure. Something in him was being threatened, that seemed certain). He knew things were never what he thought they were. But, it also seemed that he still had to go through the emotions of it all. He still had to suffer the disappointments even though he knew that things were never what they first appeared to be.



“What did the three talk about?” thought the son, laying on the bed where the father’s little chihuaha, Spud, had peed just a couple of hours ago. The wet spot had spread “What was important? What happened there? More importantly, what was being said by the Universe as the three of them came together yesterday? What was the take home? 



The man placed his black and red computer bag under the table as he found his seat. In the bag was Rumi, and Hafiz, and the book about the Christ that the Christ did no write. Also in the bag, his laptop, this story, the musings that were saving his life. Now he sat facing Northwest. The table sat at a forty five degree angle to the lines of the building. Dave was across from him facing South-East. Eileen was to the man’s right, facing South-West.



The son, lay in the quiet of the back room at his father’s house. The silver ceiling fan turned over head. Would he be able to hear what Dave and Eileen had to say today? More importantly, would he be able to receive the Universal message that was mixed in with what Dave and Eileen were saying. “We’ve all got these egos,” thought the aspiring writer, “we all project and reflect. The question is: Can I experience the Universal Presence in and through others?” There was a part of him that had been quite terrified as he listened to Dave and Eileen yesterday—a part of him that was threatened. “So let’s allow that part of us to dissolve. Let’s allow that part of us to come home. Let’s allow that threatened one, the prodigal son, to return home,” he proposed. 



He wondered if Dave had shared these writing tips because he had noticed some kind of deficiency in his voice style. The word, “marketable,” was mentioned. The aspiring writer—the sensitive artist—the threatened son was not sure how he was feeling about what had transpired yesterday between himself and Dave and Eileen (Eileen and Dave).



“Who is my audience?” thought the man who lay there on the bed in his father’s back room. This morning, as he showered (so much happened in the shower) he understood his audience to be his descendants. As the warm water poured over the man’s body, he hoped and imagined that, in this story, he was leaving an inheritance for his children and his children’s children. He wanted to let them know that he had been here. He wanted to let them know that he was waking up. He was concerned for the future generations. He wanted them to be well. He imagined these words would be a prayer for their awakening.



He wondered if this writing project was falling apart underneath him. He had secretly hoped that he was finding his footing in a new calling or a new profession. But the meeting with Dave and Eileen at the pressroom seemed deconstructive (deconstructing that which can be threatened?). He met with Dave and Eileen, two writers who had been writing and marketing for quite some time apparently, for how long he did not know. He sat at the pressroom with the owners of a publishing company, two people who are in the business of creating something that is marketable, and he could hear that in their voices, and he felt threatened (may all that can be threatened return home to the Great I AM). 



He sensed his own inexperience in his relationship with them. He could sense them relating to him through his inexperience. These are the best words that the aspiring, student-writer had to describe how he felt about the experience with Dave and Eileen yesterday. His drive home was brutal. He body was trying to fall asleep. He felt that he’d lost all his momentum. “What was the purpose of the Rucker Brothers Album?” he now wondered. The Rucker Brothers album was the creative music project that he self-published with his friend back in 2006. The man continued wondering, “It was never published. Was it ever heard? Did it make a difference in this world? Did it make a difference in my world? It was an excellent album—I can hear the heart of the album. I can hear the excellence of it today, thirteen years later. But, it was not marketable. Or, at least, we did not know how to market it. The Rucker Brothers album was produced and distributed in an ineffective grass roots fashion with seemingly no effect whatsoever on the world (that judgment is probably a little harsh). But his daughter had asked for a copy this morning. 



“Daddy,” she had said

“Yes daughter,” said the man in the olive jacket as he was driving them to lunch at Louie’s on lake Hefner in his little blue Toyota. (his son-in-law sat in the back seat with the man’s guitar and mandolin.)

“Do you have a copy of this CD that I can have? I don’t have one.”

They were listening to the Rucker Brothers album as they drove down the Kilpatrick Turnpike. They took the elevated curveed to the South, transporting them to the Hefner Parkway.



“Father?” said the son, “Is this the purpose of the album? What does this album mean to your daughter? Could this be enough?”



“Purposes are hard to nail down from your current perspective,” said the father, “The world is a complex and interconnected place. It’s hard for you to see the whole purpose and effect of your actions. The important thing is just that you bring this creative Spirit into the world. The important thing is that you continue this birthing process, that you say yes to birthing the Christ Child into the world, whether you are doing it at an inn or a manger. Just keep letting me get you pregnant (Oh my God, is it the father that gets the son pregnant?) and keep birthing the Christ child into the world. It changes you in the very least.”



“Father?” said the man again, “And what was the purpose of the meeting yesterday with Dave and Eileen? Was it so I could be reminded to “Show, don’t tell”?



“Do you remember what the course in miracles was telling you this morning?” said the Father.



“Yes,” said the son, “A course in miracles was telling me that my thoughts were meaningless. It didn’t ask me to believe that my thoughts were meaningless all day long. It just asked me to to consider that my thoughts were meaningless for one minut, five times in a day. 



Then the blue book chimed in, “That’s right, not all the time. Just five times for one minute at a time, remind yourself that your thoughts are meaningless. Just allow that to be. Can you let all of this go right now? Can you let all this search for meaning go for just a minute right now?” said the course in miracles. “Can you do that right now? For yourself? Can you just allow yourself to be? This practice will help release you from all that you believe.”



“But the TV is loud in the next room and I’m afraid of my dad,” thought the son who lay there under the silver ceiling fan.



“Just for one minute, remind yourself that it’s okay for all your thoughts, your dreams, your desires, your needs to become meaningless. Let’s try. Come on.”



My thoughts about Dave and Eileen do not mean anything

My thoughts about this book do not mean anything

My thoughts about myself do not mean anything

My thoughts about that swimming pool do not mean anything

My thoughts about my father do not mean anything

My thoughts about my ancestors do not mean anything

My thoughts about my descendants do not mean anything

My thoughts about psych units and treatment centers…they don’t mean anything

My thoughts about my hands on this computer don’t mean anything

My thoughts about the dupytren contracture in my hand don’t mean anything



“Can I do myself the favor of releasing all of these thoughts that don’t mean anything?” thought the son who was writing this book at his father’s house. The son who was now in bed, facing South, repeatedly bumping his head on the only piece of art on the North wall. The decoration was a large arrangement of concentric circles, all differing in size and overlap. The piece was four feet high and two feet wide. The man kept bumping his head.



“Am I available? Am I? I AM?” said the man in the hooded olive jacket that felt like home.



“Can I listen to one breath, without placing any words in its mouth?” The man did just that.



“Can I drop these identities for a moment? 

Can I allow myself to let them go?

Can I let this book go?

Can I touch my fingers with my thumb? Can I see what that feels like?”



The generative nurturing adult asked himself these questions. And in the asking of these questions, he allowed those fearful parts of his being--those parts of his being that felt threatened—those fragmented parts of his being were given the space and the time that they needed to reintegrate. The man in the hooded olive jacket that he bought from Wal-Mart for a poorly planned hitchhike was learning to let go. He was learning to dialogue with himself, and he was learning to write dialogue thanks to Harbor Dave and the Univeral (Ei) Lean.



And so it came to pass that the man kept with this form. So it came to pass that he continued collecting these thoughts under the title of The Moth, The Mountain, and the Middle-Aged-Man. So it was that he continued in the compassionate meaninglessness. 



“What is important here? What is really going on? What is the nature of reality in this moment?” These are the questions that he continued to ask. 



And so it came to pass that the man found himself asking the Univeral questions as he moved forward with the writing project



“Father?” asked the son.

“Yes, Son?” the father responded

“what time is it? I want to be a writer, father.” The son blurted out before allowing any space between the questions.

“Do you, son? Are you sure that’s what you want to be? I’d like you to consider your desire? Just sit with that for a while. Is that what you really want to be? Or is there something more that you desire?”



The middle-aged man rose up from his reclined position facing South. The man transferred his laptop and the wooden lap desk (provided by the man’s father) to a North facing seated position in a brown swivel-chair textured with spirals. The swivel chair was a little wobbly. The wooden lapdesk provided the appropriate support for his writing. He looked out onto his father’s back yard where he saw a swimming pool populated with plastic lilies and two orange-billed ducks . This was where his children learned to swim. Beyond the pool, he saw a garden decoration swaying in the wind, a bright yellow plastic sunflower towering above the green monkey grass. 



“Father?”

“Yes, son?”

“What kind of trees are those?”

“let’s ask,” said the father.



After twelve days of writing and relatively little sleep the middle-aged man was tired. He was looking for some kind of resolution. He was searching for the end of this real-time journey. But, he was also not ready to give this journey up prematurely. He felt that he was falling apart. He felt small after his visit with Eileen and Dave. He felt inexperienced. He felt naïve. He wanted to be held. His father was in the next room. His father, the man who was never held, the man who could never hold him.



The man clung to his project, a life raft of form in a world that was dying around him. His world was passing away, and he was documenting its passing. When the man dropped his nets to follow the Christ he had actively said “yes” to this death. Yet, he clung to this project even as he was unable to find a through line. He clung to the project as he showered. He clung to the project in the car. he clung to the project as he ate with his family at Louie’s on lake Hefner. He clung to it as he became willing to let it go. He clung to it because he trusted the dialogue that was being born in himself. He clung because this was the salvation that Life offered. He clung because it was his artist’s instinct to crawl into the liferaft that floated by.



His father belched in the living room as he watched TV. The gastrointestinal explosion bounced off the hard tile and sheetrock. The man remembered those belches from his childhood. The man was tired. Here he was at his father’s home where he intended to spend the night. 



He remembered something that he read several months ago. “If you want to find out just how awake you really are, go spend a week with your parents. See what happens.” 



“It doesn’t matter if you remember exactly what the people said,” said Dave, “just as long as you get to the heart of the dialogue.” (This was not exactly what Dave had said, but it was exactly the point).



“What would be the dialogue between the man and his father if he chose to stop streaming these words and go in there with the man who belched?” thought the man



Dave and Eileen spoke to the man yesterday as if they knew and he did not. That is what he kept feeling from Dave and Eileen. It appeared to the man yesterday that they really weren’t reading what he had sent them. Why was he so hurt? Is that even the appropriate question right now? The man felt threatened. The man felt hurt. The man felt small. The man felt scared. The man felt that he was not being heard, and that he would never be heard.



His father belched again in the next room.



“What about the trees in the back yard? That might be a good place to start a dialogue?” said the father—said the generative, nurturing Adult. The man was aware that his father had cut down many trees in order to make that backyard the hospitable place that it now was.



The man in the olive jacket felt that he was out on the edge. This felt like one of the most dangerous places for him to be. His mother knew it. She was worried. He felt it. Was he afraid that he was going to die here? Was there a part of him that felt threatened, like a small child while he was around his father? 



There were no mushrooms. There was no Eli. There was no Dan. And the man’s mother was all the way across town. He sat looking out the sliding door in his father’s extra bedroom. He wanted to be rescued--Rescued by these words. Rescued by meaning. Rescued by purpose. Rescued by an identity. He wanted to feel like he was a writer. But he did not feel that way. He felt like a man with no job who was at his father’s house, the one who belches over and over as he watches TV.



“Will that kind of thinking do you any good?” said the generative nurturing Adult.

“It will not serve me”, said the man.



He got on his knees and prayed the third step prayer which he’d learned from his friends in AA. Then he went out to meet his father for the first time, again.

 

God, I offer myself to you

Build with me

Do with me as you will

Relieve me of the bondage of self

That I may better do your will

Take away my difficulties 

That those I bear witness to 

May experience your love

Your power 

And your way of life

May I do your will today

May I do your will always



“Is this the miracle today, Father?”

“To speak of wildness is to speak of wholeness. We humans come from that wholeness.” Zen Poet, Gary Snyder

North—healing. Building. Creating. Serving people and greater earth community. Eco-centric (nature centered). Member of the greater earth community.

Yesterday I sent a message

You that turn stoniness to gold

As the writer transcribed the voice recording that he’d made from his trip to Bentonville the day before, he acknowledged the quiet coming from the house. Stillness. He listened in for a moment.

# Day 13

6:00 AM



The Traveller—the Son---The middle-aged man--awoke from a dream of the Universal Eileen. He was unable to remember the dream. He scrolled back in his draft to the message that he received yesterday this morning to read again what she had spoken to him last night. Maybe there was something she wanted to add. She did, and you, my dear descendent have already read it (if you’ve been approaching this text chronologically).



The traveller was scheduled to meet with another oracle this morning. The man called, Tim whose family had held him so many years ago. This man Tim, around whom the young man was experiencing so much insecurity, feeling somewhow that he was not trusted, or somehow unworthy of this man’s trust. The feeling had to do with the mushrooms. It had to do with the divorce. It had to do with how Tim didn’t have a good feeling about the man walking away from his job. It had to do with the fact that maybe Tim was still a fundamentalist (but maybe not, the middle-aged-man certainly didn’t want to do any name calling here). It had to do with the fact that Tim wanted to meet him at the International House of Pancakes in contrast to the open invitation into his home that the man had enjoyed for most of his adult life. 



It had do with the fact that the middle-aged-man was feeling threatened. “What did I know about feeling threatened?” the man asked himself. The very first lesson from the ACIM text came to him, as it had so many times before.



“Nothing that is real can be threatened.”

“Nothing that is unreal exists.”



This, the middle-aged-man who now sat cross-legged on the inflatable mattress at his father’s house, is how Christ made that walk with the cross. This is how Christ hung there with the nails through his hands and feet. He became this message. He was this message. “What was that he said?” asked the man, his fingers curled over home-row.



“If you try to save your life, you will lose it

But if you give up your life, you will surely save it”



“It turns out okay either way,” thought the man, “because as we try to save our life we are lead right in to the necessary misery that allows us to eventually surrender our lives. At least that’s what my experience has shown me.”



The son could hear his father piddling around the house (that’s what his grandfather used to call it, “piddling”. It was the way a body moved about without any specific conscious purpose, doing what a body does in its surroundings, tending to its belongings and its environment. That was what the man understood the word “piddling” mean. Praise be to the piddling Grandfather. The one they called Vince).



The man was torn now between his writing and his piddling father in the next room. He took the word “torn” to be the most recent manifestation of the binary. The fork in the road. The fork in the snake’s tongue. The left or the right. So, he waited. 



He acknowledged that which was beyond the binary. He acknowledged that which was beyond shame, and guilt, and obligation, and duty. He acknowledged the non-path. He acknowledged the synthesis. He offered himself some space. He gave himself permission to be exactly where he needed to be. He asked for help from a deeper source. He allowed the communion to happen. He came to that place of rest on the floor. He found the ancient water droplet, the one who shines from deep within. The one who evaporates. The one who sinks into the soil. The one who has no jealousy for the stream. The one who is still. The one who moves at the speed of life.



The son became the water droplet. The son evaporated into the living room where his father was no longer piddling, but sitting in the dark. “Hey,” said the son. There was no response from the father who was not just sitting, he was sleeping. The son walked past the father and took a seat on the neighboring couch, facing South toward the Wild Indigenous one. The sun was rising in the East, The glowing horizon could be seen through the silhouettes of the innumerable naked branches of his father’s backyard. Closest to the horizon was a brilliant orange, which gradated to a brilliant white, which then transmuted into deep midnight blue. The stones in the gas fireplace glowed red as they were excited by the flames, which contined in them all the deeps bues and oranges of the sunrise. His father, silently breathing from his Westerly position was the most still that the son had seen him, in possibly forever. The son felt that he had entered into the old man’s sacred sleep, as if he were observing a moment in the life of this sacred being that had happened a thousand times, and my happen a thousand more. A clock ticked from the kitchen in the North. The old man stirred. He coughed. He reached for a drink. His cell phone was now in his hand and he was entering text. Spud, the chihuaha growled his entrance. The ol man rose from his slumber, to let the yellow animal pee in the front yard. The father left the door open and the cold air touched the son’s feet. The father closed the front door and made his way back to his chair. They had yet to acknowledge one another. The son sat in silent breath, his hands curled over home row.



The sky was soft yellow now on the horizon which slowly faded into a grey blue as seen through the higher branches of the back-lit trees. A single bird lit upon a branch, then he was gone. The heater kicked on. The father flipped through a scrolling screen on his device. His wife stirred in her room on the North-East corner of the house. Tuesday was the day that she spent all day at Synagogue. According to the father, she had a fervent messianic-judaism practice. Peace to the Jew who showed us how to give it away! Peace to the woman in the Norht-East room. Peace to the father who sat silently, scrolling through his cell phone.



The middle-aged-man had found his own stillness in his father’s home, and he had observed his father in a rare moment of stillness. The man could not ever remember seeing his dad asleep when he wasn’t snoring. The man was able to hear his father’s breath that morning. Praise be to Yaweh, the breath of God. Praise be to the One Being. Praise be to the peace that the father and son were holding in that moment. Praise be to the orange and blue fire which excited to stones to glow. Praise be to the little yellow Spud who brought joy to the old man’s heart. 



The man placed his laptop to the side and lowered himself to the large living-room rug where he planned to stretch his hamstrings. As he entered into a relaxed dialogue with his father, he found himself grateful. He stretched hamstrings and quads and found himself in all manners of novice yogic activity as witnessed by his father that morning, all of which felt the most natural in terms of conversation and physical exertion.



He breathed deeply in his father’s presence. He read his father the excerpt that he had written as the sun rose and the father was sleeping. They spoke together in the quietest of tones in which the son ever remembered speaking to his father. Kathy joined them and they laughed in the tile -floored sharply reverberating living room.



The son shared with Kathy of his most recent public baptism. She encouraged him to root himeself in the Word. The son was able to agree with her concerning the importance of being rooted in the Word. He showed her his new bible. The son shared with her how he was writing scriptures of his own, which appeared to mometarily strike fear in Kathy’s eyes, but the son was quickly able to reassure her that he had no need for her to believe as she did, and in so doing, side-stepped a clash of fundamentals. The son congratulated Kathy that she had found her peace in her church home. Kathy congratulated the middle-aged-man on his new found baptism, then she pointed sideways toward her husband and with half-hushed tones indicating the need to get the old-man on board. “We are all on board! We are all on board!” with laughter in his chest. the middle-aged man repeated the statement for emphasis, in agreement with the all-inclusive and broadening expanse of the Universal Christ consciousness. It was in this way that the middle-aged-man made peace with Kathy as she participated in the form that was working for her that day. It was in that way that the middle-aged-man began his day of making peace with old friends and old wineskins



Shantaram

Gregory David Roberts
