# Day 13

5:05PM



At precisely the speed of life the young man (for he truly felt young that day) steered his car into the IHOP parking lot. He found his silver-haired Timothy waiting at a booth in the Northwest corner of the restaurant. The young man embraced the older man with a smile on his face and true gratitude in his heart.



After exchanging their initial greetings Timothy expressed to the young man how he never wanted him to interpret his lack of enthusiasm in text and phone conversations as a slight toward him. The younger man let him know that it was sometimes a challenge when his texts and voice mails sometimes went unanswered, but it was a challenge which he was willing to face in exchange for a true friendship. The young man also acknowledged the growth that this challenge had brought into his life over the last weeks.



“Would you mind if I placed my phone right here in front of you to record your voice Tim?” said the younger man.



“No, not at all,” Timothy said.



It was in this way that the younger man hoped that he honored the older man’s experience and wisdom while continuing his study of dialogue. Tim was an Evolutionary Christian Mystic who was still bound by some of the trappings of fundamentalism (as we all inevitably are bound by these forms that holds us). The younger man knew that Timothy was right where he needed to be. The younger man had chosen to participate in form. Timothy was one of the chiefs that he had seen in the Kachina dolls on that night of his first medicine journey. The younger man said “yes” to Timothy as Timothy said “yes” to him for more than twenty years. It was understandable that Timothy was right where he was, considering the circles in which he currently walked and where he had come from. It was understandable that the younger man was right where he was. Today, the younger man accepted his silver haired friend. He acknowledged the great wisdom and grace that abides deeply within.



Tim explained to the younger man that because he was involved, on some level, in so many people’s lives that sometimes he engaged in multi-tasking.



Here are some excerpts from the conversation as recorded that day as the two old friends sat in the Northwest corner of the IHOP:



Timothy: …Multi-tasking bothers some people because they think you’re not paying attention to them, or you’re not telling them what they want to hear. Some people think it’s rude if you’re doing something else at the same time that you’re talking to them, but really it’s just true, that’s the way your brain’s working all the time anyway. 



I remember when I was back in school, trying to pay attention to the teacher and I’d look outside and I’d get fascinated with something going on out there. I could still hear her, but I was carrying on a conversation over here too. And I found that you can only do this so much, but the average person does this more than we are willing to admit.



Younger man: I’ve been on a different path of really being right here with one thing at a time.



Timothy: Sometimes that’s the only way to fix something, is to focus and totally isolate everything else. That’s alright. That’s an engineer way of doing it.



Younger man: It’s BOTH/AND



Timothy: I don’t think anyone is supposed to do one or the other, they’re both important.



Younger man: And here’s something I’ve been learning when I come to the fork in the road. It’s like this: ‘Yes’, to the right. ‘Yes’, to the left, and then the non-path presents itself.



Timothy: Here’s something you haven’t seen yet.



Younger man: (Laughing) Right. Exactly. The path that you did not see.



Timothy: Sometimes I think I’m going the wrong way and when it’s really more in-the-plan than I thought. Other times it’s the opposite; you think you’re going the right way and everything crashes and we interpret that as wrong instead of, ‘this is what I’m supposed to be experiencing.’ And that causes a lot of people to get double-minded.



2:04 time indicator



Name changes 4min





The middle-aged-man still felt a kind of sadness that he could not go back to a more open time with Timothy, a time when he felt the closeness with him and his family in which he could call any time and Tim would answer, that time when he enjoyed the liberty of just dropping in on them any time. But Tim did not extend that invitation today, and neither had his wife Jolee in their last facebook messenger exchange. The man sat with that reality for a moment. He sat with it. He let it be exactly what it was. Then, he wondered what would happen if he applied the ACIM lesson of the day to this situation:



“My meaningless thoughts are showing me a meaningless world.”



For the moment, the middle-aged-man preferred to understand his thoughts this way. What if it was true that his thoughts were meaningless? What if these meaningless thoughts were showing him a meaningless world?



The middle-aged-man questioned himself, “How long will I allow myself to be insecure about the change in my relationship to these people who were once such a huge part of my life? How much room does one need to grieve a loss? Who is it that is grieving the loss? Who is the ‘myself’ that is insecure over this loss? Can I bring Presence to this loss? What does this loss feel like in my body? Where is this loss located? What is it like to bring Presence to this loss? What is that experience like? Can I get curious about that? Can I allow that to happen? Is this what these fragmented parts of my being require? Presence? What is this proces like?”



Whose the enemy?

Satan.

What does Christ ask us to do to our enemy?

Love your enemy

Love satan?



Why all this again? What is the point of this blasphemy? More meaningless thought? Possibly.



The middle-aged man recognized the reverence with which he had treated Timothy. Timothy had been the nearest approximation (representation? Embodiement?) of Christ, or the tangible embodiment in this world that most looked like Christ to the young man. 



So, What’s it like to sit with that man, Timothy, and see his faults? Is that how we want to see this? Faults? Is there another way to ask that question? What’s it like to see Timothy as a man who is still maturing and to see places where Tim may be stuck in his progression? Maybe that’s not even the right way to say this. I’m hesitant to nail this down. What’s it like to love Timothy? I think I’m getting closer now. What’s it like to love that man? What’s it like to come back to him in love and acceptance? What’s it like to accept him as you accept yourself? What’s it like to see him in the context of spiral dynamics? What’s it like to feel him as an equal? What’s it like to know your way around your Self in his presence? Here’s one to try on for size…dare I say it?....What’s it like to have gone deeper than your mentor? Let’s try again. Let’s try it this way…What’s it like to know a bigger Christ than Tim knows? What’s it like to experience the Christ as Universal? What’s it like to have left the bible belt? Am I speaking foolishly now? Can I take these risks? Am I willing to risk trying out these statements? Can this be part of my process? What’s it like to love that man? I want to come back to that one.



Timothy still talks of the “saved” and the “lost”. “I asked him what those words meant to him, didn’t I?” the man questioned himself, although he already knew the answer.



Timothy had the check for the meal in his hand.



“I’ll get the tip,” said the younger man as he laid a twenty dollar bill down on the table.



“That’s not a tip,” said Timothy, batting the bill toward his old-disciple.



“Yes, it is,” said the younger man, “That’s my tip today. I’m sowing some seeds. I know you understand that.”



“Yes, I do,” said Timothy



The younger man noticed that, although his bank account was dwindling with no more money scheduled to come in, that he did not feel so scared as he laid the twenty down on the table. And yesterday, as he passed a ten dollar bill to a homeless-looking couple on the street corner, he felt no fear. He who gives up his life, gains it. He who gives up the money, gains his freedom from it.



“Okay, said Tim. I’ve got to get to this dentist appointment.” Several times during their conversation the silver-haired man had applied some anbesol to his gums.



“Yes,” said the younger of the two, “let’s get you there.”



“Oh, wait!” said the younger man, “Could you please sign this for me?” He slid his new blue bible with the vine-textured cover over to Timothy.



Timothy took a few thoughtful moments to write in the front cover of the younger man’s new bible which had his name embossed in silver on the front.



“Okay,” said Timothy, “It was great to see you, my friend.



“Oh, no,” said the younger man, “I’m not leaving you yet. I want to get every moment I can with you. I’m so grateful that you took the time to sit down with me today.”



And so they waited in line. Timothy paid the bill.



As they turned toward the double doors, the younger man placed his arm over Timothy’s shoulder and spoke these words: “I’m here to blow you up Tim, because that’s what you’ve prayed for.” The two men laughed. These were words that were spoken with affection and humor. These two men had a history together. Timothy was with the young man when he was kicked out of his first church. Timothy and his family had held the young man as he as his family left the church of the bible belt to discover what was then a complete mystery, the Cosmic Christ. These two men were accepting the death and resurrection process. These two men were accepting the trembling that came with this process of inviting the Word into one’s very being. They were saying “yes” to life. They were saying yes to one another.



As they emerged from the Internation House of Pancakes into the morning light, they laughed and exchanged good-byes. They parted ways.



“Call me when it’s time to play!” The younger man was strumming his air guitar, walking backwards across the parking lot.



The man in the hooded olive jacket got in his little blue Toyota with the extremely cracked windshield. His next waypoint seemed obvious to him. He was the hunter-gatherer looking for the next berry. He was the following the herd. He turned his little car South-East down the Northwest Expessway. He headed South on Rockwell toward his old place of employment, where he hoped he would meet his old friend and boss, Brian.



Inkling Design



The man is heading South on Rockwell. He is nostalgic. He knows these streets, or at least he once knew them. The people that he left behind here have been travelling these streets the whole time that he has been gone. He left this town like Moses having slain the Egyptian. Into exile in the desert. Not exile. Refuge? Refuge in the desert. The man crosses over that street. What is the name of that street? It’s not wilshire, right? Wilshire runs parallel to Rockwell, does it not. It’s the street that you enter the Bence’s neighborhood from. It’s the last main intersection that you cross through before you get to Brian’s shop when you’re coming from this way.



I’m awake. Sitting here in this room facing North. Trying to make sense. Is that what I’m trying to make sense? Maybe that’s a problem? I wanted to write “the” problem, but I felt that was a little too absolute. 



The man scrolled back down to the real time in which he belonged.

# Day 13

December 31, 2019

11:37PM



The dying-author awoke just before the dawn of a new decade, a dawn that had already cracked on much of the world to his East--A midnight which had already come to many of his fellow human beings. The dying author acknowledged the new year in this way, crafting these sentences slowly as the minutes passed before him on the small clock in the lower right-hand- corner of his laptop. He celebrated this new year somberly, by himself, but not alone dear reader. He was mostly unafraid of what life was offering in this moment, and he felt grateful for it all.



His father’s house was quiet. The middle-aged man had napped for over three hours after another conversation with Kathy…



 As he heard the fireworks, an audible expression of the new year, he thought of his children, and it seemed just right to send them a group text:



Father: “Happy New Year! Thinking of you as the dawn of a new decade arises upon us, my dear children! I heard the fireworks and thought, “I bet that’s what my kiddos are doing right now!” Peace to you and all our fellow human beings. Peace to this waking world and all its expressions of arising consciousness.”



The middle aged man admitted to himself the loneliness that he currently felt in his being. He had considered venturing out into the world earlier, but he had not. Instead, he asked Kathy about her synagogue. He had the conversation that his friend Jeremy advised him not to have just before he’d left the college-cow-town those five days ago.



 “So Kathy,” began the middle-aged-man, “you call your assembly place a synagogue? Is that correct? Am I getting that right?”



“Yes,” she said, “I call it a church sometimes so others can understand what I’m talking about.”



“Ahh, I see,” he responded, “And you find your peace there, participating in that form?”



“Yes, I do. Very much so. I have friends there. I enjoy the ceremonies. I feel supported there. I feel loved. I am cared for within those walls.”



“Oh, that sounds lovely, Kathy. I am so happy for you,” he encouraged her to continue.



“Yes, I love my synagogue and the people in it. We recognize the appropriate feasts as indicated in the old testaments. We do Davidic dancing…”



“Davidic dancing?” the man interrupted, “Do you mean that you dance with abandon?”



“Oh no, we don’t believe in that kind of thing, Davidic dancing is a structured group dance with very specific steps,” she explained, “It’s really beautiful. I’d have to show you a video.”



“Yes, I’d like to see that,” he said



She went on, “At our synagogue, we try to avoid the traditions of man by observing the bible as it is written. Things go wrong when man comes in and tries to change things. When we stray from what’s written in the Word, that’s when things go wrong. We do our best to observe the Judaic traditions as they are set out in the Old Testament. The first Christians were Jewish people. If you just stick with the old testament, you can’t go wrong. You know, like Christmas, it’s a Pagan holiday, so we don’t celebrate that.”



“Do you ever find that you are inventing your own traditions despite your efforts to prevent them from coming in? I just ask because that was my experience as I did my best to give myself to the holy scriptures?” He asked.



“Oh yes, that’s always a danger. But we just stick to the Word. You can’t go wrong if you just stay with what’s written there.”



And so this interaction between the middle-aged-man and his father’s wife began. They found common ground in their recognition of the name that cannot be spoken, Y-W-H, the breath of God, the unspeakable name. They also agreed that the annointed one was never called Jesus while he walked the earth, Yeshua being a closer representation of the name of the human-being that was called Messiah over two-thousand years ago. 



The middle-aged-man shared with her about the Universal Christ, the all inclusive One whose arms are wide open, the One who does not exclude anything or any one.



She responded, “I don’t understand this Universal Christ that you are talking about. That doesn’t make much sense to me.”



“That’s okay,” said the man, “I’m not trying to get you to believe anything. It’s okay with me that you don’t understand. My experience has lead me to see the Christ in everything and in every one. There is nowhere I can go to escape the all-encompassing embrace of Christ...”



The middle-aged-man dared to go on. He shared with her how he saw the Christ in his vipassana practice as he observed the breath, and how he saw the Christ in the Buddha. Then, he shared with her how he saw the Christ in his spirit animal, Snake, as he practiced therapeutic shamanism. He shared with her how he saw the Christ in the Hindu Gods and Goddesses.



She continued, “I just know that God said to have no idols before him. Moses went up on the mountain for forty days and the people formed a golden calf, because that’s what we do. We make false idols, and so that’s why I think it’s very important to follow the Word.”



“I think I understand what you are saying. There was a time in my twenties when I tried to live my life as I interpreted the scriptures literally,” He said.



“Well, what do you think of the bible? How do you see the scriptures? What do you believe?” she said.



The middle aged man paused. He began to explain. He stopped. He paused again, realizing how important this one was, for himself, that he be clear of any need to prove anything to Kathy. He was walking a fine line in this conversation. He tried to share only his experience, his strength, his hope. He did not want her to feel threatened or attacked.



“I can’t speak about what I believe, because belief never really helped me as much as I wanted it to,” he continued at last, “I can only speak about my experience. I once read the scriptures literally, and that lead to a type of madness, a death that came naturally as a result of that whole process.” 



The man backed up. He tried again. 



“Let me see if I can say this another way. Really, I just want to be held, Kathy. I never felt that I was held the way I needed to be. And my father was never held like he needed. And his father before him. And this is how I came into the church. I wanted to be held and I was told that I would be held by a literal interpretation of the bible. And I truly was held in that tradition, in that form, for a while. But, eventually, my literal understanding of the holy scriptures was not enough to hold me. When we sold all of our possessions, I gave myself to that form completely, but in the end, I didn’t feel held, so I felt that I had to move on. 

I moved on in my search. I moved on to find the next form, or practice, that would hold me. And this way of being fits me, maybe because I am one of those people that you might call an artist. It’s about the creative process for me. And that’s why it’s so important that I can see the Christ in the Buddha, or Snake, or the Hindu Gods and Goddesses. I never know where I’m going to see the Christ, and I can’t control where this provision of grace through the Cosmic Christ will come from. I know that these ideas may be disturbing to you, and I don’t mean to offend you at all, but I’m even going to take this a step further. You may need to cast me out, and if you do, I understand, but I’m going to speak some blasphemy right now, just to make a point. Here goes: Who is the enemy? Satan. What does Christ tell us to do for our enemies? Love them. So who do we love? We love Satan.”



The man stopped speaking. There was a long pause.



Finally Kathy speaks. “I just know that Jesus did a lot of casting out of demons. There is an enemy and I don’t think that we can love Satan. We have to fight Satan…”



“Okay,” said the man, “But what does the fight of a follower of Christ look like? Isn’t our only weapon love? How do we fight these evil principles and principalities? Do we literally put on God’s armour? And if so, what does that armour look like?”



“You can’t love Satan, that’s all I know.” She said.



“That very well may be so,” he said, “And fortunately I’m not trying to convince you of anything tonight. I’m just sharing my experience with you. I’m just using these words so that maybe we can both see something greater than ourselves. I’m being open and honest with you about my experience. I pray tonight, as I have been praying, that anything false in me will be burned up. Anything not genuine. Anything not authentic. I pray that these things will be burned up in me. And I thank you for your prayers of healing. I welcome them. I have suffered deeply, Kathy, and this is just who I find my Self to be today. I am aware of my need to be held by this all-inclusive, all-encompassing, Creative, Intelligent, and fully-Compassionate Universal Christ. Today I feel that I am in communion with this Christ. This is my experience. I hope that you can feel my respect for your experience today. I don’t need you to be anything different than what you are right now. I don’t need you to be anywhere different than where you are right now. Thank you for allowing me to stay in your home.



“I think I understand, Maybe we can just watch Edward Scissor-hands,” she suggested.



The man sat to watch…



Edward Scissor-hands. The young man who was isolated from his community at the end of the cul-de-sac. The Avon lady came calling. She brought him home. The religious lady was afraid of him. He cut himself. He poked a hole in the water bed. He had trouble dressing and acting right. Everyone seemed curious at best. Suspicious at worst.



But the middle-aged-man grew sleepy. He excused himself to his bedroom to nap, truly hoping that he would get to finish the movie another day. And this is the story of how the middle-aged-man woke up just twenty-three minutes before midnight and began writing as the decade passed before his eyes.

# Day 14

3:12 AM



The writer gave his body a chance to sleep. He awoke from what he estimated to be a ten minute dream.



I am standing in a physical therapy gym. There is an older man in the parallel bars. He beckons me over. He is an older Asian man. He asks me a question. What is he saying? I am leaning in. I can’t understand him now, but I understood him when I was dreaming. He is telling me that he is unable or unwilling to do something that he said he would? Is that what it is? I stop him mid-sentence. I do not want to hear any more. I get the point. I understand. You have told me enough. I want you to stop talking. I am annoyed. No More explanation in necessary, old man. I don’t want to hear it any more. Why is your hand on my left thigh. I want you to remove your hand from my thigh. Then the question returns. The Question. There’s a deeper question. What is it? What are you asking me, old man? Something to do with physical therapy? Why can’t I remember the question? I am listening. Am i listening? I cannot hear the question now. I knew what it was then. I heard it. The man collapses. He goes to his knees outside the parallel bars. I look up at the crowd of my coworkers, there are many. Someone call 911! Everyones’ phones are out they are all calling at once. 911 will be flooded with calls. The cel phones make the faces of my coworkers glow. Everyone is dialing. “The patient is still breathing,” I announce. 



I awake in fear that I will have no insurance. I wake in fear of my rotting teeth. Tim’s toothache. I have no structure. Joseph’s words are in my ears, “how will you care for yourself?” Who will care for me? I am the overly-bearded man who shows up at Brian’s shop, my job is fading from me. What if I don’t return on the sixth for my Dr appointment. I have an appointment with Renita borders, my new therapist in a couple of days too. Do I go home now? Do I run home? Can I continue facing my father. My mother is calling, offering chowder and a “safer” place to be. My father’s house is a sad house where the televisions run constantly. I am very tired now. Depleted. Exhausted. My body is getting tired from never sleeping more than three hours at a time. I want to go home. Where is home? Father, what time is it? Mother invited me over for clam chowder tomorrow night. I want to see my mother before I go home. I am scared. I am lonely. I do not like the way the television sounds in this house. I do not like the isolation and sadness here. I am afraid that my father will be mad in the morning because I did not spend enough time with him yesterday. This is the home where people shut themselves in rooms and turn the television on all evening. The place they rarely leave. I want to go home. Where is home? Who will take care of me?



The writer sat on the light-tan leather couch in his father’s spare bedroom. He was facing North, toward the concentric circles at the head of the bed where he had just dreamed of the Asian man. The dying Asian man.? The Asian man who had a heart attack in the parallel bars. Was he from the East? The innocent sage? Of Bill Plotkin. The Trickster? The fool?



The writer scolled back to his writings from the day before. He wanted to tell the story of Brian and Nash and Inkling design.



The man sat on the light tan couch at 3:52AM. He faced North. He observed a breath. And another one. The Y-W-H. the observance of the I AM. That which the Kathy cannot understand. He wondered if he was sinking too far into the soil, like he had done on Christmas day, one week ago. The one week anniversary of the Christmas day that the man was convinced of his death by the “lethal dose” of psilocybin mushrooms. The medicine that showed him what it might be like to face his death. 



The man had a story to tell. At least that’s what he thought he might be doing here. Or maybe he was just writing to save himself. Maybe he was writing so that he could be saved. That’s one question that he’d asked Tim yesterday.



“These words, ‘saved’ and ‘lost,’ what do they mean to you now after all these years?



The writer himself certainly felt saved these days. “Saved from what?” he mused of his own being. Was that honest? That last sentence. Was that an honest use of the word “muse.” It was moments like these when he remembered that writing had very little to do with writing and everything to do with that question that was famous within the realms of his own being, “How will I live with myself.”



The next question is sometimes this, “who is this self that you are trying to live with?”



Harbor Dave told the aspiring writer that he had written thousands of pages (or was it just a thousand that he’d estimated. I think it was just a thousand) that would never be published. The writer now realized that he had also written many pages that would never be published. 



“Do I have the courage to continue in this writing project even if it were to never be published?” he asked himself. Do I have the courage to call all these thought meaningless. Let’s try it for just a minute, just as ACIM has recommended on day 10. And day 11 which states, “My meaningless thoughts are showing me a meaningless world.” Ha! The greatest insult to a storyteller, right?



This made him think of his friend, Janice, back in Portales. The woman who he ha once called muru (mutual guru). The woman who he’d cut out of his life after he read three-quarters of a book about codependencey. He stopped reading the book after he’d blocked his brother, his father, and three friends, including Janice, who he had been scheduled to meet with that morning.



He floundered now in this writing project, although he’d just completed writing a couple of significant chunks. His cell phone sounded a text. He leaned over to see who was contacting him at 4AM in the morning (that’s what his ex-wife used to say when she used the AM. He felt that it was redundant in nature to say AM and ‘in the morning’ as well. AM was sufficient. It bothered him that she did this over and over again. He felt that being an English teacher that she must be held accountable for these types of infractions). His cell phone signaled yet another text. That was three. This time, he really did reach over the couch to pick up the cell phone, which was plugged into the wall charging. There he goes. He’s about the reach.



It was his brother. The man was tired. His head felt foggy. He didn not know if he was ready to engage his brother right now. The man missed the showers at the adobe house on Avenue Q. The man wondered if he was sinking in to the soil. He wondered if he was too far gone to come back. “What is required of me to complete this process,” He wondered. “How far do I have (get) to go.” He wondered again. 



It was writing like this that connected him to something deeper than this writing project that he really did hope to get published. Oh, the impossibilty of that. Or rather, that felt like the impossible. How long had it been since the man had written of the miracles? The form was always passing through for the man. Transient form. Constantly changing. Ah, to be one of those people who finds a form and rests in it. This was not how the man experienced life. Even as he wrote, his form and voice were changing. They had to change in order for him to experience (there’s that word again) his own honesty. 



“Am I really ready to die this death?” he asked himself. (he wrote the phrase “he wondered to himself” but he sensed that he’d already used that phrase several times recently). Writing was a constant effort to not say the same thing, the same way, twice, especially in the same sentence or the same paragraph. And then, if he noticed that a word was used frequently (i.e. experience) then it must somehow be acknowledged. He wondered what he would find if he looked up the word “experience” in a thesaurus. 



What about Stan and David in Cloudcroft? Was that a place he needed to be? Was there something there for him? Was there some “experience” that he needed in Cloudcroft? Why was that word experience so important. “Experience is important because it is through experience that we experience the change that we so deeply need,” first person writer answered third-person writer. “You just used the word “experience” twice in that one first-person sentence…no…actually three times.” The writer’s head was spinning. He opened google to find a thesaurus.



The writer needed to feel the warmth of a shower. He wanted to feel the warmth of the shower. He did, as the writer’s father slept just a few feet away, he showered. It was a mainly uneventful shower, mostly just the cleaning of his body. He did, however, sit down for a bit and feel the warm water as he allowed himself to come into contact with this breath and his body (btw, “contact” was one of the synonyms for “experience” in the thesaurus). As he dried off he remembered one of the teachings of his Pema, which was “Go to the places that scare you.” Was that not the teaching of the Christ when he asked the rich young man to sell all of his possessions and give to the poor? Was the Christ not asking the rich young man to “go to the places that scared” him? 



“Oh,” thought the writer, “a shower in close proximity to my father. I think that qualifies as one of those places. Could it be possible after all these years that when you are around your father you are still a scared child?”



The writer suddenly wanted to run back to the comfort of the medicine. “The comfort of the medicine!?” he thought loudly. “Are you serious? The medicine that made you feel like you were going to die?” Now the writer was answering himself in second person. They say that’s a sign of true insanity. “Who is ‘they’?” the writer questioned.



“Pema?” the writer asked….



Let’s try that again…



“Pema?” the son asked



“Yes, son?” said the Pema



“How long do I stay in these places that scare me?”



“Pema?”



“Yes, Son?”



“What time is it?”



“Do you remember when you went to the mountains?” asked his Pema.



“Which time?” the son asked (knowing exactly which time she was referring to).



“That time that you went all by yourself, son. That time that you drove all the way up to the Santa Fe National forest by yourself. Your son wasn’t with you and that was a pretty big deal, and you knew the deal would get bigger. And do you remember how, on the trail register, someone had written, ‘watch for cougars! Stay with your party!’. And you were all alone, weren’t you, son?”



“Yes, Pema, I was,” Said the son.



“And how did that make you feel,” asked his Pema.



“I felt scared, my Pema,” confessed the son.



“And what did you do?” she asked.



“I signed the trail register and I started my backpack adventure.”



“Yes, that is how I remember it too,” she said.



“And what happened next, son,” Pema asked.



The son responded, “I hiked and hiked all day long. I was all by myself and the sun was shining down on me in the forest as I hiked through the changing landscape. I hiked through tall grasses. I hiked past all different kinds of wild flowers and dandelions. I hiked through open, flat fields, and rocky, slanted ascents. I hiked past large rocks. I hiked past uprooted trees. I hiked past tall, sticky pines. I saw a horny toad. I rested and ate packets of tuna. I hiked through green ferns and aspens. And the whole time I wondered about wild cats. Well, not the whole time, I finally got too tired to care much about the cougar that might be stocking me. But, she was there with me the whole time. And I got so tired. I got tired and a lot of emotions came up and I started crying and hiking at the same time. Then my tears turned into prayers. And I came to that place where I didn’t want to go any further, and I wondered why in the heck I’d come in the first place, but by then I had gone too far to turn back…”



“Right there,” said Pema, “That’s exactly how far you have to go. You get to go so far our that you can’t come back. That’s what they call ‘past the point of no return.’ That’s the place that scares you. And that’s the only place where you can overcove your fear. Because it’s right there where you have no choice but to work with yourself. That’s the place where your practice pays off. So, are you there yet?”



“I don’t know, Pema. Am I there yet?” the son felt like he was in the back seat of Pema’s car crying, “Are we there yet, Pema?”



“Just keep talking about what happened next, son.”



“Thank you,” said the son.



“What are you thanking me for?” said his Pema.



“For calling me son?” said the son.



“You are very welcome. That’s what you are, isn’t it? A son?”



“Yeah, I know,” said the son, “but I know that you are a non-theist and the ‘son’ thing, well that’s kind of my thing and not yours.”



“I am the Universal Pema,” she said, straightening her yellow Pema robes, “I AM all forms, and I am no forms. Now get on with your story, because you’ve got a point to make here.”



“Yes, Pema, I will.” Said the Universal Son. “I had ascended past the point of no return, up past ten-thousand feet now. I was all by myself. I hadn’t seen another hiker all day. I cried as I was hiking. I cried for my own loneliness. I missed my son on the trail because he was my trail partner who’d been with me on every trip. We helped each other get our packs on and off and talked to one another and watched out for one another, and he wasn’t there. And that lonelineess started to press in on me.



And all day I had wondered about the large cat that might be sneaking up behind me. And sometimes I stopped and I listened very carefully, and I turned around to look behind me, scanning the trees and underbrush for any movement or color difference. And the more tired I got, the more intense the sense of loneliness and loss became. It was grief, that’s what I was feeling so intensely. Grief: when your happiest memories become your most painful ones; that’s how I had come to define it for myself, and miss Du’bois, at work, when I explained it to her that way, she told me that I should write a book. So there I was, past the point of no return and the grief kept mounting up. And I kept turning around to see if there was a big cat behind me, knowing that any big cat worth their salt would never give away its position to a lumbering human with a forty pound pack on his back. I knew I would never see her coming. And I didn’t have a knife, but I did have my dragon-tooth necklace, and when that moment came I planned to gouge her in the eyes with my dragon tooth necklace. I don’t know what that was about because I did have a knife in my pack, yet still I planned to gouge the attacking cougar with my dragon-tooth necklace that the mountain climber from the Life Healing Center had made just for me. 



My tears, at some point turned into prayers. I prayed for my ex-wife and I prayed for the woman from Bermuda who I had put on a plane—the woman who I had left my ex-wife for. That thing I had done that I was still coming to terms with. This was before I knew that Sapphos had returned to Lesbos island. Anyway, I prayed for these women long and hard. I asked God that these women would be given the strength to recover from the harm that I had done to them. I especially remember praying for the woman from Bermuda who I wanted so deeply, the woman that I tried so hard to give myself away to, but something inside of me would just not allow it to, no matter how hard I tried. It was for her that I remember praying for the most fervently. Up and up I went that day.



I came with the intent that night of meeting Kali Ma on the mountain. She is a Hindu Goddes with blue skin and at least four arms who cuts mens head off with a scythe. I was praying for the death of my false self. The head represented the ego to me. And it was with the specific intention of making love to Kali Ma in this way that I had come to the mountain.



After nine hours of physical and emotional exertion, I arrived at lake Johnson which was over eleven-thousand feet. I made my camp. The making of that camp was one of the loneliest and saddest things I had ever done. There were other campers. My son was not with me. I was well past the point of no return. I was in up to my neck, the neck that I prayed Kali Ma would sever that night. I pitched the tent. I prepared wood for the fire. I cooked some shrimp flavored Ramen. I rolled out my sleeping bag. I got everything organized for the night. Having completed all the camp chores, I was ready to go meet her.



 

I knew where I was going. Me and my son had been to this very lake just two weeks before. I followed the stream up into the forest, past where anyone might find me if something were to go wrong. There was a lush, green, ground covering up there. There were these giganitic boulders too, with little bodies of water around them. A couple of these boulders were fifteen or twenty feet high. They were gigantic. 



This place held a lot of mystery. These boulders had spirits in them. And the green ground covering too. And the stream. It was all alive. It was all breathing. And there was the spirit of the cougar there with me the whole time, the one who stalks me. She was there. She was always there. There was one place where when I stepped, the ground sounded hollow. I had on my black combat boots, the same pair that I would leave behind at the ENMU brick wall when I took my hitchike months later. Anyway, these black combat boots, when I stomped the ground made this incredibly strange thunking sound in the earth. I began stomping and dancing. I began calling on the spirit of Kali Ma. “Kali Ma! Kali Ma! Kali Ma! I yelled out time and time again. Her name rang through the valley. And when I stopped calling her name the quiet was just as loud. And I thought that she would surely come in the form of a the mother cat. And it was in this way that I summoned the spirit of Kali Ma, saying yes to the death that I knew I must die. And it was there also that I cried out the name of the others that had helped me. I called on the name of Yeshua. I called on the Buddha. I called on Shiva and Shakti, the male and the female. It was in this way that I made myself vulnerable that night on the mountain. It was in this way that I made myself vulnerable in both spirit and in my physical being. 



I made my way back to camp as the sun was setting. It was dusk and getting duskier. I lit the great fire that I had made from large branches an the trunk of a tree. The fire was nestled where two large rocks met. The fire was sheltered from the wind. And I saw that there was a curious animal hole right there by my camp. It was a tunnel that went into the earth. I was curious. 



I drank water. I ate more food. The night came. The fire roared. I fell sound asleep. When I woke up the fire was out. That’s when I heard the mysterious clicking sound that I spoke of earlier—the strange clicking from which would eventually arise the Exquisite Stillness.



“Pema?” said the son, “Are you there?”



“Ask him to take you to see the cats,” said Pema.



“The cats?” said the son (knowing exactly the cats that she was talking about)



(So there must be a Louie’s scene now in which the cats are mentioned?)



“Yes, son. The cats that were so important to him that he told you about during the meal a Louie’s. Ask him if he’ll take you to see those cats. See what happens. Go to the places that scare you. You’ve got to go past the point of no return.”

# Day 14

9:58AM



Dear reader, the writer comes to you for company this morning. Dear Pema, thank you for you support this morning. Dear Mother, Dear Father, the son acknowledges the blessing that you are in his life.



A miracle came to pass in the life of the middle-aged-man, one that may be somewhat difficult to articulate so early in its development. 



The writer had learned in the last two weeks that it was often the less direct approach to the miracle which brought the deepest results. And so this is the way he began that morning in a South facing position at his Mother’s house.



The first time that the son remembered his father blaming him for his misery was when he was five. It made a lasting impression on the little boy. His mother helped him to understand that his Daddy wa sad because of something that he did. 



What does it do in the heart of a child when the father is unable to give himself the approval that he needs? What does it do in the heart of a maturing young adult when the father, once again, blames his son for his own suffering? What does it do?



What does it do to a son to be attacked by the father? The sone knew. He was experiencing the results this very moment. He knelt in one of his mother’s two extra bedrooms as he was typing. It was the Northern-most bedroom. He knelt to the west. The beloved-muse according to Bill Plotkin. 



He knelt with fear in his heart that he would be overwhelmed by the memory of his father this morning as he, once again, attempted to withdraw his blessing from the child (child? Is that what the writer just wrote? Yes. That is what just came out). The writer clung to this form, recording the passing of this moment. He faced the west in a half-water-droplet position. He retrieved two pillows from the surface of the bed above him. He propped his chest, rested his elbows on the ground, and resumed typing from this position. Every word was his life line. Every word was the life raft of form that held him out of the turbulent waters. His feet tingled now as the blood began to flow back in to them. 



Images of his suffering father’s face filled his mind as he woke up from the very short nap which allowed him now to resume his writing. Each word that came from his fingers a blessing. Each word transporting him through this moment, a tactile prayer for his finger tips. He breathed in deeply and typed the next words as he allowed the oxygen to escape his lungs. The writer waited for the next miracle. He had already seen miracles happening today. He watched his father attack. He watched himself as he did not return the attack. He watched himself pray for his father. He watched himself give thanks to his father as he left his home. The writer allowed some saliva to drip from his mouth as a distraction, just another tactile experience that carried him one moment further into the present. 



“Am I of a right mind?” the writer questioned himself (the writer? Yes that is what he called himself. He clung to this form for life). He waited for a moment when he could find himself in the simplicity of being. Exhaustion. Sadness. He watched his father’s eyes fill with desperation and anger. He watched him as he recounted a whole new layer of pain within himself. These were stories that the son had not yet heard. The father recounted how his elder brother of six years consistently reminded him that he was an accident. My father was the one who was not supposed to come. He was the one who was not held. His parents had no energy for him. His brother relished shooting his cats with a shotgun when they became ill. The father still carried all this loss within him. The little boy (his father) left for overnight trips, sleeping under railroad bridges, his parents not knowing that he was gone and never knowing of his absence. These were the new stories of his childhood that he was now telling. Why doesn’t the father reach out for help? Why doesn’t he go and talk to a counselor? The father recounted his pain to his son as he stood in the kitchen. This was after the jerky had been put in the oven. This was after the father made the son a rice bowl. The father had been disappointed by the son yesterday because the son did not give him the attention that he desired. The father was lashing out at his son now. The father told his son that he was disappointed in him because he was on medical leave and he was not providing for his family. The father, in a mocking tone, hoped the son made his money as a writer soon so that he could fulfill his responsibilities. These fresh memories. What was the son to do with them now? These fresh woundings from the father who still insisted on blaming his son for making his life miserable. If the son would have shared the grandchildren more, then he would not be this way, everything would have been better. If his son would have been a better son, the father would be happier. If the son was a better son then he would not suffer.



Each keystroke now, he allowed the sensory experience. The man did not know where this was going. He was being stripped down by this attack from his father. What did the son do during this attack. His heart beat fast. He could feel it in his chest. He could feel those fearful parts of his being. He witnessed the father becoming a hurt child again. He witnessed this transformation. The typing human. The human on the floor. The one waiting for a miracle. 



This human held his form as best as he could during the father’s breakdown. The son bore witness to the man’s suffering. At one point he remembered the Christ and the suffering and sickness that he became on the cross. He felt as if he was taking on the suffering of his father, just in witnessing it. He felt now that he had taken it on. “Is this the process?” he wondered. Would he be able to return? He got up to retrieve his guitar. He had a vision of how he had walked himself out of darkness one week ago on Christmas day. His music was a strong form. He allowed God’s strength to take him to his guitar, which was still out in his car, parked in the street in front of his mother’s house.



The son handled himself well in the time during and directly following the attack. He breathed as he watched his father’s pain sending him into attack mode. He prayed for their awakening. When the son had heard all he could stand, he politely dismissed himself from his seat at the kitchen bar. Why was the son surprised that this was happening? The son watched the situation unfold with a calmness while his heart beat strongly and fast in his chest. After the son dismissed himself from the table, he made his way back to the room where he began packing. He packed calmly and quietly. After he packed he went out the sliding glass door to the back porch. He found a seat in a metal rocking chair. It was there that he began to pray for his father. It was there that he said, “Father forgive him because he does not know what he’s doing.” The words are a burden now as the son stands in front of the screen trying to recall what happened just hours ago. 



The mirror that the son now stands in front of can only reflect the bottom half of his face. His beard, the mustache hanging well below the upper lip.



The man, having retrieved his guitar made his way out to the backyard to the porch where he began the song that had been his liferaft just one week ago as he was bringing him self back from the great folding from which he felt he may never return. That christmas day when he truly felt that he might die. 



The sonback at his father’s house now had sat on the back porch and prayed for his father, the prayer of the cross. “Father, forgive him because he doesn’t know what he’s doing.” This pain will pass. It is fresh. You know that it passes. 



As the son watched his father he understood the christ for a moment taking on all the sin and sickness of the world. Just witnessing his father’s pain was anguish for the son, because it was connected to the old man’s pain. The son watched as the father traced the lineage of his pain from deep in his childhood all the way up to the point in his timeline when the father’s pain began to intersect with his son’s. The son watched his father’s eyes intently, wondering if there would be a recognition of what was happening. The father was reliving his own pain in front of his son. His eyes were tearful and desperate, the desperate eyes of a sixty-seven year old man who had never been held, or if he had it had been short and never enough. The son watched the story of the father’s suffering unfold in stories that he’d never heard before, as if a new layer of pain had been unearthed within the father’s psyche. The son wondered what would happen when their pain became one. What woud happen.



 The father spoke of the physical abuse that was heaped upon him. The father was ill. He was mocking his neighbors, there was a mocking tone in the voice that the son knew. The son began to speak of his own pain. He spoke of how he had once abused the animals, how he had shaken a little dog until it shit. It was at this moment that the father showed horror in his eyes toward the son, as if he’d seen a monster. The father recoiled from the son in disgust and the words “How could you? How can you live with yourself? Those words were of a self-righteous attitude in the son’s heart. And at that moment their pain merged and the son’s heart was now hurting. But the son held form. He held. He did not attack. The father was horrified by the son’s confession at having shaken the dog, maybe because he loved his little dog so much. It was his own self-righteousness, that which upheld the father in place of the free flow of the spirit. Although the son knew that there was a dog that the father beat with a newspaper when he was young, yet there is still self-righteous. And the father can not see that the son was just showing that the curse of the generations had apprehended him too. But the father judges in this moment. And the father recoils, which causes a recoil in the son. And then the father asks the son, “Did I ever shake you?” and ther is something in the father’s voice that is justifying himself. And if the son answers something will be made right. But the son is unwilling to say anything. The son is speechless, unwilling to talk. The father is blaming the son and the son has just listened to his pain. That is all that he is done. And now it is the father in his own self-righteousness who is deflecting all responsibility and he wants to presure the son in to absolving him. And the son wants his father to be absolved, that’s why he came? Is that why he came? He came to make peace with the old man. And then the son explains to the father why he is hurt, because he feels that he has been judged by his past acts of the dog. 



The son, who is now typing just wants this to all be over. He took his guitar outside and gave himself away to the sun and the birds and the wind in the trees



And then the man moved himself outside with Lina the mandolin, the gift from the universe. The man sat on the grass playing in the sunshine. The floaters danced in front of his closed with the orange background of warmth. He played and felt the other-worldliness of the music. And then he saw a miracle. There were two boys who were watching him from the street. He continued playing with increased enthusisasm knowing that they were watching him. He played and sang with his mandolin. The boys remained for well over a minute. The man arose with this gift from the Universe strapped over his shoulder. He played as he approched the two twelve year old boys. They had matching scooters. “Are you Marl’s son,” said the bigger of the two boys. “No,” I’m Lorri’s son,” said the man.” And with that the man knew that recovery from this pain was possible. He would see the light again. “What’s your name,” said the man. “Sebastian,” said the larger of the two. “And what’s your name?” he said to the other. “Jackson,” the thinner framed boy said. “how long have you two been friends?” said the man? “About a decade,” said sebastian, “We’ve known each other since pre-school.” 

“Are these scooters Christmas gifts?” asked the man.

“Yeah,” they said in unison.

“And do they have motors on them?” asked the man.

“mm hmm, yeah,” they said.

“Can they even go uphill?” asked the man?

“Oh yeah,” said sebastian.

“They both gunned their throttles and headed up the hill, where Jackson turned up an even steeper embankment on one of the neighbors driveways.”

“Wow!” said the man, “That is so cool! How long does the battery last?”

“Eleven miles,” said Jackson.

“I think it’s eighteen,” Jackson said proudly.

“Well do you ride these things to school,” the man asked.

“No, My school’s on a highway, so that wouldn’t be so good,” said Sebastian.

 

The man never stopped playing his mandolin. He just kept picking away. Any non-song would do. He continued acknowledging the miracle in the restorative energy that he felt in these two boys. He would stay with them in this moment as long as they were willing to hold it with him. This moment was part of his most recent salvation.



“aaahhh, I’m so sorry. I’m real bad at names the man said. Can you please tell me your names again. They did, and the man was glad.



“Well Sebastian, where do you live?” said the man.



“I live right there,” he pointed to the grey house next door to his mothers’. 



“And how ‘bout you?” he asked of Jackson.



“I live in Quail creek.”



“Doesn’t that sun fee nice today?” Proclaimed the man.



“yeah,” chorused the two boys in white T shirts.



“You’re wearing shorts today, Sebastian. You must be warm blooded.” Smiled the man.



“Yeah,” he said, “I get hot real easy.”



The man continued to play the mandolin for the sunshine and the wind and the two boys who had brought him his salvation at 2:30 PM on that New Years day as the man was, once again in recovery.



Despite his efforts to accept the situation immediately for what it was, the words of his father were causing great discomfort in the man. He had the opportunity to work with those fearful and fragmented parts of his being. 



He turned to page one of the ACIM text. He scanned for one of the fifty principles that felt in to what he had just experienced.



There it was: “Miracles are healing because theysupply a lack: they are performed by those who temporarily have more for those who temporarily have less.”



Those two boys had supplied a miracle for him in becoming his audience on that first day of January 2020.

# Day 15

5:59



The man slept. He came home from a meeting with an old friend at IHOP and he slept. He slept for seven hours that night, the longest that he’d slept in over two weeks.



“Past the point of no return,” were the words that were in his stomach, the words so tangible that they pushed out a bowel movement that morning.



And he wanted to see the cats that he and his father didn’t get to see together. The feral cat colony on lake Hefner. He wondered if they were still there, the cats that lived in the rocks on the bank of lake Hefner that his father told he and his children about at Louie’s.



The night before he sat at IHOP with his old friend, a friend who had listened to him very closely when he was younger, a friend who had followed him and his wife down to southern Oklahoma when they’d moved down there to farm and ranch for her father-in-law.



Past the point of no return 



Those were the words that were with him this morning



At IHOP with his old friend, the one who had followed him to southern Oklahoma, the one who had followed he and his wife. The man who had followed. The man who had rearranged his life, and convinced his own wife to follow them to southern Oklahoma. This is the one who the middle-aged-man sat with now at IHOP.



This man who he sat with now had once allowed the feminine in to come to the surface. When he was younger, he dressed like a woman and allowed the feminine to exist in his being, he had lingered with the tree Goddess, one might say. This is one thing that the middle-aged man knew about his friend.



Renita Borders…the man had an appointment with his new therapist today in New Mexico. There was a very significant part of him that wanted to go back to New Mexico and see this woman who listened to him. But today, as he woke up with these solid words that pushed out a bowel movement, he had come to feel quite certain that he needed to call and cancel that appointment with her, the beatiful dark skinned woman with the thick braided hair who listened to him speak his heart and mind. The man loved a good woman therapist who listened. The man loved a woman who listened. And this was exactly what his friend was doing for him as they sat at IHOP.



His friend had always listened very intently to the middle-aged-man. The middle-aged-man enjoyed being heard by men and women alike. At IHOP last night, he’d allowed something to express its Self from within him. As he spoke to his friend the Christ arose. He told his friend about the snake in the garden, the spiral dynamics, how Christ and his band of followers had made love to the earth, Yeshua’s conversation with Petra., the kundalini wound at the root and rising through the Chakras to light that crown above the head. He spoke of the tree Goddess that had emerged from within and the men who worked just through the trees as he quivered to orgasm in her form. He told him the story of the day in which he had continued thanking his father, even from his knees as the father towered over him, as the father attempted to revoke the blessing that can’t be revoked, as the father tried to humiliate his son,.



“Did you take my cell phone?” the father raged, “Is my cell phone in your pocket? Kathy! Get in here and help me find my cell phone before he leaves!” he yelled.



The son checked his pockets,“I don’t have your cell phone, Dad.”



“Do you know how you and your brother have disappointed me? Do you know what it’s like to have two sons who haven’t figured it out yet? You two are the reason for my misery.”



The son listened and continued to thank his father.



“I thank you for all the gifts that you have given me,” he said repeatedly



The son prayed for his father as he gathered his belongings. The son prayed for his father as his father spewed curses upon him.



“You say that sometimes you’re afraid of me?” said the father, “Well, I’m afraid of you too. How’s that? How do you like that. Yeah, I’m afraid that when you come over here your’e gonna murder me and Kathy. That’s right. How do you like that? I’m afraid of you.” Said the raging father.



“I love you, Dad, I’m grateful for all that you have ever given me.”



“Do you know how disappointing it is to have a son who can’t take care of his family? I hope this writing thing works out for you. I hope you start making some money real quick, because that’s what you need, isn’t it? You’re gonna need money, aren’t you? If you’re gonna support that family of yours, if you’re gonna give your wife the child support and support those kids in college. You’re gonna need money, right? I hope you start making some money real quick. Do you know how disappointing it is, having a son who goes on medical leave and can’t support his family?” 



The father was doing his best.



“And also,” said the father, “Thanks so much for spending so much time with me yesterday.”



The son had, in fact, not spent very much time with his father yesterday. He visited friends. He was sleepy when he came home to his father’s house. His father wanted him to watch “The Nutty Professor” with him, but as the son sat down in the living room, his eyes were closing, his body asking for quiet sleep. The son did not have the heart to watch Jerry Lewis be a nutty professor. The son excused himself to his father’s back room where he napped.



The son prayed silently as he gathered his things from the bedroom that his father had prepared for him with a comfortable inflatable mattress, the bedroom where the wooden lap desk sat on the leather couch, the lap desk that his father let him use while he was there. The son gave thanks in his heart as the father raged with accusation. The son gave thanks to his father. The son gave thanks for his father. The son did not defend himself. The son did not attack. The son said one thing to the father.



“You are the father who continues to blame his children for his own misery.”



And then the son continued to calmly packed his things, including the weighted blanket that his daughter had given him as a Christmas gift just five days, including the leather bound journal that his youngest daughter had given him, including the uniquely shaped and stained piece of wood that his son gave him, his son who was also concerned about how his father would make his way without someone to care for him as his ex-wife had.



Kathy helped her suffering husband find his cell phone. The middle-aged-man gave his best smile to Kathy and hugged her goodbye.



“Thank you for your hospitality,” he said to her before he turned to pick up his belongings. “Thank you.” 



The man’s heart was beating wildly in his chest as he made the two trips required to load up his car. The son remembered a similar incident ten years ago, when the father followed his son out into the driveway, taking the son’s head in his hands, and holding on tightly, not releasing him when it became obvious that the son wanted to be free from the grasp of his father’s hands. 



But the father did not follow the son into the driveway. And the son knew now that he was free from the father’s grasp. He opened the hatch-back of his little blue toyota as his heart beat strongly in his chest. “Everything is going to be okay,” he reminded those parts of his being that were terrified, “I’m gonna take good care of you,” the generative-nurturing-adult reminded those fearful and fragmented parts of his being. 



And so the man walked back through the threshold of his father’s house to retrieve the rest of his belongings that sat there by the front door that the father opened every morning so the little yellow Chihuahua could go outside to use the bathroom. And there sat the chair closest to the front door, the chair in which his father had rested so soundly the morning before, where the son was able to hear the father breathing so peacefully, and the sun rose with orange, and white, and midnight blue, as those white fireplace stones glowed bright.



The son picked up his things, turned and walked out of his fathers home as calmy as was possible for him on that particular day. He gave thanks as he placed one foot in front of the other on the curving sidewalk that led to the driveway where his little blue car waited, the hatchback extended toward the sky.



The son placed his items in the car. He closed the dirty hatchback, feeling with his fingers the dirt and grime that covered his car. He opened the front car door. He slid into his seat. He noticed the roll of quarters that his father had given him for the turnpike. “Thank you, Father,” said the son.



“Thank you, Father, that your blessing cannot be revoked. Thank you for the blessing that cannot be taken from me, the blessing that is me. Thank you for the well of being that flows from deep within me. Thank you for all the gifts that man has given me. I pray as Christ did on the cross, ‘Father, forgive him, because he doesn’t know what he’s doing.’”



The man gave thanks in this way as he started his engine, shifted into reverse and backed out of the unusually shaped driveway, being careful not to strike the mailbox or run off the curb. The man continued to give thanks in this way as he called his mother to see if he could stay with her again. The man gave thanks in this way as he used the quarters that his father had given him for the turnpike. The man gave thanks with a pure heart. He prayed for the wholeness of his father. He prayed for his father’s restoration. He prayed that the generational curses that rest upon his father’s heart would be removed. He gave thanks for the gift that his father had given him that day. # Day 15

8:58 AM



The writer recalled how he’d realized that he was a Hindu, and how he had eventually come to call upon Kali Ma that day on the mountain after he followed the small stream up to the large boulders which rested among the thick and sprouting green beings of the soil:



As the man continued his awakening process over the years he gained many tools. He read many books and integrated the life experience of the “other” into his own practice. After Penny had shared with him that he was “one of the top five self-bludgeoners” that she’d ever met, the man tried to discover for himself the love that he so desperately needed. Penny gave him a book: The Pocket Pema Chodron. He read a book by Thich Nhat Hanh called The Art of Power. From these two great teachers he came to experience the power of silence. He began to observe on a deeper level what was actually going on in his mind and in his body. He also rediscovered a medicine in his beloved marijuana plant.



The man found this song upon his lips:



“There’s a beautiful green leaf that grows upon the earth. 

It helps us to sing and encourages mirth

But the man says no and there’s a reason why

He doesn’t want us to see what we can see when we are high”



The herb connected him with himself. He was able to experience joy, once again, in a world that seemed to be crushing him. In a marriage where he often times felt guilty for being himself, the marijuana came to him and offered him peace and love and joy within himself. It also gave him ample opportunity to face his fears. The chronology of all of this was impossible for the writer to untangle as he sat at his mother’s home writing on the Thursday morning, the second day of the year two-thousand-and-twenty. But he saw the healing process that had happened in his heart.



There was Thich Nhat Hanh first. The vietnamese monk who had watched so many of his friends and family die in the war that ravaged his country. The man who had been exiled from his country. The man who taught his readers to breathe. The man who described the beauty and the simplicity and the freedom that may be experienced in the breathing-in and the breathing-out. It was in this book that was given to his wife by a great icelandic princess that the man discovered that he was breathing and that it mattered. The awakening that happened in the heart of the buddha showed the way to the breath and the universal consciousness that we may all experience as we turn our attention toward that simplest of all human experience which we all have in common. The breath, that form which none of us will abandon until our body finally stops breathing. 



It was Thich Nhat Hanh who first helped the man to see this. And then there was Pema in this little book that Penny gave him. Pema was simple and digestable. She kept bringing him back to the here and the now. She kept urging the awakening man to go to the places that scared him. She invite him to let things be when he thought they needed to change to his liking. She invited him to accept his birthright, the gift of this moment, that which is beyond the resolution that we all think will finally satisfy us. She invited him to sit with his loneliness. She dared him to discover himself and to accept himself and his attitudes and his thoughts for exactly what they were. She gave him permission to just allow himself to be. She gave him permission to stop trying to fix himself. She asked him to speak to his fear with respect. She wondered what would happen if he just stuck his head right in that demons mouth instead of trying to cast him out. She invited him to go deeper when the world was telling him to go higher. She asked him to sit as fear was screaming in his face, trying to tell him what he had to do. She told a simple story of the Tigers and the Strawberries which went something like this:



There was a young woman who was travelling through the forest when she discovered that she was being pursued by tigers. She ran as fast as she could to escape the terrifying creatures who chased her. As she ran she came to a cliff. She climbed down a vine which was growing down the cliff-face. As she climbed down the vine she looked down. Below her she saw yet another group of growling tigers. “Oh my,” said the young woman to herself, “there are tigers above me and below me. What will I do now?” It was in that moment that she noticed some mice above her. These mice were gnawing through the vine which held her there suspended above and below the hungry tigers. It was in this moment that she saw something else. It was a little strawberry plant with a single little berry growing from its green body. So, the woman simply reached out, and she ate that strawberry.



Yes. That is the end of that story. The story with the non-ending. The story without resolution. The story with a happy ending. The story with a tragic ending. The story of the woman who reaches out and plucks the strawberry from the vine. Praise be to the tigers and the strawberries and the mice who gnaw on the vine. Praise be to the one who eats the strawberry.



It was in this way that the man began his meditative practice. It was in this way that the man found himself eating every strawberry that he found as he dangled above and below the tigers that chased him through life. It was in this way that the man found a new teacher and he dedicated himself to her teachings. He carried his Pema around with him in the right side-pocket of his cargo pants. It was in this way that the man continued to make a deeper peace with himself and the world in which he lived. Praise be to the Pema who asks for no such praise, the one who did not hold herself accountable to any deity.



And so it was inscribed on the inside cover of the pocket Pema:



“To Travis,

Be the one you dream you can be.

Penny”



And it was in this way that Pema and Penny became the same being to him. It was in this way that the man also gave himself to the teachings of Penny who always gave him unconditional positive regard (Praise be to the one who was called Carl Rogers!).



The doorbell rang at his mother’s house. The man wondered if it was his father who had finally come to put that bullet in his head. He heard no violence as his mothe’s husband answered the door. He heard no gunshots. He chose, once again, the strawberry that was before him.



The man was never fully faithful to the Vipassana practice given to him. He phased in and out. This man was never faithful at anything, even the things that he claimed to love the most, like his music or his family. But, the man did continue.



It was in this way that the man found himself on occasion sharing this joy with the world. He and two friends started a meditation group. They read together. They sat together. They talked together. They read again.They sat again. They talked again. And that was their form. That was the form that they held together. Together, they gently practiced and learned from one another. They learned to listen. They learned to give space for what was said instead of trying to fix things or give advice. They gave each other the gift on one another’s presence. It was in this way that they practiced on-again and off-again for four years, sometimes drinking tea, sometimes just meeting for breakfast, sometimes reading TNH, sometimes reading Joseph Campbell.



And so it came to pass that the son, one day shared with his father the joy of the salvation that he had experienced in this practice. And this is how it happened that the father mocked the son and called him a Hindu as if it was a dirty word. And this is how the son hung up the phone with his father that day with a hurting heart because of the father that mocked him. And this is how the son continued his practice on-again and off-again not understanding why the man’s father would ever think he was a Hindu, and not at all thinking he was a Hindu and not even really very aware at all of the historical connection between Buddhism and Hinduism. Pema certainly never mentioned any Hindu Gods or Godesses, she herself describing her worldview as non-theist (not anti-theist because there was no position against anything that would bring true peace into being).



And then it came to pass that months later the man found himself talking to an old friend in front of the Wal-Mart with whom he was sharing his most recent spiritual awakening (for there had certainly been many in his precious and sacred lifetime). The old friend was very glad that the man was doing well and she shared with him how she had been concerned about his well being for quite some time.

“I heard that you had become a Hindu,” she whispered to the man as they stood there beside the sliding doors in front of the Wal-Mart.



“That’s strange,” thought the man, who honestly recoiled at the idea himself. “I do not understand why people think that I am a Hindu.”



And so it came to pass that the younger man went home where he brought his groceries in from the little blue Toyota, unpacked them, and made himself a nice lunch of lentil soup and strawberry shortcake with coconut milk for lunch. A meal that fit his current vegan diet (a diet that he made no vows to continue forever, but one which he currently embraced with a joyful and appropriate zeal).



It was in this way that he found himself doing a google search for “Hinduism,” after which he found himself reading Wikipedia which helped him to understand this: The name Hindu was not a name that was adopted by any one people or religious group. It was actually a description that foreigners assigned to the people who generally lived by the Indus River, “Indus” meaning a great body of water, in this case a great flowing body of water. 



It was in this simple way that the man munching on lentil stew, at that moment, as he sat in front of the computer in the great adobe house, came to understand that he how he truly was a Hindu. He was one of a Universal people who draw their Life from the Great River. 



And it was in this way that the man became curious about Hinduism (however broad that spectrum may be). It was in this way that he came to ask Shiva, the divine feminine to arise from within him, to uncoil the great serpent that he had felt quivering at the root of his being. It was in this way that he called for a marriage of the divine masculine, who was Shiva, to marry the divine feminine, Shakti in his being. It was in this way that he continued to see the diving in all that is. It is in this way that he came to see the Christ in the Hindu gods and goddesses. It is in this way that he met Kali Ma and asked her to come and couple with him. It is in this way that he was aroused by the possibility of backpacking by himself up to a mountain lake which was fed by a stream which he would follow as far as he could, at which point he would stomp the ground and summon the great Kali Ma to come and destroy him. It was in this way that he would eventually (ironically?) rediscover this prayer. 



I want to know the Christ

The power of his resurrection

The fellowship of sharing in his suffering

Becoming like him in his death

And so somehow to receive

A resurrection from the dead



It was in this way also that the man, earlier in the year, in April as Easter approached, began to invite death to come and take that which death had a rightuful claim to. It was in this spirit that the man wrote thes words:



I wept for the women who’d lost me

As I waited in the oneness I had found

I forgave all those deities who’d crossed me

As I lead my body to the burial ground

As I laid my body in the ground



And this is how the man came to recognize himself as the Universal, the Hindu, one who lives by a great flowing body of water from which he draws true life.



Praise be to Shiva and Shakti who unite within us, making us whole. Praise be to Kali Ma who lops off our heads and our ego. Praise be to the serpent who is coiled and quivering, ready to open an travel up to the crown. Praise to the She. Praise to the He. Praise be to the Christ whose arms open to receive us all.



Praise be to the Great River, that which nourished us all. The Universal River! Praise be to the Hindus who live on its shores and are baptized in its waters.



Amen

Selah
